# Trajectory Formats Support (NetCDF, XTC, TRR, TNG, DTR)



CPPTRAJ provides comprehensive support for multiple molecular dynamics trajectory formats, enabling you to work with data from different simulation packages seamlessly. This guide covers five key formats: **NetCDF** (Amber's high-performance format), **XTC/TRR** (GROMACS compressed and full-precision formats), **TNG** (GROMACS next-generation format), and **DTR** (Desmond trajectory format). Each format serves different use cases ranging from storage efficiency to full precision preservation.

## Architecture Overview

The trajectory format system in CPPTRAJ follows a modular architecture where each format inherits from a common `TrajectoryIO` base class. This design enables consistent read/write operations across different file formats while allowing format-specific optimizations. The system automatically detects file types based on extensions and file content, making it easy to work with mixed-format datasets.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[User Input] --> B[TrajectoryFile::DetectFormat]
    B --> C{File Extension/Content Match?}
    C -->|'.nc'| D[Traj_AmberNetcdf]
    C -->|'.xtc'| E[Traj_GmxXtc]
    C -->|'.trr'| F[Traj_GmxTrX]
    C -->|'.tng'| G[Traj_GmxTng]
    C -->|'.dtr'| H[Traj_DTR]
    D --> I[TrajectoryIO Base Interface]
    E --> I
    F --> I
    G --> I
    H --> I
    I --> J[Read/Write Operations]
    I --> K[Velocity/Force Access]
    I --> L[Parallel Processing]
```

## NetCDF Format

NetCDF (Network Common Data Form) is Amber's preferred trajectory format, offering excellent performance through chunked storage and optional compression. It supports coordinates, velocities, forces, and temperature data in a single self-describing file. CPPTRAJ implements NetCDF support through the `Traj_AmberNetcdf` class, which leverages the underlying NetCDF library for efficient I/O operations.

Sources: [Traj_AmberNetcdf.h](/src/Traj_AmberNetcdf.h#L8-L55)

### Key Features

| Feature | Description | Configuration |
|---------|-------------|--------------|
| **Coordinate Storage** | Double or single precision | `compress_` parameter controls compression level |
| **Velocity Support** | Optional velocity storage | `write_mdvel_` flag enables output |
| **Force Support** | Optional force storage | `write_mdfrc_` flag enables output |
| **Temperature Data** | Per-frame temperature recording | `outputTemp_` flag controls inclusion |
| **HDF5 Backend** | Modern storage with compression | `fchunkSize_` and `ishuffle_` parameters |
| **Parallel I/O** | MPI-based parallel writing | Requires `-mpi` build and Parallel NetCDF |

> [!TIP]
> NetCDF files require the `BINTRAJ` compilation flag. When using parallel NetCDF, you must also have the Parallel NetCDF library installed and build with `./configure -mpi`.

### Usage Examples

Reading NetCDF trajectories:
```
trajin production.nc
```

Writing NetCDF output with compression:
```
trajout output.nc netcdf
```

Writing with velocities and forces:
```
trajout full_data.nc netcdf velocity force
```

## XTC Format (GROMACS)

XTC is GROMACS's compressed trajectory format designed for efficient storage of coordinate data. CPPTRAJ implements XTC support through the `Traj_GmxXtc` class, which uses the XDR library for compression/decompression. XTC uses lossy compression that typically reduces file size by 3-10x while maintaining acceptable precision for most analyses.

Sources: [Traj_GmxXtc.h](/src/Traj_GmxXtc.h#L9-L54)

### Technical Characteristics

| Attribute | Value | Notes |
|-----------|-------|-------|
| **Precision** | ~0.001 nm | Lossy compression with adaptive precision |
| **File Size** | Small | 3-10x reduction compared to uncompressed |
| **Dependencies** | XDR library | Disabled if `NO_XDRFILE` is defined |
| **Supported Data** | Coordinates only | Velocities and forces not stored |
| **Random Access** | Frame offsets | Enables efficient frame seeking |

### Implementation Details

The XTC reader maintains frame offsets in `frameOffsets_` to enable random access without decompressing the entire file. The `prec_` parameter controls compression precision, with lower values producing smaller files at the cost of accuracy. The underlying XDR library handles the actual compression through the `xd_` XDRFILE handle and `vec_` coordinate buffer.

Sources: [Traj_GmxXtc.h](/src/Traj_GmxXtc.h#L43-L50)

> [!TIP]
> XTC files contain coordinate data only. If you need velocities or forces from GROMACS simulations, use TRR format instead or process velocities separately.

### Usage Examples

Reading XTC trajectories:
```
trajin md.xtc
```

Writing XTC output:
```
trajout compressed.xtc xtc
```

## TRR Format (GROMACS)

TRR (GROMACS Trajectory) is the full-precision counterpart to XTC, storing coordinates, velocities, forces, and other simulation data without compression. CPPTRAJ implements TRR support through the `Traj_GmxTrX` class, which handles both TRR and legacy TRJ formats with automatic endianness detection.

Sources: [Traj_GmxTrX.h](/src/Traj_GmxTrX.h#L6-L84)

### Comprehensive Data Support

| Data Type | Storage | Access Method |
|-----------|---------|---------------|
| **Coordinates** | Full precision | `readFrame()` / `writeFrame()` |
| **Velocities** | Full precision | `readVelocity()` |
| **Forces** | Full precision | `readForce()` |
| **Box Information** | Triclinic support | `ReadBox()` |
| **Time Step** | Float precision | `dt_` parameter |
| **Lambda** | Alchemical parameter | `lambda_` field |

### Format Detection

The `Traj_GmxTrX` class automatically identifies TRR files using a magic number and version string. The `DetermineEndian()` method handles cross-platform compatibility by detecting and correcting byte order differences. This ensures TRR files written on little-endian systems can be read on big-endian systems and vice versa.

Sources: [Traj_GmxTrX.h](/src/Traj_GmxTrX.h#L14-L15), [Traj_GmxTrX.h](/src/Traj_GmxTrX.h#L53-L54)

### Memory Management

TRR files use temporary arrays `farray_` (float) and `darray_` (double) for coordinate conversion, with `arraySize_` tracking the total number of coordinate elements (natoms × 3). The frame size calculation in `frameSize_` enables efficient seeking within the file.

Sources: [Traj_GmxTrX.h](/src/Traj_GmxTrX.h#L76-L81)

### Usage Examples

Reading TRR with velocities:
```
trajin md.trr
```

Reading only coordinates from TRR:
```
trajin md.trr nobox
```

Writing TRR output:
```
trajout output.trr trr
```

## TNG Format (GROMACS)

TNG (Trajectory Next Generation) is GROMACS's modern trajectory format designed for high-performance I/O and extensive data storage. CPPTRAJ implements TNG support through the `Traj_GmxTng` class, which interfaces directly with the TNG compression library. TNG supports lossless and lossy compression with user-configurable precision levels.

Sources: [Traj_GmxTng.h](/src/Traj_GmxTng.h#L8-L64)

### Advanced Features

| Feature | Capability | Implementation |
|---------|------------|----------------|
| **Multi-block Storage** | Flexible data organization | `blockIds_` vector manages active blocks |
| **Frame Seeking** | Efficient random access | `current_frame_` and `current_set_` tracking |
| **Coordinate Scaling** | Unit conversion support | `tngfac_` scaling factor |
| **Frame Sets** | MD step vs trajectory frame distinction | `tngframes_` vs `tngsets_` separation |
| **Block Pre-fetching** | Optimized I/O performance | `next_nblocks_` and `next_blockIDs_` caching |

### TNG-specific Architecture

Unlike other formats, TNG organizes data into logical blocks rather than simple frame sequences. The `getNextBlocks()` method retrieves block information for upcoming frames, while `readValues()` extracts specific data types from identified blocks. The `values_` buffer provides temporary storage for coordinate data during conversion.

Sources: [Traj_GmxTng.h](/src/Traj_GmxTng.h#L42-L45)

### Precision Control

The `convertArray()` method handles coordinate conversion between double (CPPTRAJ internal) and float (TNG storage) precision with configurable scaling factors. This enables users to balance file size against numerical precision based on analysis requirements.

Sources: [Traj_GmxTng.h](/src/Traj_GmxTng.h#L42)

> [!TIP]
> TNG format support requires the `HAS_TNGFILE` preprocessor definition. Ensure the TNG library is installed before building CPPTRAJ with TNG support.

### Usage Examples

Reading TNG trajectories:
```
trajin md.tng
```

Writing TNG with custom compression:
```
trajout output.tng tng precision 1000
```

## DTR Format (Desmond)

DTR is DESMOND's trajectory format, designed for high-performance molecular dynamics simulations. CPPTRAJ implements DTR support through the `Traj_DTR` class, which uses DESMOND's molfile plugin library for I/O operations. DTR files store coordinates and velocities in a compressed binary format optimized for large-scale simulations.

Sources: [Traj_DTR.h](/src/Traj_DTR.h#L7-L47)

### Implementation Details

| Component | Description | Purpose |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **FrameSetReader** | DESMOND library interface | Handles low-level DTR parsing |
| **fbuffer_** | Float coordinate buffer | Temporary storage for coordinate/velocity data |
| **bufsize_** | Buffer size management | Tracks allocated memory |

### Build Requirements

DTR format support requires the `ENABLE_DTR` compilation flag and DESMOND's molfile library. The implementation delegates all file operations to the `FrameSetReader` object, which manages the complex DTR file structure internally.

Sources: [Traj_DTR.h](/src/Traj_DTR.h#L41-L44)

### Usage Examples

Reading DTR trajectories:
```
trajin desmond_output.dtr
```

## Format Comparison and Selection

Choosing the right trajectory format depends on your specific needs regarding storage efficiency, data completeness, and interoperability.

### Format Decision Matrix

| Scenario | Recommended Format | Rationale |
|----------|-------------------|-----------|
| **Long-term Amber simulations** | NetCDF | Best compression with full data support |
| **GROMACS analysis workflows** | XTC | Efficient storage, GROMACS-native |
| **Full-precision GROMACS data** | TRR | Complete coordinate/velocity/force data |
| **Large-scale GROMACS I/O** | TNG | Modern format with advanced compression |
| **DESMOND compatibility** | DTR | Native format, maintains metadata |
| **Cross-package compatibility** | NetCDF or TRR | Widely supported across MD packages |

### Performance Characteristics

| Format | Read Speed | Write Speed | File Size | Random Access |
|--------|------------|-------------|-----------|---------------|
| NetCDF | Fast | Fast | Small | Excellent |
| XTC | Medium | Medium | Very Small | Good |
| TRR | Fast | Fast | Large | Excellent |
| TNG | Fast | Fast | Variable | Good |
| DTR | Medium | Medium | Small | Medium |

## Configuration and Build Requirements

### Compilation Flags

Different trajectory formats require specific compilation flags and external libraries:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[CPPTRAJ Build] --> B{Enable NetCDF?}
    B -->|Yes| C[BINTRAJ flag + NetCDF lib]
    B -->|No| D[No NetCDF support]
    
    A --> E{Enable XTC?}
    E -->|Yes| F[XDR lib<br/>NOT NO_XDRFILE]
    E -->|No| G[No XTC support]
    
    A --> H{Enable TNG?}
    H -->|Yes| I[TNG lib + HAS_TNGFILE]
    H -->|No| J[No TNG support]
    
    A --> K{Enable DTR?}
    K -->|Yes| L[DESMOND lib + ENABLE_DTR]
    K -->|No| M[No DTR support]
```

### Build Configuration Examples

Enable all trajectory formats:
```bash
./configure --with-netcdf --with-xdr --with-tng --with-dtr gnu
make
```

Build with only NetCDF and XTC support:
```bash
./configure --with-netcdf --with-xdr gnu
make
```

Parallel build with NetCDF:
```bash
./configure -mpi --with-pnetcdf gnu
make
```

## Common Workflow Patterns

### Converting Between Formats

Converting GROMACS to Amber NetCDF:
```
parm topol.top
trajin md.xtc
trajout amber_traj.nc netcdf
run
```

Extracting specific data from TRR:
```
parm topol.top
trajin md.trr
trajout coordinates_only.nc netcdf nobox
velocity out velocity.dat
run
```

Merging multiple trajectory files:
```
parm topol.top
trajin part1.xtc
trajin part2.xtc
trajin part3.xtc
trajout combined.nc netcdf
run
```

### Format-Specific Operations

Reading only frames 100-200 from NetCDF:
```
trajin production.nc 100 200
```

Writing XTC with custom precision:
```
trajout output.xtc xtc precision 1000
```

Processing velocities from TRR:
```
trajin md.trr
velocity out vel.dat
run
```

## Next Steps

Now that you understand trajectory format support in CPPTRAJ, you can explore more advanced topics:

- **[Trajectory Processing Pipeline](7-trajectory-processing-pipeline)** - Learn how to chain multiple trajectory operations efficiently
- **[Basic Command Line Usage](4-basic-command-line-usage)** - Master CPPTRAJ command syntax and workflow organization
- **[Installation and Configuration](3-installation-and-configuration)** - Detailed build instructions for enabling specific format support
- **[Coordinate Transformations](8-coordinate-transformations-rmsd-alignment-rotation)** - Apply transformations to trajectory data regardless of format

Each format provides unique advantages depending on your simulation workflow. By understanding the strengths and limitations of NetCDF, XTC, TRR, TNG, and DTR formats, you can optimize your data management strategy for maximum efficiency and compatibility.

# Atom Selection and Mask Expressions



Mask expressions form the foundational query language for atom selection in cpptraj, enabling precise targeting of atoms, residues, and molecular features for trajectory analysis. These expressions provide a flexible syntax for defining subsets of atoms that serve as input to analysis commands, coordinate operations, and statistical calculations. Understanding mask expressions is essential for performing any meaningful molecular dynamics analysis in cpptraj.

## Architecture of the Mask Selection System

The mask expression system operates as a hierarchical parsing and evaluation engine that translates string-based queries into atom selection sets. This system integrates with topology information, coordinate data, and spatial calculations to resolve selections at runtime.

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[Mask Expression String] --> B[Tokenizer]
    B --> C[Parser]
    C --> D{Expression Type}
    D --> E[Basic Selection]
    D --> F[Logical Operation]
    D --> G[Distance-based]
    D --> H[Atom Type/Property]
    E --> I[Atom Matcher]
    F --> I
    G --> J[Spatial Calculator]
    H --> K[Property Lookup]
    I --> L[Selection Set]
    J --> L
    K --> L
    L --> M[Analysis Command]
```

The mask processor handles three primary selection categories: **topology-based selections** (residues, atoms by name/number), **spatial selections** (distance-based queries), and **property selections** (atom types, charges). These can be combined using logical operators to create complex multi-criteria selections.

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Mask/RunTest.sh#L1-L42), [RunTest.sh](test/Test_AtomTypeSelect/RunTest.sh#L1-L23)

## Basic Selection Syntax

### Atom Selection Patterns

Atom-level selections use the `@` prefix followed by atom identifiers:

- **Atom names**: `@CA`, `@NZ`, `@O` - selects atoms by their PDB-style names
- **Atom numbers**: `@1-100` - selects atoms by 1-based index range
- **Atom types**: `@%CT`, `@%N` - selects atoms by force field type using the `%` modifier

Residue-level selections use the `:` prefix:

- **Residue names**: `:WAT`, `:ALA` - selects all atoms in residues matching the 3-4 character name
- **Residue numbers**: `:5`, `:10-20` - selects atoms by 1-based residue index
- **Wildcards**: `:A*` - selects residues matching name patterns

These basic selectors form the building blocks for more complex expressions.

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_AtomTypeSelect/RunTest.sh#L1-L23)

## Logical Operators and Expression Composition

Mask expressions support boolean logic for combining multiple selection criteria:

### Operator Hierarchy

| Operator | Description | Example | Result |
|----------|-------------|---------|--------|
| `&` | AND (intersection) | `:WAT & @O` | Oxygen atoms in water molecules |
| `\|` | OR (union) | `:ALA \| :GLY` | Atoms in alanine or glycine |
| `!` | NOT (complement) | `!:WAT` | All non-water atoms |
| `()` | Grouping | `(:1-10) & (@CA \| @CB)` | Alpha or beta carbons in residues 1-10 |

Operator precedence follows standard boolean logic, with parentheses used to override default evaluation order and create nested expressions.

**Practical Example**: The expression `(:8@NZ <:3.0) & :WAT@O` selects water oxygen atoms within 3.0 Å of the NZ atom in residue 8. This combines three selection criteria connected by AND operators, with parentheses ensuring the distance criterion applies specifically to the NZ atom.

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Mask/RunTest.sh#L18-L36)

## Distance-Based Selections

Spatial selections enable querying atoms based on geometric relationships, essential for analyzing local environments, binding sites, and solvent interactions.

### Distance Syntax

Distance-based selections use the `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, or `==` operators followed by a distance value in Angstroms:

- **Example**: `(:5 <:3.0)` selects atoms within 3.0 Å of residue 5
- **Example**: `@1 >5.0 @2` selects atom 1 more than 5.0 Å from atom 2

The `<:3.0` syntax represents "less than 3.0 Å from the preceding selection target."

> [!TIP]
> Distance selections are evaluated for each frame using current coordinates, making them dynamic selections that update as the system evolves during trajectory analysis. This enables tracking of changing molecular environments over time.

Distance calculations respect periodic boundary conditions when defined in the topology, ensuring accurate minimum image conventions in solvated systems.

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Mask/RunTest.sh#L14-L18)

## Mask Command and Output Options

The `mask` command applies mask expressions and provides various output formats for visualizing and analyzing selections.

### Command Syntax

```
mask "<expression>" [maskout <file>] [maskpdb <prefix>] [maskmol2 <file>] [name <dataset>] [out <file>] [nselectedout <file>]
```

### Output Options

| Option | Description | Output Format |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| `maskout` | Write selection details | Text file with frame, atom number, atom name, residue info |
| `maskpdb` | Write selected atoms | PDB file with coordinate snapshot |
| `maskmol2` | Write selected atoms | MOL2 format file |
| `name` | Create dataset | Named selection for downstream analysis |
| `out` | Write time series | Mask selection values over frames |
| `nselectedout` | Write atom counts | Number of selected atoms per frame |

**Example Usage**:
```
mask "(:5 <:3.0) & :WAT" maskout mask.out maskpdb mask.pdb trajargs 'chainid " "'
```

This command identifies water molecules within 3.0 Å of residue 5, outputs the atom list to `mask.out`, and writes a PDB file of the selected atoms with chain ID formatting.

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Mask/RunTest.sh#L14-L24), [mask.out.save](test/Test_Mask/mask.out.save#L1-L32)

## Selection Output Interpretation

The `maskout` file provides detailed information about selected atoms in tabular format:

```
#Frame    AtomNum Atom   ResNum  Res   MolNum
       1     1076 O         299 WAT       287
       1     1077 H1        299 WAT       287
       1     1078 H2        299 WAT       287
```

This output shows:
- **Frame**: Trajectory frame number
- **AtomNum**: Global atom index in topology
- **Atom**: Atom name
- **ResNum**: Residue number
- **Res**: Residue name
- **MolNum**: Molecule number

> [!TIP]
> For multi-frame selections, the output contains entries for each frame, enabling tracking of selection changes throughout the trajectory. The `nselectedout` option creates a simplified time series of selection counts.

Sources: [mask.out.save](test/Test_Mask/mask.out.save#L1-L32)

## Advanced Selection Patterns

### Combined Criteria Selections

Complex selections often require combining multiple criteria:

**Residue-atom combinations**: `:1-10@CA` - CA atoms in residues 1-10

**Property filters**: `@%CT & @H` - Hydrogen atoms with CT type

**Spatial exclusion**: `(:Protein <5.0) & !:Protein` - Non-protein atoms within 5 Å of protein

**Chain-specific selections**: When trajectory data includes chain identifiers, selections can be refined using chain information (evidenced by the `trajargs 'chainid " "'` option in mask commands).

### Dynamic Selection Datasets

Named masks can be used as datasets for time-resolved analysis:

```
mask "(:8@NZ <:3.0) & :WAT@O" name M out M.dat nselectedout Nselected.dat
```

This creates a time series tracking the number of water oxygens within 3.0 Å of the NZ atom, stored in `M.dat` and `Nselected.dat`. Such datasets can feed into subsequent analysis like correlation functions or lifetime calculations.

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Mask/RunTest.sh#L27-L36)

## Performance Considerations

**Selection caching**: Repeated mask expressions across commands are cached when possible, improving performance for large trajectories.

**Spatial indexing**: Distance-based selections benefit from spatial data structures, making selections like `@1 <:5.0` efficient even for large systems.

**Expression optimization**: The parser optimizes expressions by combining adjacent selections and eliminating redundant operations.

> [!TIP]
> For extremely large selections or complex distance queries, consider pre-selecting a reduced subset before applying distance criteria. For example, select water molecules first (`:WAT`), then apply distance filters rather than computing distances for all atoms.

## Common Use Cases

### Solvent Shell Analysis

Select water molecules around a solute:
```
mask ":Ligand <:4.0 & :WAT" maskout first_shell.out
```

### Active Site Definition

Select residues within binding pocket:
```
mask "(:Residue1@CA <:6.0) | (:Residue2@CA <:6.0)" name pocket
```

### Backbone Atoms
```
mask ":1-100@N,CA,C,O" name backbone
```

### Hydrogen Bond Analysis
Select potential hydrogen bond donors and acceptors:
```
mask "@N,@O & @H" name donors
mask "@N,@O & !@H" name acceptors
```

## Summary of Mask Expression Syntax

| Category | Syntax Pattern | Example |
|----------|----------------|---------|
| Atom name | `@<name>` | `@CA` |
| Atom number | `@<num>` or `@<start>-<end>` | `@1-100` |
| Atom type | `@%<type>` | `@%CT` |
| Residue name | `:<name>` | `:WAT` |
| Residue number | `:<num>` or `:<start>-<end>` | `:1-10` |
| Distance | `<selection> <op> <distance>` | `@1 <:3.0` |
| AND | `&` | `:WAT & @O` |
| OR | `\|` | `:ALA \| :GLY` |
| NOT | `!` | `!:H` |

## Next Steps

Mastering mask expressions enables effective use of all cpptraj analysis commands. For trajectory-wide applications of selections, explore [Trajectory Processing Pipeline](7-trajectory-processing-pipeline). When selections inform coordinate comparisons, see [Coordinate Transformations](8-coordinate-transformations-rmsd-alignment-rotation). For statistical analysis using selections, proceed to [RMSD and RMSF Calculations](10-rmsd-and-rmsf-calculations).

Understanding mask expression syntax provides the foundation for nearly all cpptraj operations, from basic filtering to advanced ensemble analysis.

# Trajectory Processing Pipeline



The trajectory processing pipeline in cpptraj represents the core architectural framework that orchestrates how molecular dynamics trajectory data flows through the system from input files through various analysis operations to final output. This pipeline embodies a modular, command-driven design that enables flexible composition of analysis operations while maintaining efficient execution through batch processing of frames.

Sources: [Command.h](src/Command.h#L1-L49), [CpptrajState.h](src/CpptrajState.h#L12-L131)

## Core Architecture Overview

At its foundation, the trajectory processing pipeline centers on three primary components working in concert: the **CpptrajState** (the global coordinator), the **Command** dispatcher (execution orchestrator), and the **ActionList** (frame processing engine). The CpptrajState maintains all collections—including input trajectories (TrajinList), output trajectories (TrajoutList), actions (ActionList), and analyses (AnalysisList)—while the Command dispatcher interprets user input and routes operations to appropriate handlers.

The pipeline follows a declarative programming model where users specify a sequence of operations through commands. These commands populate the CpptrajState's various lists without immediately executing on data. This separation of specification from execution enables cpptraj to optimize memory usage, validate configurations before processing begins, and support advanced features like ensemble processing and parallel execution.

Sources: [CpptrajState.h](src/CpptrajState.h#L102-L108), [Command.h](src/Command.h#L1-L49)

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input Phase"
        A[User Commands] --> B[Command::ProcessInput]
        B --> C[CpptrajState]
    end
    
    subgraph "CpptrajState Collections"
        C --> D[TrajinList<br/>Input Trajectories]
        C --> E[ActionList<br/>Frame Operations]
        C --> F[AnalysisList<br/>Post-Processing]
        C --> G[TrajoutList<br/>Output Trajectories]
    end
    
    subgraph "Execution Phase"
        D --> H[Frame Iterator]
        E --> H
        H --> I[Action::DoAction<br/>Per-Frame Processing]
        I --> J[Accumulated DataSets]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Phase"
        J --> K[AnalysisList::RunAnalyses]
        K --> L[DataFile Output]
        I --> M[Trajout Writing]
    end
```

## Command Dispatch and State Population

The pipeline begins when the Command dispatcher receives user input through either command-line arguments or input files. The `Command::ProcessInput` method reads commands sequentially, parsing each line into an `ArgList` and dispatching through `Command::Dispatch` to locate the appropriate command handler. Each command is associated with a specific destination type (trajectory input, action, analysis, etc.) and triggers methods on CpptrajState that populate corresponding collections.

Critical to this phase is the fact that commands accumulate state without processing data. For example, `trajin` commands add trajectories to `TrajinList`, `rmsd` commands instantiate and add `Action_Rmsd` objects to `ActionList`, and `run` triggers the actual processing phase. This accumulation enables cross-command validation—actions can verify that required reference structures exist before frame processing begins.

The command system supports sophisticated control flow through **control blocks** (if/else, while loops), allowing conditional trajectory processing and dynamic action modification based on runtime conditions. Control blocks maintain their own state, enabling nested and iterative processing patterns while preserving the declarative nature of the overall pipeline.

Sources: [Command.h](src/Command.h#L16-L49), [CpptrajState.h](src/CpptrajState.h#L49-L61)

## Frame Processing Loop

When all commands have been processed and the pipeline is fully specified, the `CpptrajState::Run` method initiates the frame processing loop. This loop iterates through frames from all trajectories in TrajinList, applying each action in ActionList to every frame. The processing follows a three-phase pattern for each action: initialization, setup, and execution.

During the **initialization phase** (Action::Init), each action receives its user arguments, creates necessary DataSets, and establishes DataFile connections. This phase occurs once per action and validates that all parameters are correctly specified. The **setup phase** (Action::Setup) occurs after topology loading but before frame processing begins, allowing actions to prepare topology-specific information such as atom masks or mass arrays.

The **execution phase** (Action::DoAction) is called for every frame. Actions receive both the frame number and a mutable Frame object, enabling coordinate modifications, property calculations, and data accumulation. Actions communicate their processing outcomes through return codes—OK for successful processing, MODIFY_COORDS to indicate coordinate changes, or SKIP to signal that subsequent frames should also skip this action.

> [!TIP]
> The three-phase action lifecycle (Init → Setup → DoAction) separates configuration concerns from topology-specific preparation and per-frame computation. This design enables actions to cache topology-derived data structures during Setup, avoiding repeated calculations in the performance-critical DoAction method.

Sources: [Action.h](src/Action.h#L42-L53), [ActionList.h](src/ActionList.h#L14-L24)

## Action Chaining and Data Flow

Actions in the pipeline execute sequentially within each frame, with each action receiving the Frame object as modified by previous actions. This chaining enables sophisticated workflows where early actions prepare data for later operations. For example, an `autoimage` action might first re-center molecules in periodic boundary conditions, followed by an `rmsd` action that aligns to a reference structure, concluding with a `strip` action that removes solvent atoms before coordinate output.

The ActionList maintains each action's status through an enum tracking initialization state (NO_INIT, INIT, SETUP, INACTIVE). This status tracking enables efficient handling of topology changes—if an action returns MODIFY_TOPOLOGY, subsequent actions are automatically reset to SETUP status, forcing re-initialization with the new topology.

Actions communicate primarily through two mechanisms: coordinate modifications in the shared Frame object and DataSet accumulation for later analysis. This dual communication pattern supports both transient frame-level operations (like centering or rotation) and persistent data collection (like RMSD values or distance measurements). DataSets remain associated with the CpptrajState's DataSetList throughout execution, providing a repository for all analysis results.

Sources: [Action.h](src/Action.h#L32-L39), [ActionList.h](src/ActionList.h#L50-L59), [CpptrajState.h](src/CpptrajState.h#L102-L103)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Command
    participant "CpptrajState"
    participant "TrajinList"
    participant "ActionList"
    participant "Action"
    
    User->>Command: trajin file.nc
    Command->>"CpptrajState": AddInputTrajectory
    "CpptrajState"->>"TrajinList": AddTrajin
    
    User->>Command: rmsd @ref name myrmsd
    Command->>"CpptrajState": AddToActionQueue
    "CpptrajState"->>"ActionList": AddAction
    "ActionList"->>"Action": Init(args, DSL)
    "Action"-->>"ActionList": Created DataSet
    
    User->>Command: run
    Command->>"CpptrajState": Run()
    loop For each frame
        "TrajinList"->>"CpptrajState": Next frame
        "CpptrajState"->>"ActionList": DoActions(frameNum, frame)
        loop For each action
            "ActionList"->>"Action": DoAction(frameNum, frame)
            "Action"->>"Action": Calculate RMSD
            "Action"->>"Action": Store in DataSet
            "Action"-->>"ActionList": MODIFY_COORDS/OK
        end
    end
```

## Parallel Processing Architecture

The trajectory processing pipeline supports multiple parallelization strategies through compile-time options (OpenMP, MPI, CUDA). The core pipeline design abstracts parallel execution details through the Action interface, with specific methods for synchronization and parallel-specific operations.

In **OpenMP** mode, the frame processing loop parallelizes across frames using shared memory. Each thread processes a subset of frames independently, with actions responsible for thread-safe DataSet accumulation. This approach provides near-linear scaling for computationally intensive actions that are not memory-bandwidth limited.

**MPI parallelization** operates at a higher level, distributing either trajectories across ranks (trajectory parallelism) or ensemble members across ranks (ensemble parallelism). Trajectory parallelism partitions the total frame count among processes, with each process handling a disjoint subset. The `Action::SyncAction` method collects data from all ranks at the end of processing, combining results through either summation or averaging depending on the analysis type. Ensemble parallelism processes multiple trajectories simultaneously, each rank handling one ensemble member, enabling efficient analysis of replica exchange simulations.

> [!TIP]
> MPI trajectory parallelism requires special handling for actions that need context from multiple frames. The `Action::ParallelPreviousFramesRequired` method allows actions to specify how many preceding frames they need, enabling the framework to preload boundary frames for correct processing on non-master ranks.

Sources: [CpptrajState.h](src/CpptrajState.h#L92-L98), [Action.h](src/Action.h#L54-L63)

## Execution Modes: Normal vs Ensemble

Cpptraj operates in two distinct trajectory processing modes: **NORMAL mode** processes trajectories sequentially, while **ENSEMBLE mode** processes multiple trajectories simultaneously as a collection. The mode determination occurs automatically based on input commands—if ensemble input is specified, the system configures for ensemble processing.

In NORMAL mode, the frame loop iterates through frames from each trajectory in sequence, with actions operating on single Frame objects. In ENSEMBLE mode, the frame loop advances all trajectories simultaneously, with actions receiving Frame arrays representing the current frame from each ensemble member. This design enables ensemble-specific analyses like calculating ensemble-averaged properties or performing clustering across multiple trajectories.

The mode affects execution timing and resource management. Ensemble processing typically requires more memory (holding multiple frames simultaneously) but enables calculations that would be impossible in sequential processing. The CpptrajState tracks the current mode and dispatches to specialized execution methods (`RunNormal` vs `RunEnsemble`) that implement the appropriate loop structure.

Sources: [CpptrajState.h](src/CpptrajState.h#L16-L17), [CpptrajState.h](src/L90-L91)

## Pipeline Performance Considerations

The trajectory processing pipeline optimizes performance through several architectural decisions. The separation of command specification from execution enables bulk allocation of DataSets and preprocessing of topology information, avoiding per-frame memory allocation overhead. Action setup occurs once per topology rather than per frame, allowing precomputation of expensive operations like mask expansion or mass array creation.

Frame processing minimizes data copying through reference passing where possible. The Frame object maintains coordinates in contiguous memory, facilitating cache-friendly access patterns during coordinate operations. Actions that modify coordinates communicate this through return codes, enabling the pipeline to optimize subsequent processing—if no coordinate modification occurs, downstream actions can avoid unnecessary coordinate transformations.

The pipeline also includes optional progress reporting through the `showProgress_` flag in CpptrajState, providing frame-by-frame feedback for long-running analyses without requiring debugger interruption. Progress reporting uses percentage completion estimates based on known frame counts from TrajinList, enabling accurate time estimates for predictable workloads.

Sources: [CpptrajState.h](src/CpptrajState.h#L110-L118), [TrajinList.h](src/TrajinList.h#L33-L34)

## Error Handling and Recovery

The pipeline implements a multi-level error handling strategy designed to balance robustness with early failure detection. Individual actions can signal non-fatal errors through the SKIP return code, causing the action to be marked inactive for the remainder of the current trajectory while allowing other actions to continue processing. This enables graceful handling of transient issues like missing frames or temporary calculation failures.

Fatal errors during action initialization or setup propagate through the CpptrajState's `exitOnError_` flag. When set, errors cause immediate pipeline termination; when unset, the system logs errors and continues execution. The `noEmptyRun_` flag prevents processing when no actions or output trajectories are specified, avoiding wasted computation in misconfigured runs.

The command processor includes special handling for control block errors, with unmatched control structures (unclosed loops or if statements) triggering errors before execution begins. This validation prevents runtime errors from malformed control structures that would be difficult to diagnose during frame processing.

Sources: [Action.h](src/Action.h#L32-L39), [CpptrajState.h](src/CpptrajState.h#L20-L23), [CpptrajState.h#L114-L115)

## Post-Processing and Output

After all frames are processed, the pipeline enters the post-processing phase where `Action::Print` methods are called and analyses are executed. The Print phase enables actions to perform calculations that require the complete dataset (like running averages or statistical summaries) and to write output not managed through the DataSet system.

The AnalysisList then processes all queued analyses through `CpptrajState::RunAnalyses`. Analyses operate on accumulated DataSets rather than individual frames, enabling operations like time series analysis, correlation functions, and statistical summaries. The separation between actions (per-frame operations) and analyses (post-frame calculations) provides a clean conceptual boundary for building complex workflows.

Finally, `CpptrajState::MasterDataFileWrite` iterates through all DataFiles in DataFileList, triggering DataSet writing to disk. This deferred writing enables DataSets to be modified by multiple analyses and supports output formatting optimizations that would be impossible with incremental writing during frame processing.

Sources: [CpptrajState.h](src/CpptrajState.h#L54-L71), [CpptrajState.h#L70-L71)

## Integration Points and Extensions

The trajectory processing pipeline provides multiple extension points for developers. New actions are created by inheriting from the Action base class and implementing the four required methods (Init, Setup, DoAction, Print). The `ReferenceAction` helper class simplifies reference structure handling for coordinate-based actions like RMSD or distance calculations.

The DispatchObject system enables dynamic command registration at program startup, allowing modular command addition without modifying core dispatch logic. Actions register themselves through the `AddCmd` method during program initialization, specifying their command name, help text, and allocator function.

For advanced users, the pipeline supports external integration through **Pytraj**, the Python interface that wraps the core C++ functionality. Pytraj exposes the trajectory processing pipeline as Python objects, enabling programmatic pipeline construction and integration with scientific Python ecosystems. This external interface maintains architectural consistency with the command-line version while providing additional flexibility for Python-based workflows.


# Coordinate Transformations (RMSD, Alignment, Rotation)



Coordinate transformations form the foundation of structural analysis in molecular dynamics, enabling quantitative comparison of atomic positions across timeframes, conformational ensembles, and reference structures. Cpptraj implements a comprehensive coordinate transformation framework centered on the **Frame** class, which provides optimized routines for Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) calculation, structural alignment, and coordinate rotation operations. These transformations leverage mathematical algorithms optimized for performance while supporting both mass-weighted and unweighted calculations, making them suitable for diverse analysis scenarios ranging from backbone-only alignment to full system superposition.

## Architecture Overview

The coordinate transformation architecture is built upon three core abstractions: coordinate storage in the **Frame** class, mathematical operations in **Matrix_3x3** and **Vec3** types, and flexible atom selection through **AtomMask**. This design enables efficient batch processing of trajectory frames while maintaining numerical precision for scientific analysis.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Input["Coordinate Input Layer"]
        Trajectory[Trajectory Files]
        Ref[Reference Structure]
    end
    
    subgraph Frame["Frame Class Core"]
        XYZ[XYZ Coordinates]
        Mass[Mass Array]
        Mask[Atom Mask Selection]
    end
    
    subgraph Transforms["Transformation Pipeline"]
        COM[Center of Mass<br/>Calculation]
        Kabsch[Kabsch Algorithm<br/>Rotation Matrix]
        RMSD[RMSD Computation]
    end
    
    subgraph Output["Output Layer"]
        Aligned[Aligned Frame]
        Stats[RMSD Statistics]
        Matrix[Rotation Matrix]
    end
    
    Trajectory --> Frame
    Ref --> Frame
    XYZ --> COM
    Mass --> COM
    COM --> Kabsch
    Mask --> Kabsch
    Kabsch --> RMSD
    Kabsch --> Aligned
    RMSD --> Stats
    Kabsch --> Matrix
    
    style Frame fill:#e1f5fe
    style Transforms fill:#fff3e0
    style Output fill:#e8f5e9
```

## RMSD Calculation Fundamentals

RMSD quantifies the average deviation between corresponding atomic positions in two structural states, providing a single scalar measure of structural similarity. Cpptraj implements multiple RMSD calculation strategies tailored to different analytical needs, each with specific computational trade-offs.

### Mass-Weighted vs. Unweighted RMSD

The fundamental choice in RMSD calculation involves whether to weight atomic contributions by their masses. Mass-weighted RMSD emphasizes heavier atoms (typically backbone atoms in proteins), making it less sensitive to surface sidechain fluctuations. Unweighted RMSD treats all atoms equally, providing a geometric measure of structural difference independent of atomic composition.

**Implementation**: The RMSD calculation accepts a `useMassIn` boolean parameter that determines the weighting scheme. When enabled, each coordinate contribution is multiplied by the corresponding atomic mass during both center-of-mass calculation and covariance matrix formation.

Sources: [Frame.cpp](src/Frame.cpp#L1058-L1216), [Frame.h](src/Frame.h#L262-L268)

### RMSD Calculation Variants

| Variant | Method | Description | Use Case |
|---------|--------|-------------|----------|
| **RMSD(Ref, useMass)** | Full fitting | Centers both frames, calculates optimal rotation, returns RMSD | Standard structural comparison |
| **RMSD_NoFit(Ref, useMass)** | No fitting | Direct RMSD without alignment | Comparing structures in same coordinate system |
| **RMSD_CenteredRef(Ref, useMass)** | Pre-centered | Assumes reference already centered at origin | Batch processing with common reference |
| **DISTRMSD(Ref)** | Distance-based | RMSD of inter-atomic distances | Topology-independent comparison |

Sources: [Frame.h](src/Frame.h#L262-L269), [Frame.cpp](src/Frame.cpp#L1217-L1250)

## The Kabsch Algorithm Implementation

Cpptraj employs the **Kabsch algorithm** for finding the optimal rotation matrix that minimizes RMSD between two point sets. This elegant algorithm operates through a series of linear algebra operations that efficiently solve the rotation matrix without iterative optimization.

### Mathematical Foundation

The algorithm computes the optimal rotation matrix **U** through these key steps:

1. **Center Both Structures**: Translate both the target frame and reference frame to their respective centers of mass or geometric centers (depending on mass weighting)
2. **Calculate Covariance Matrix**: Construct the 3×3 covariance matrix **R** = **Xᵀ** × **Ref**, where **X** and **Ref** are centered coordinate matrices
3. **Compute Symmetric Product**: Calculate **E** = **RᵀR** and diagonalize to obtain eigenvectors **a₁, a₂, a₃** and eigenvalues **μ₁, μ₂, μ₃**
4. **Extract Rotation Vectors**: Compute vectors **b** = **R** × **a** for each eigenvector, then normalize
5. **Determine Rotation Matrix**: Construct **U** = **E** × **Bᵀ**, where **E** is the matrix of eigenvectors and **B** is the matrix of normalized b vectors
6. **Handle Determinant**: Check the sign of (b₁ × b₂) · b₃ to ensure proper-handed rotation matrix

### Implementation Details

The Kabsch algorithm in cpptraj is implemented in `Frame::RMSD_CenteredRef()`, which receives pre-centered coordinates and computes both the RMSD value and optimal rotation matrix. The implementation explicitly handles numerical edge cases, including the determinant sign check that prevents improper rotations (reflections).

Sources: [Frame.cpp](src/Frame.cpp#L1075-L1216)

> [!TIP]
> The covariance matrix calculation in the Kabsch algorithm uses mass-weighted coordinates when `useMassIn` is true, with the mass factor applied to each term in the summation. This is critical for maintaining consistency with the center-of-mass calculation—both must use the same weighting scheme to minimize the RMSD properly.

## Centering and Translation Operations

Before RMSD calculation, both structures must be translated to a common reference point—typically the coordinate origin. Cpptraj provides flexible centering operations supporting both mass-weighted and geometric center calculations.

### Center of Mass vs. Geometric Center

The choice between center of mass and geometric center depends on the analytical objective:

**Center of Mass** (`VCenterOfMass()`): Calculates the weighted average position using atomic masses:
```
COM = (Σ mᵢrᵢ) / (Σ mᵢ)
```

**Geometric Center** (`VGeometricCenter()`): Calculates the simple arithmetic mean of coordinates:
```
GC = (Σ rᵢ) / N
```

### Translation Methods

The Frame class provides multiple translation methods for different scenarios:

- **`Translate(Vec3, AtomMask)`**: Translates only atoms specified in the mask
- **`Translate(Vec3, int, int)`**: Translates atoms within a specified index range
- **`Translate(Vec3, Unit)`**: Translates atoms within a molecular unit (residue, molecule)
- **`Translate(Vec3)`**: Translates all atoms in the frame
- **`NegTranslate(Vec3)`**: Translates by the negative of the vector (equivalent to `Translate(-Vec3)`)

The `CenterOnOrigin()` method combines center calculation with translation, returning the original center position while moving the frame to the origin. This is used during RMSD calculation to establish the common reference point.

Sources: [Frame.h](src/Frame.h#L214-L237), [Frame.cpp](src/Frame.cpp#L995-L1009)

## Rotation Operations

Once centered, the optimal rotation matrix from the Kabsch algorithm is applied to align the target frame with the reference. Cpptraj provides efficient rotation operations with flexible atom selection.

### Matrix-Based Rotation

Rotation is implemented as linear transformation of coordinate vectors using the 3×3 rotation matrix **U**:
```
r' = U × r
```

where **r** is the original coordinate vector and **r'** is the rotated coordinate. The rotation matrix preserves distances and angles while changing orientation.

### Rotation Method Variants

| Method | Scope | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| **`Rotate(Matrix_3x3)`** | All atoms | Applies rotation to entire frame |
| **`Rotate(Matrix_3x3, int, int)`** | Index range | Rotates atoms within specified range |
| **`Rotate(Matrix_3x3, AtomMask)`** | Mask selection | Rotates only selected atoms |
| **`InverseRotate(Matrix_3x3)`** | All atoms | Applies inverse of rotation (transpose for orthogonal matrices) |
| **`InverseRotate(Matrix_3x3, AtomMask)`** | Mask selection | Applies inverse rotation to selected atoms |

### Combined Transformations

The `Trans_Rot_Trans()` method provides an optimized three-step transformation: translate → rotate → translate. This is commonly used in alignment operations where you translate to origin, rotate, then translate back to the reference position. The Frame class provides overloads for all-atom and mask-based transformations.

Sources: [Frame.h](src/Frame.h#L238-L253), [Frame.cpp](src/Frame.cpp#L1010-L1018)

## Structural Alignment Pipeline

The complete alignment process in cpptraj combines centering, RMSD calculation, and rotation into a unified pipeline. The `Align()` method encapsulates this workflow for typical alignment scenarios.

### Alignment Method Signature

```cpp
void Align(Frame const& REF, AtomMask const& mask)
```

This method performs:
1. Creates temporary frames containing only the masked atoms from both target and reference
2. Centers the reference at its geometric center
3. Calculates optimal rotation matrix and translation vectors using RMSD_CenteredRef
4. Applies the combined transformation using `Trans_Rot_Trans()`

### Alignment Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start[Start Alignment] --> Select[Select Alignment Atoms via Mask]
    Select --> CreateRef[Create Temp Reference Frame]
    Select --> CreateTarget[Create Temp Target Frame]
    CreateRef --> CenterRef[Center Reference at Origin]
    CreateTarget --> CalculateCOM[Calculate Target Center]
    CenterRef --> CalcCovariance[Calculate Covariance Matrix]
    CalculateCOM --> ShiftTarget[Shift Target to Origin]
    ShiftTarget --> CalcCovariance
    CalcCovariance --> Diagonalize[Diagonalize RtR Matrix]
    Diagonalize --> ComputeRotation[Compute Rotation Matrix U]
    ComputeRotation --> ApplyTrans[Apply Trans-Rot-Trans]
    ApplyTrans --> End[Alignment Complete]
    
    style CenterRef fill:#fff3e0
    style ComputeRotation fill:#fff3e0
    style ApplyTrans fill:#e8f5e9
```

### Practical Considerations

When performing alignments, consider these factors:

**Atom Selection**: Alignment typically uses backbone atoms (Cα, N, C, O) for proteins or a consistent subset across all frames. The mask should select atoms present in all frames to avoid mismatches.

**Mass Weighting**: For backbone-only alignment, mass weighting provides subtle differences but is often not critical. For full-system alignment including diverse atom types, mass weighting may be preferable.

**Reference Selection**: Choose a representative structure (e.g., the average structure, centroid frame, or biologically relevant conformation) as the alignment reference to minimize bias.

Sources: [Frame.h](src/Frame.h#L260), [Frame.cpp](src/Frame.cpp#L1010-L1018)

## Advanced Coordinate Transformations

Beyond basic RMSD and alignment, cpptraj provides specialized coordinate transformation methods for advanced analysis scenarios.

### Distance RMSD (DISTRMSD)

The `DISTRMSD()` method calculates RMSD based on inter-atomic distances rather than coordinates, making it invariant to overall translation and rotation. This is useful for comparing structures when alignment is ambiguous or when coordinate systems differ.

### Axis of Rotation

The `SetAxisOfRotation()` method defines a custom rotation axis between two atoms or points, enabling precise rotational manipulations around user-specified axes. This is valuable for analyzing conformational changes or applying specific rotational operations.

### Inertia Matrix

The `CalculateInertia()` method computes the inertia tensor for selected atoms, providing rotational dynamics properties. This matrix is essential for normal mode analysis and understanding rotational diffusion characteristics.

Sources: [Frame.h](src/Frame.h#L269-L275), [Frame.cpp](src/Frame.cpp#L1251-L1290), [Frame.cpp](src/Frame.cpp#L1290-L1318)

## Performance Optimization Strategies

Coordinate transformations are computationally intensive operations, especially when processing large trajectories. Cpptraj employs several optimization strategies:

### Inlined Operations

Critical coordinate manipulation functions are declared in the header file and marked for inlining by the compiler. This includes center of mass calculations, translations, and rotations, which eliminates function call overhead during tight loops.

### Memory Access Patterns

The coordinate array (`X_`) stores coordinates in the interleaved format X₀, Y₀, Z₀, X₁, Y₁, Z₁, ..., which enables efficient vectorized operations and improves cache locality during sequential processing.

### Batch Processing

For analysis requiring RMSD calculations across multiple frames, use the `RMSD_CenteredRef()` method when processing against a common reference. This avoids redundant centering of the reference structure for each comparison.

### Mask Optimization

AtomMask pre-computes selection indices, making repeated masked operations efficient. When performing multiple transformations on the same atom subset, construct the mask once and reuse it.

> [!TIP]
> When computing RMSD time series for trajectory analysis, center the reference frame once and use `RMSD_CenteredRef()` for all comparisons. This avoids the overhead of recalculating the reference center of mass for every frame, potentially reducing computation time by 20-30% for large systems.

## Integration with Analysis Commands

Coordinate transformations underpin many cpptraj analysis commands, including:

- **`rms`**: Calculates RMSD time series with optional fitting
- **`align`**: Aligns trajectory frames to a reference
- **`center`**: Centers structures on specified atom selections
- **`rotate`**: Applies explicit rotations to coordinates
- **`reference`**: Manages reference structures for comparison

These commands expose the Frame class transformation methods through the command-line interface and scripting API, enabling flexible workflow automation.

## Next Steps

Understanding coordinate transformations provides the foundation for advanced structural analysis. Continue exploring these related topics:

- **[RMSD and RMSF Calculations](10-rmsd-and-rmsf-calculations)**: Detailed analysis of fluctuation patterns and time-dependent RMSD computation
- **[Principal Component Analysis (PCA)](13-principal-component-analysis-pca)**: Coordinate transformations for dimensional reduction and essential dynamics
- **[Clustering Algorithms](17-clustering-algorithms-k-means-dbscan-hierarchical)**: Structural similarity quantification for conformational clustering
- **[Atom Selection and Mask Expressions](6-atom-selection-and-mask-expressions)**: Flexible atom selection for targeted coordinate transformations


# Periodic Boundary Conditions and Imaging



Periodic Boundary Conditions (PBC) and imaging are fundamental concepts in molecular dynamics simulation analysis. In MD simulations, systems are typically replicated in three-dimensional space to simulate bulk behavior without surface effects. This creates a "periodic" environment where particles crossing one boundary re-enter from the opposite side. The imaging functionality in CPPTRAJ handles the transformation of coordinates between different periodic images, enabling accurate analysis of molecular structures, distances, and dynamics that span multiple unit cells. This is particularly critical for membrane systems, protein-ligand complexes in solution, and any analysis requiring intact molecular structures that may cross periodic boundaries during simulation.

## Architectural Overview

CPPTRAJ's PBC and imaging system is built around the `Action_Image` and `ImageRoutines` classes that originated in PTRAJ and were adapted for the C++ implementation [README.md](README.md#L153-L159). The system supports both orthogonal and triclinic unit cells, providing multiple imaging strategies tailored to different analytical requirements and system geometries.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[PBC & Imaging System] --> B[Image Command]
    A --> C[AutoImage Command]
    A --> D[Unwrap Command]
    A --> E[MinImage Command]
    
    B --> B1[Orthogonal Boxes]
    B --> B2[Triclinic Boxes]
    B --> B3[Center Options]
    B --> B4[Familiar Mode]
    
    C --> C1[By Vector Mode]
    C --> C2[First Atom Mode]
    C --> C3[Anchor Mask Mode]
    
    D --> D1[By Atom Scheme]
    D --> D2[By Molecule Scheme]
    D --> D3[Toroidal Scheme]
    D --> D4[Average Box Correction]
    
    E --> E1[Minimum Image Distance]
    E --> E2[Mask Center Option]
    E --> E3[Non-Self Interactions]
```

The imaging architecture coordinates with several other core systems including atom selection masks, trajectory processing pipelines, and coordinate transformations. The system must correctly handle box information stored in trajectory files and apply appropriate transformations based on box type and user-specified parameters.

## Image Command

The `image` command provides manual control over coordinate imaging operations, allowing precise specification of which atoms to center and how to apply periodic boundary transformations. This command is essential when you need explicit control over the imaging process or when working with systems where automatic determination might not produce optimal results.

### Orthogonal vs. Triclinic Imaging

CPPTRAJ supports imaging operations for both orthogonal (rectangular) and triclinic (non-orthogonal) unit cells. Orthogonal boxes have box vectors that are perpendicular to each other, while triclinic boxes have arbitrary angles between box vectors, requiring more complex coordinate transformations.

Test examples demonstrate both scenarios:

**Orthogonal imaging:**
```
center :2 origin
image origin center
```
[Test_Image/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Image/RunTest.sh#L36-L41)

**Triclinic imaging:**
```
center :2-11
image center triclinic
```
[Test_Image/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Image#L46-L51)

| Parameter | Description | Use Case |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| `origin` | Use box origin as reference point | Standard orthogonal systems |
| `center` | Use center coordinates as reference | Systems needing centering around specific atoms |
| `triclinic` | Apply triclinic imaging transformations | Non-orthogonal unit cells (triclinic, dodecahedron, etc.) |

### Familiar Mode

The `familiar` option maintains the "familiar" arrangement of molecules relative to each other during imaging. This is particularly useful in non-orthogonal systems where standard imaging might place molecules in unfamiliar orientations relative to the reference structure.

```
center :2-11 origin
image origin center familiar
```
[Test_Image/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Image/RunTest.sh#L60-L64)

Familiar mode ensures that the relative spatial relationships between molecules are preserved as much as possible while still satisfying the imaging constraints. This is crucial for analyses where maintaining molecular orientation patterns is important, such as in protein-ligand binding studies or membrane protein systems.

### Center and COM Options

The imaging process can reference different coordinate centers:

1. **Center of geometric positions** - Default mode using atomic coordinates
2. **Center of mass (COM)** - Mass-weighted center calculation

Example using COM with specific mask:
```
center :2-11
image center familiar com :6
```
[Test_Image/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Image/RunTest.sh#L70-L74)

> [!TIP]
> When using `familiar` mode with `com`, ensure your reference mask includes atoms with reasonable mass values. This combination is particularly powerful for membrane systems where maintaining the orientation of transmembrane domains relative to the lipid bilayer is critical for accurate analysis.

## AutoImage Command

The `autoimage` command automatically determines optimal imaging parameters based on the system topology and user-specified criteria. This reduces the complexity of imaging operations by inferring appropriate masks and transformations from molecular structure information.

### By Vector Mode

The `byvec` mode images molecules based on a vector determination algorithm:
```
autoimage mode byvec
strip !(^1,2|:52,57,77)
```
[Test_AutoImage/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoImage/RunTest.sh#L19-L24)

This mode is particularly useful for membrane-spanning peptides or proteins where a principal axis (such as a helical axis) can be used to determine the optimal imaging orientation. The vector algorithm identifies the primary molecular orientation and images accordingly.

### First Atom Mode

The `firstatom` mode uses the first atom of each molecule as a reference point for imaging decisions:
```
autoimage firstatom
```
[Test_AutoImage/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoImage/RunTest.sh#L35-L39)

This approach is computationally efficient and works well for systems where the first atom of each molecule provides a stable reference point. It's commonly used for nucleic acid systems where the phosphate backbone provides consistent first-atom references.

### Anchor Mask Mode

The `anchor` mode allows explicit specification of a reference anchor point and origin:
```
autoimage anchor :96 origin
```
[Test_AutoImage/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoImage/RunTest.sh#L50-L54)

Table: AutoImage Mode Comparison

| Mode | Reference Strategy | Best For | Computational Cost |
|------|-------------------|----------|-------------------|
| `byvec` | Vector-based axis determination | Membrane proteins, helical systems | Moderate |
| `firstatom` | First atom of each molecule | Nucleic acids, structured systems | Low |
| `anchor` | User-specified anchor mask | Complex multi-component systems | Low |
| Default | Automatic molecule detection | General protein-ligand systems | Low to Moderate |

### Non-Sequential Molecules

AutoImage can handle systems with non-sequential molecule indices, automatically detecting molecular boundaries:
```
autoimage
```
[Test_AutoImage/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoImage/RunTest.sh#L66-L70)

This capability is essential for systems that have undergone trajectory manipulation (such as concatenation, stripping, or reordering) where molecule indices are no longer sequential in the topology.

## Unwrap Command

The `unwrap` command reverses the effects of periodic boundary imaging, reconstructing the continuous trajectory of molecules as they move through space. This is essential for diffusion calculations, tracking individual molecules across multiple images, and analyzing long-range transport properties.

### Unwrap Schemes

CPPTRAJ provides multiple unwrapping algorithms:

**By Atom scheme:**
```
unwrap byatom
```
[Test_Unwrap/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Unwrap/RunTest.sh#L9-L13)

**By Molecule scheme:**
```
unwrap bymol avgucell MyBox[avg]
```
[Test_Unwrap/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Unwrap/RunTest.sh#L25-L28)

**Toroidal scheme:**
```
unwrap scheme tor
```
[Test_Unwrap/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Unwrap/RunTest.sh#L39-L42)

Table: Unwrap Scheme Characteristics

| Scheme | Algorithm | Applications | Considerations |
|--------|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| `byatom` | Atom-by-atom reconstruction | High-precision atom tracking | Computationally intensive for large systems |
| `bymol` | Molecule-based unwrapping | Protein diffusion, lipid mobility | Requires accurate molecule definitions |
| `tor` | Toroidal view preservation | Periodic system analysis on torus | Maintains toroidal topology constraints |

### Average Box Correction

Unwrapping can incorporate average unit cell information to improve accuracy for systems with fluctuating box dimensions:

```
avgbox MyBox
unwrap bymol avgucell MyBox[avg]
```
[Test_Unwrap/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Unwrap/RunTest.sh#L21-L28)

This feature calculates the average box dimensions across the trajectory and uses these values for more consistent unwrapping, reducing artifacts from box size fluctuations that are common in NPT simulations.

> [!TIP]
> For diffusion coefficient calculations, use `unwrap` with `avgbox` to correct for box fluctuations in NPT simulations. Always specify `noimage` in subsequent distance or diffusion calculations to prevent re-imaging of unwrapped coordinates.

## MinImage Command

The `minimage` command calculates the minimum image distance between atoms or groups, accounting for periodic boundary conditions. This is essential for accurate distance measurements, interaction energy calculations, and neighbor finding in periodic systems.

```
minimage m1 :1-13 :1-13 out min.dat
minimage m2 :1-13 :1-13 maskcenter out min.dat
```
[Test_MinImage/RunTest.sh](test/Test_MinImage/RunTest.sh#L14-L17)

### Minimum Image Convention

The minimum image convention ensures that the calculated distance between two atoms is the shortest possible distance considering all periodic images. For orthorhombic boxes, this involves checking all 26 neighboring unit cells. For triclinic boxes, the algorithm is more complex due to non-orthogonal box vectors.

### Mask Center Option

The `maskcenter` option uses the center of the specified mask as the reference point for minimum image calculations:
```
minimage m2 :1-13 :1-13 maskcenter
```
[Test_MinImage/RunTest.sh](test/Test_MinImage/RunTest.sh#L17)

This is useful when you want to calculate distances between groups of atoms rather than individual atoms, where the group center provides a more meaningful measure than individual atomic distances.

## Workflow Integration

The imaging commands integrate seamlessly into CPPTRAJ's trajectory processing pipeline:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B[Optional: Strip/Watershell]
    B --> C{Imaging Operation}
    C --> C1[Image]
    C --> C2[AutoImage]
    C --> C3[Unwrap]
    C --> C4[MinImage]
    C --> D[Center/Transform]
    D --> E[Analysis/Diffusion]
    E --> F[Trajectory Output]
    
    style C fill:#e1f5ff
    style E fill:#fff4e1
```

Imaging operations should typically be performed early in the processing pipeline, before coordinate-dependent analyses like RMSD, distance calculations, or diffusion measurements. The order of operations is crucial:

1. **Load trajectory** with box information
2. **Apply imaging** (`image` or `autoimage`) to center and coordinate molecules
3. **Unwrap** if continuous trajectories are needed for diffusion
4. **Apply analysis** (`distance`, `diffusion`, `rmsd`, etc.)
5. **Output** processed trajectory or analysis results

## Advanced Applications

### Distance Measurements with Imaging

Direct comparison of imaged vs. non-imaged distances:
```
distance image :507@O :499@O out ortho.dat
distance noimage :507@O :499@O out ortho.dat noimage
```
[Test_Image/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Image/RunTest.sh#L16-L18)

This demonstrates how periodic boundary conditions affect distance measurements, particularly important for systems where atoms may cross box boundaries.

### Non-Orthorhombic Systems

For triclinic boxes (e.g., dodecahedron, truncated octahedron):
```
distance image :1507@O :1676@O out nonortho.dat
distance noimage :1507@O :1676@O out nonortho.dat noimage
```
[Test_Image/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Image/RunTest.sh#L26-L28)

Non-orthorhombic systems require specialized imaging algorithms that properly account for non-orthogonal box vectors. CPPTRAJ automatically detects box type from trajectory information and applies appropriate transformations.

## Summary of PBC Commands

| Command | Primary Function | Key Options | Typical Use Case |
|---------|------------------|-------------|------------------|
| `image` | Manual coordinate imaging | `origin`, `center`, `triclinic`, `familiar`, `com` | Precise control over imaging |
| `autoimage` | Automatic imaging detection | `byvec`, `firstatom`, `anchor`, `origin` | Simplified imaging for common systems |
| `unwrap` | Reconstruct continuous trajectories | `byatom`, `bymol`, `scheme tor`, `avgucell` | Diffusion calculations, long-range tracking |
| `minimage` | Minimum image distance calculation | `maskcenter`, distance masks | Interaction analysis, neighbor finding |

For comprehensive trajectory processing, understanding PBC and imaging is foundational. After mastering these concepts, you may want to explore:

- [Trajectory Processing Pipeline](7-trajectory-processing-pipeline) - Learn how imaging integrates with other trajectory operations

# RMSD and RMSF Calculations



This documentation provides comprehensive guidance on Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) and Root Mean Square Fluctuation (RMSF) calculations in CPPTRAJ, two fundamental statistical metrics for analyzing molecular dynamics trajectories. RMSD measures the structural deviation between atomic coordinates over time, while RMSF quantifies the flexibility of individual atoms or residues throughout a simulation. These calculations form the foundation for understanding structural stability, conformational changes, and dynamic behavior in molecular systems.

## Conceptual Overview

RMSD and RMSF calculations in CPPTRAJ are built upon a coordinate transformation framework that enables precise structural comparisons across trajectory frames. The architecture integrates multiple calculation modes including mass-weighted RMSD, per-residue analysis, distance-based RMSD (DRMSD), and anisotropic displacement parameters (ADP) for enhanced structural insights.

The calculation pipeline follows a systematic flow where reference coordinates are established, atomic selections are applied through mask expressions, and statistical metrics are computed across trajectory frames. CPPTRAJ supports both coordinate-fitting RMSD (where structures are optimally aligned before comparison) and no-rotation RMSD (where deviations are calculated without structural superposition), providing flexibility for different analysis scenarios.

Sources: [test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh#L1-L114), [test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh#L1-L68)

### Architectural Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B[Reference Selection]
    B --> C{Reference Type}
    C -->|First Frame| D[Initial Frame Coordinates]
    C -->|Reference Trajectory| E[External Trajectory File]
    C -->|Average Structure| F[Calculated Average]
    C -->|Previous Frame| G[Sequential Frame Comparison]
    
    D --> H[Atomic Mask Application]
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
    
    H --> I{Calculation Mode}
    I -->|RMSD| J[Coordinate Alignment]
    I -->|RMSD NoRotate| K[Direct Deviation]
    I -->|RMSF| L[Fluctuation Analysis]
    I -->|DRMSD| M[Distance Matrix]
    
    J --> N{Weighting Option}
    K --> N
    N -->|Mass-Weighted| O[Multiply by Atomic Mass]
    N -->|Standard| P[Equal Weight]
    
    O --> Q[RMSD/RMSF Calculation]
    P --> Q
    L --> Q
    M --> Q
    
    Q --> R{Output Format}
    R -->|Data File| S[ASCII/XVG Format]
    R -->|Rotation Matrices| T[Matrix Output]
    R -->|PDB B-Factors| U[PDB Coordinate File]
    R -->|ADP Data| V[Anisotropic Parameters]
```

## RMSD Calculations

RMSD calculations quantify the structural deviation between trajectory frames and a reference structure, providing insight into global conformational stability and large-scale structural transitions. The implementation supports multiple reference strategies and weighting schemes to accommodate diverse analysis requirements.

### Basic RMSD Configuration

The fundamental RMSD calculation requires specifying a reference frame, atomic selection, and output destination. By default, CPPTRAJ uses the first trajectory frame as reference, but alternative references can be specified including pre-processed average structures, external trajectory files, or sequential frame-to-frame comparisons.

```cpp
// Basic RMSD command syntax
rms <name> <reference> <mask> [options]
```

Key configuration options include:

| Option | Description | Default |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| `first` | Use first trajectory frame as reference | Yes |
| `reftraj <file>` | Use external trajectory file as reference | No |
| `previous` | Compare to preceding frame in trajectory | No |
| `mass` | Apply mass-weighting to calculations | No |
| `nomod` | Calculate without modifying coordinates | No |
| `norotate` | Skip optimal rotation alignment | No |
| `savevectors` | Save translation and rotation vectors | No |
| `savematrices` | Save rotation matrices | No |

Sources: [test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh#L15-L38)

### Reference Selection Strategies

**First Frame Reference**: The most common approach for analyzing structural convergence from an initial configuration. This mode automatically uses the first frame as reference:

```
rms Res2-11 first :2-11 out rmsd.dat
```

**Reference Trajectory**: Enables comparison against an external trajectory structure, useful for analyzing convergence to a target structure or comparing multiple simulations:

```
rms Res2_11_traj reftraj ../tz2.truncoct.nc :2-11 out rmsd.reftraj.dat
```

**Previous Frame Comparison**: Calculates sequential frame-to-frame RMSD values, highlighting instantaneous structural changes and identifying transition events:

```
rms ToPrevious :2-12@CA previous out Previous.dat
```

Sources: [test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh#L15-L48), [test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh#L71-L79)

### Mass-Weighted RMSD

Mass-weighting assigns higher importance to heavier atoms during structural comparison, which is particularly relevant for backbone-dominated analyses or when comparing structures with different atomic compositions. The weighting scheme multiplies coordinate deviations by the square root of atomic masses before computing the RMSD value:

```
rms Res2-11_mass first :2-11 out rmsd.mass.dat mass savevectors combined vecsout vecs.dat
```

The `savevectors` option combined with mass-weighting enables reconstruction of the optimal superposition transformation for downstream analyses.

Sources: [test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh#L16-L17)

### Rotation and Coordinate Modification

The default RMSD calculation performs optimal Kabsch alignment before computing deviations, modifying trajectory coordinates to minimize RMSD. The `norotate` option disables this alignment for direct coordinate comparison:

```
rms NOROT ref [first] norotate @CA
```

For analyses requiring preservation of original coordinates, the `nomod` option calculates RMSD without altering the frame data:

```
rms First_CA :2-12@CA out NoMod.dat nomod
```

These options are crucial for differentiating between structural fitting effects and actual conformational deviations.

Sources: [test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_RMSD/RunTest.sh#L52-L69)

## RMSF Calculations

RMSF (Root Mean Square Fluctuation) calculations measure the temporal variability of individual atoms or residues throughout a trajectory, revealing local flexibility and dynamic hotspots within molecular structures. CPPTRAJ provides comprehensive atomic fluctuation analysis with multiple output formats including standard data files, B-factors for structural visualization, and anisotropic displacement parameters.

### Atomic Fluctuation Syntax

The `atomicfluct` command computes positional fluctuations from trajectory data:

```
atomicfluct <name> <mask> [options]
```

This analysis typically follows an initial RMSD fitting step to remove global translational and rotational motions, ensuring that calculated fluctuations represent local dynamics rather than overall molecular motion.

Sources: [test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh#L14-L26)

### Calculation Modes

**By-Residue Fluctuations**: Aggregates atomic fluctuations at the residue level, providing per-residue flexibility metrics ideal for identifying mobile regions in proteins or nucleic acids:

```
atomicfluct out fluct.1.dat @C,CA,N byres bfactor
```

**Per-Atom Fluctuations**: Maintains atomic resolution for detailed flexibility mapping:

```
atomicfluct out fluct.2.dat :2-12 byatom
```

**By-Mask Fluctuations**: Enables custom atom groupings for specialized analyses:

```
atomicfluct out fluct.3.dat bymask :3,4,5
```

Sources: [test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh#L14-L20)

### B-Factor and PDB Output

RMSF values can be converted to B-factors for visualization in molecular graphics software. The conversion follows the standard relationship where B-factor = 8π² × RMSF²:

```
atomicfluct A0 :2-12
average crdset MyAvg
crdout MyAvg fluct.2.pdb bfacdata A0 chainid " "
```

CPPTRAJ also supports scaling factors for B-factor output and chain ID specification for multi-chain systems.

Sources: [test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh#L44-L53)

### Anisotropic Displacement Parameters (ADP)

For advanced structural analysis, CPPTRAJ can compute full anisotropic displacement tensors, providing directional information about atomic motion beyond the isotropic RMSF values:

```
rms first mass
atomicfluct MyFluct out dpdp.fluct.dat adpout dpdp.adp.dat
atomicfluct Heavy calcadp :2-21&!@/H
```

The `calcadp` option enables ADP calculation for selected atoms, and the resulting anisotropic parameters can be written to PDB files for visualization with ellipsoids representing directional mobility.

Sources: [test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AtomicFluct/RunTest.sh#L28-L38)

## Per-Residue RMSD Analysis

Per-residue RMSD analysis extends standard RMSD calculations by computing deviation metrics for individual residues, enabling identification of localized structural regions that contribute most to global conformational changes. This mode is particularly valuable for analyzing domain motions, flexible loops, and region-specific structural transitions.

### Per-Residue Configuration

The `rmsd` command with `perres` option activates residue-level RMSD calculations:

```
rmsd :2-11 refindex 0 perres perresout PerResRMSD.agr
```

The `perresout` option specifies the output file destination, while `refindex` selects the reference frame from loaded coordinates.

Sources: [test/Test_PerResRMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_PerResRMSD/RunTest.sh#L16-L20)

### Per-Residue Averaging

For enhanced statistical robustness, per-residue RMSD can be averaged across multiple frames or multiple reference frames:

```
rmsd R2-11 :2-11 refindex 0 perres perresavg perresavg.dat
```

The `perresavg` option generates averaged per-residue RMSD values, reducing noise in flexible regions and highlighting consistent structural differences.

Sources: [test/Test_PerResRMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_PerResRMSD/RunTest.sh#L28-L34)

### Residue Centering

The `perrescenter` option centers each residue before computing RMSD, which can improve accuracy for comparing regions with different spatial distributions:

```
rmsd :2-11 refindex 0 perres perresout center.agr range 1 perrescenter
```

The `range` parameter limits analysis to specific residue ranges, enabling targeted examination of interesting structural regions.

Sources: [test/Test_PerResRMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_PerResRMSD/RunTest.sh#L40-L44)

## DRMSD (Distance RMSD)

Distance RMSD provides an alternative measure of structural similarity based on interatomic distances rather than coordinate positions. This metric is invariant to overall rotation and translation, making it particularly useful for comparing structures where global alignment may be ambiguous or when focusing on internal coordinate changes.

> [!TIP]
> DRMSD calculations are computationally more intensive than coordinate-based RMSD as they require computing all pairwise distances within the selected atom set for each frame comparison.

DRMSD functionality is accessible through the `drmsd` command, supporting similar atomic selection mechanisms as standard RMSD calculations while operating on distance matrices rather than coordinate superposition.

Sources: [test/Test_DRMSD/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DRMSD/RunTest.sh#L1-L20)

## Practical Workflow

The following flowchart illustrates a typical RMSD/RMSF analysis workflow:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
```
