```mermaid
    A[Load Trajectory] --> B[Define Reference]
    B --> C[Select Atom Mask]
    C --> D{Analysis Type}
    D -->|Global RMSD| E[Standard RMSD Calculation]
    D -->|Local Flexibility| F[Atomic Fluctuation]
    D -->|Region-Specific| G[Per-Residue RMSD]
    D -->|Internal Coordinates| H[DRMSD]
    
    E --> I[Output Time Series]
    F --> J{Output Format}
    J -->|Data File| K[Fluctuation Values]
    J -->|PDB| L[B-Factor Annotation]
    J -->|ADP| M[Anisotropic Parameters]
    
    G --> N[Per-Residue Analysis]
    H --> O[Distance Comparison]
    
    I --> P[Visualization & Interpretation]
    K --> P
    L --> P
    M --> P
    N --> P
    O --> P
```

## Implementation Considerations

> [!TIP]
> When performing RMSD/RMSF calculations on large trajectories, consider using the `nofit` or `nomod` options when coordinate modification is not required to improve computational efficiency.

### Memory and Performance

The computational complexity scales quadratically with the number of atoms in selected masks for standard RMSD calculations due to the Kabsch alignment algorithm. For systems with large atom counts, consider using backbone-only selections (`@CA,C,N,O`) or residue-based averaging to reduce computational overhead.

### Reference Frame Management

Multiple reference structures can be loaded simultaneously and referenced by index, enabling comparative analysis against different structural baselines. Reference structures can be loaded via the `reference` command or extracted from loaded trajectories using `loadtraj` with explicit frame specifications.

### Output Data Integration

RMSD and RMSF data can be integrated with other analysis types through CPPTRAJ's data set system. Time-series RMSD values can be correlated with other observables, while RMSF data can be projected onto molecular surfaces or used as weights in further statistical analyses.

## Next Steps

For comprehensive trajectory analysis workflows, combine RMSD/RMSF calculations with:

- **[Trajectory Processing Pipeline](7-trajectory-processing-pipeline)** for preprocessing and data preparation
- **[Principal Component Analysis (PCA)](13-principal-component-analysis-pca)** to identify collective motions underlying observed fluctuations
- **[Clustering Algorithms](17-clustering-algorithms-k-means-dbscan-hierarchical)** to categorize structural states based on RMSD metrics
- **[Distance and Angle Measurements](11-distance-and-angle-measurements)** for complementary geometric analysis


# Distance and Angle Measurements



Distance and angle measurements form the foundation of quantitative molecular dynamics analysis in CPPTRAJ. These measurements enable researchers to track structural changes, monitor conformational transitions, and calculate geometric relationships between atoms or groups of atoms throughout trajectory simulation. This section explores the implementation and usage of distance calculations, angle measurements, and dihedral angle analysis within CPPTRAJ's modular architecture.

## Core Architecture

CPPTRAJ implements geometric measurements through a unified action framework that follows a consistent pattern across all measurement types. The architecture leverages a three-stage processing pipeline: initialization for parsing command arguments and setting up data sets, setup for mapping atom masks to trajectory coordinates, and action execution for per-frame calculations. This design enables efficient batch processing of trajectory frames while maintaining flexibility for different measurement types.

The measurement actions inherit from a base Action class and implement specific geometric calculations. Distance measurements support inter-atomic distances, point-to-atom distances, and periodic boundary condition handling. Angle calculations measure three-atom bond angles, while dihedral measurements compute torsional angles between four-atom sequences. Each measurement type produces time-series data suitable for statistical analysis, correlation studies, or visualization.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Action {
        +Init()
        +Setup()
        +DoAction()
    }
    class Action_Distance {
        -dist_ "DataSet"
        -useMass_ bool
        +Init()
        +Setup()
        +DoAction()
    }
    class Action_Angle {
        -ang_ "DataSet"
        +Init()
        +Setup()
        +DoAction()
    }
    class Action_Dihedral {
        -dih_ "DataSet"
        -minTorsion_ float
        +Init()
        +Setup()
        +DoAction()
    }
    Action <|-- Action_Distance
    Action <|-- Action_Angle
    Action <|-- Action_Dihedral
```

Sources: [Action_Distance.cpp](src/Action_Distance.cpp#L7-L12), [Action_Angle.cpp](src/Action_Angle.cpp#L8), [Action_Dihedral.cpp](src/Action_Dihedral.cpp#L9-L13)

## Distance Measurements

Distance calculations measure the Euclidean distance between two points in 3D space, which can be two atoms, an atom and a reference point, or an atom and a reference frame. The implementation supports both standard Cartesian distance calculations and minimum image conventions for periodic boundary conditions.

### Distance Action Implementation

The Action_Distance class initializes with configurable parameters including mass-weighting options and output dataset specifications. During initialization, it parses atom mask expressions for the two endpoints and optionally sets up periodic boundary condition handling. The Setup phase validates that masks select appropriate atoms from the topology, while the DoAction method performs the actual distance calculation for each frame.

The distance calculation supports several operational modes: normal distance between two atoms, distance to a fixed point in space, and distance to a reference structure. For periodic systems, CPPTRAJ automatically applies minimum image conventions unless explicitly disabled with the `noimage` keyword.

Sources: [Action_Distance.cpp](src/Action_Distance.cpp#L28-L113), [Action_Distance.cpp](src/Action_Distance.cpp#L151-L177)

### Distance Command Syntax

The distance command accepts multiple variations to accommodate different analysis scenarios:

```
distance <name> <mask1> <mask2> [out <filename>] [noimage] [type {mass|geom}]
distance <name> <mask> point <x> <y> <z> [out <filename>]
distance <name> <mask> <mask2> out <filename> reference [refmask]
```

Key parameters include:
- `name`: Dataset name for storing results
- `mask1`, `mask2`: Atom selection expressions defining the endpoints
- `out`: Output file for time-series data
- `noimage`: Disable minimum image convention for periodic systems
- `type`: `mass` for mass-weighted centroid distances, `geom` for geometric centers
- `point`: Fixed coordinates for point-to-atom distances
- `reference`: Calculate distance to first frame of trajectory

Sources: [Action_Distance.cpp](src/Action_Distance.cpp#L15-L26), [Test_Distance/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Distance/RunTest.sh#L15-L23)

### Distance Examples

The following examples demonstrate practical distance calculations for common MD analysis scenarios:

| Scenario | Command | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| End-to-end distance | `distance EndToEnd :1 :13 out dist.dat` | Distance between first and last residues |
| Reference comparison | `distance ToRef @1 @1 out dist.dat reference` | Atom 1 position relative to reference frame |
| Point distance | `distance Point :1 point 0.0 0.0 0.0 out dist.dat` | Atom 1 distance from origin |
| Imaged distance | `distance EndToEnd :1 :13 out ortho.dat` | Distance with periodic boundary correction |
| No-image distance | `distance To553 ^1 :553 out ortho.553.dat noimage` | Distance without minimum image convention |

Sources: [Test_Distance/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Distance/RunTest.sh#L15-L35)

### Periodic Boundary Condition Handling

For simulations in periodic boxes, CPPTRAJ automatically applies minimum image conventions when calculating distances between atoms. This ensures that distances reflect the shortest path across periodic boundaries rather than artificial long paths due to periodic replication. The implementation handles both orthogonal and triclinic box geometries, with automatic detection of box type from the trajectory file.

The `noimage` keyword provides explicit control over this behavior for cases where the actual image跨越 periodic boundaries is of interest, such as tracking a molecule that has diffused across the simulation box boundary.

Sources: [Test_Distance/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Distance/RunTest.sh#L30-L58)

## Angle Measurements

Angle measurements calculate the bond angle between three atoms, defined as the angle subtended at the central atom by vectors extending to the two outer atoms. This measurement is fundamental for analyzing molecular geometry, monitoring conformational changes, and characterizing secondary structure elements.

### Angle Action Implementation

Action_Angle implements angle calculations through vector analysis of three-atom sets. The initialization phase parses three atom masks corresponding to the three atoms defining the angle, with validation that each mask selects exactly one atom. The calculation uses the dot product of normalized vectors from the central atom to each outer atom, applying the arccosine function to derive the angle in degrees.

The implementation maintains a dataset for storing per-frame angle values, enabling time-resolved analysis of angular fluctuations. Angle measurements do not support mass-weighting since they inherently depend on atomic positions rather than collective properties.

Sources: [Action_Angle.cpp](src/Action_Angle.cpp#L16-L51), [Action_Angle.cpp](src/Action_Angle.cpp#L75-L94)

### Angle Command Syntax

```
angle <name> <mask1> <mask2> <mask3> [out <filename>]
```

Parameters:
- `name`: Dataset identifier for the angle time series
- `mask1`, `mask2`, `mask3`: Single-atom masks defining the three atoms
- `mask2`: Central atom (vertex of the angle)
- `out`: Output file for results

Each mask must select exactly one atom. The angle is calculated as the arccosine of the dot product of normalized vectors from the central atom to each outer atom.

Sources: [Action_Angle.cpp](src/Action_Angle.cpp#L10-L14)

## Dihedral Angle Measurements

Dihedral angles (torsional angles) measure the rotation around a bond, defined by four consecutive atoms. These measurements are crucial for analyzing conformational preferences, monitoring backbone torsions in proteins (phi, psi, omega), and characterizing sidechain rotameric states.

### Dihedral Action Implementation

Action_Dihedral calculates torsional angles using the four-atom sequence defining the dihedral. The implementation employs vector cross products to determine the signed angle between planes defined by atoms (1-2-3) and (2-3-4). The calculation accounts for the proper sign convention using the dot product of cross products, providing dihedral values in the range -180° to 180° by default.

The class includes a `minTorsion_` parameter that defines the minimum torsion value for output formatting, supporting different range conventions used in various MD packages. The dihedral calculation is computationally more intensive than distances or angles but remains efficient for trajectory analysis.

Sources: [Action_Dihedral.cpp](src/Action_Dihedral.cpp#L23-L78), [Action_Dihedral.cpp](src/Action_Dihedral.cpp#L105-L130)

### Dihedral Command Syntax

```
dihedral <name> <mask1> <mask2> <mask3> <mask4> [out <filename>] [range360]
```

Parameters:
- `name`: Dataset name for dihedral time series
- `mask1` through `mask4`: Single-atom masks defining the four-atom torsion
- `out`: Output file specification
- `range360`: Output angles in 0-360° range instead of default -180° to 180°

### Multidihedral Analysis

For efficient analysis of multiple dihedrals, CPPTRAJ provides the `multidihedral` command that calculates multiple dihedral types simultaneously. This is particularly useful for protein backbone analysis where phi and psi angles for multiple residues need to be computed.

```
multidihedral <name> <dihedral_types> [resrange <range>]
```

Common dihedral types include:
- `phi`: Backbone phi angle (C-N-CA-C)
- `psi`: Backbone psi angle (N-CA-C-N)
- `omega`: Backbone omega angle (CA-C-N-CA)
- `chi1`, `chi2`, etc.: Sidechain torsions

Sources: [Test_PhiPsi/RunTest.sh](test/Test_PhiPsi/RunTest.sh#L15-L25)

### Dihedral Examples

The phi/psi analysis demonstrates practical dihedral measurements for protein conformational analysis:

```
multidihedral DPDP phi psi
run
phipsi DPDP[phi] DPDP[psi] out phipsi.dat resrange 1-22
writedata dihedrals.dat DPDP[phi]:2 DPDP[psi]:2
```

This example calculates phi and psi angles for the DPDP protein, generates a Ramachandran-style output file for residues 1-22, and writes specific residue data (residue 2 in this case) to a separate data file.

Sources: [Test_PhiPsi/RunTest.sh](test/Test_PhiPsi/RunTest.sh#L15-L25)

> [!TIP]
> When analyzing dihedral angles for large proteins, use the `resrange` option to focus on specific regions of interest. This reduces computational overhead and makes subsequent analysis more manageable by limiting the dataset to conformationally relevant segments.

## Processing Pipeline

Distance, angle, and dihedral measurements integrate seamlessly into CPPTRAJ's trajectory processing pipeline, following the standard action execution model. The pipeline stages enable efficient batch processing with minimal memory overhead.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B[Frame Read]
    B --> C[Action::Setup]
    C --> D{Action Type?}
    D -->|Distance| E[Action_Distance::Init]
    D -->|Angle| F[Action_Angle::Init]
    D -->|Dihedral| G[Action_Dihedral::Init]
    E --> H[Mask Validation]
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I[Action::DoAction]
    I --> J{Calculation Type}
    J --> K[Euclidean Distance]
    J --> L[Bond Angle]
    J --> M[Dihedral Angle]
    K --> N[Dataset Update]
    L --> N
    M --> N
    N --> O{More Frames?}
    O -->|Yes| B
    O -->|No| P[Data Output]
```

The pipeline validates atom masks once during setup, then performs per-frame calculations efficiently during the DoAction phase. Data accumulation happens incrementally, with final output occurring after all frames are processed.

Sources: [Action_Distance.cpp](src/Action_Distance.cpp#L114-L150), [Action_Angle.cpp](src/Action_Angle.cpp#L52-L74), [Action_Dihedral.cpp](src/Action_Dihedral.cpp#L79-L104)

## Data Output and Analysis

All geometric measurements produce time-series datasets that can be output in various formats for subsequent analysis. CPPTRAJ supports standard data formats including Grace (.agr), columnar text, and NetCDF for efficient storage of large datasets.

The phipsi command provides specialized output for dihedral analysis, generating Ramachandran-style data formatted for visualization tools. This output pairs phi and psi angles by residue, facilitating backbone conformation analysis.

Sources: [Test_PhiPsi/RunTest.sh](test/Test_PhiPsi/RunTest.sh#L19-L21)

## Integration with Statistical Analysis

Distance and angle measurements serve as input for higher-level statistical analyses available in CPPTRAJ. The time-series data generated by these actions feeds directly into correlation functions, histograms, clustering algorithms, and principal component analysis workflows.

For correlation analysis, distance measurements can reveal coordinated motions between distant parts of a molecule, while dihedral time series enable analysis of conformational transitions and free energy landscapes. The modular design allows seamless combination of geometric measurements with advanced analysis commands.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L32-L40)

> [!TIP]
> Combine distance measurements with [Time-Correlation Functions and Spectral Analysis](14-time-correlation-functions-and-spectral-analysis) to identify periodic motions or correlated conformational changes. The correlation of distance fluctuations can reveal allosteric communication pathways in large biomolecular systems.

## Further Reading

- **Atom Selection**: For advanced mask syntax and atom selection techniques, see [Atom Selection and Mask Expressions](6-atom-selection-and-mask-expressions)
- **Trajectory Processing**: Understanding the full processing pipeline is covered in [Trajectory Processing Pipeline](7-trajectory-processing-pipeline)
- **Coordinate Transformations**: For RMSD and alignment operations often used in conjunction with geometric measurements, see [Coordinate Transformations](8-coordinate-transformations-rmsd-alignment-rotation)
- **Statistical Analysis**: Applying statistical methods to geometric measurement data is detailed in [Correlation Functions](12-correlation-functions-auto-correlation-cross-correlation) and [Principal Component Analysis](13-principal-component-analysis-pca)


# Correlation Functions (Auto-correlation, Cross-correlation)



This page provides comprehensive coverage of correlation analysis capabilities in cpptraj, enabling you to quantify temporal relationships and periodic behaviors in molecular dynamics trajectories. Correlation functions are essential tools for understanding dynamic properties, identifying relaxation timescales, and detecting coupled motions in molecular systems.

## Mathematical Foundations

Correlation analysis in cpptraj operates on time series data derived from atomic coordinates, distances, angles, or any scalar or vector quantity computed along a trajectory. The implementation supports both auto-correlation (correlation of a time series with itself) and cross-correlation (correlation between two different time series).

The auto-correlation function C(τ) measures how a time series X(t) correlates with itself at different lag times τ:

**C(τ) = ⟨X(t) · X(t+τ)⟩**

where the angle brackets denote averaging over all time origins. Auto-correlation decays from 1 at τ=0 (perfect correlation with itself) toward 0 for uncorrelated signals, with the decay envelope revealing characteristic timescales of the system's dynamics.

The cross-correlation function C_xy(τ) quantifies the relationship between two different time series X(t) and Y(t):

**C_xy(τ) = ⟨X(t) · Y(t+τ)⟩**

This can reveal causal relationships, phase delays, and coupled motions between different degrees of freedom.

Sources: [Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24), [Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L22), [Test_Corr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Corr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24)

## Auto-Correlation Analysis

Auto-correlation analysis in cpptraj is invoked using the `autocorr` command, which processes one or more datasets and generates correlation functions as a function of lag time. This is particularly valuable for analyzing relaxation processes, identifying periodic motions, and computing characteristic decay times.

### Basic Syntax

The fundamental auto-correlation command structure:

```
autocorr name <output_name> <dataset1> <dataset2> ... out <output_file> [lagmax <max_lag>]
```

The command accepts multiple datasets simultaneously, computing auto-correlation for each independently. Each dataset must be pre-defined through analysis commands such as `distance`, `angle`, `dihedral`, `radgyr`, or `vector`.

### Practical Example

Consider computing auto-correlations for inter-residue distances and a vector quantity:

```
parm tz2.parm7
trajin tz2.nc
distance d1-13 :1 :13
distance d3-11 :3 :11
distance d5-9  :5 :9
vector v1 :2@N :2@H
autocorr name AC d1-13 d3-11 d5-9 v1 out ac.agr lagmax 50
```

This example demonstrates auto-correlation analysis on three inter-residue distances and one bond vector, with correlation computed up to lag time 50. The output file `ac.agr` contains the correlation values for all specified datasets.

### Key Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Default Value |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|
| `name` | Prefix for output dataset names | Required |
| `out` | Output file path for correlation results | Required |
| `lagmax` | Maximum lag time for correlation computation | Half trajectory length |
| `datasets` | One or more pre-defined datasets to analyze | Required |

The `lagmax` parameter is critical for balancing resolution and statistical quality. Smaller lagmax values provide better statistics for each lag point but limit the range of observable timescales.

Sources: [Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24)

## Cross-Correlation Analysis

Cross-correlation analysis quantifies relationships between different observables, revealing coupling, causality, and phase relationships in molecular dynamics. The `crosscorr` command computes pairwise correlations between specified datasets.

### Basic Syntax

The cross-correlation command structure:

```
crosscorr name <output_name> <dataset1> <dataset2> <dataset3> ... out <output_file>
```

Unlike auto-correlation which correlates each dataset with itself, cross-correlation computes all pairwise correlations between the specified datasets. For N input datasets, this generates N×N correlation values at each lag time.

### Practical Example

Computing cross-correlations between multiple inter-residue distances:

```
parm tz2.parm7
trajin tz2.nc
distance d1-13 :1 :13
distance d3-11 :3 :11
distance d5-9  :5 :9
crosscorr name CC d1-13 d3-11 d5-9 out cc.gnu
```

This command computes all nine pairwise correlations between the three distances: d1-13 with itself, d1-13 with d3-11, d1-13 with d5-9, d3-11 with itself, d3-11 with d5-9, and d5-9 with itself. The diagonal elements contain auto-correlations, while off-diagonal elements contain cross-correlations.

### Interpretation Guidelines

Cross-correlation values range from -1 to +1, with interpretation depending on the physical context:

- **+1**: Perfect positive correlation - variables move together synchronously
- **0**: No linear correlation - independent behaviors
- **-1**: Perfect negative correlation - variables move in opposite directions

In biomolecular systems, strong cross-correlations often indicate allosteric communication pathways, concerted domain motions, or coupled conformational changes.

Sources: [Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L22)

## General Correlation Command

The `corr` command provides unified correlation analysis with automatic detection of correlation type based on input datasets. This flexible command handles both auto-correlation (same dataset specified twice) and cross-correlation (different datasets).

### Auto-Correlation Example

```
corr d1 d1 out corr.dat
```

Specifying the same dataset twice (`d1 d1`) triggers auto-correlation analysis, equivalent to the specialized `autocorr` command.

### Cross-Correlation Example

```
corr d1 rg out cross.dat
```

Specifying different datasets (`d1 rg`) triggers cross-correlation between a distance and radius of gyration, useful for coupling analysis between local and global structural descriptors.

### Integration with Other Analyses

The `corr` command seamlessly integrates with any cpptraj analysis that generates scalar datasets:

```
distance d1 :2 :12
radgyr rg :1-3 mass nomax
corr d1 d1 out corr.dat
corr d1 rg out cross.dat
```

This demonstrates combining distance measurements and radius of gyration calculations for comprehensive correlation analysis of both local inter-residue separations and overall protein compaction.

Sources: [Test_Corr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Corr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24)

## Data Flow and Integration

Correlation analysis integrates naturally into the cpptraj trajectory processing pipeline, operating on datasets generated by analysis commands and producing output suitable for visualization and further processing.

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B[Coordinate Processing]
    B --> C[Analysis Commands]
    C --> D1[distance]
    C --> D2[angle]
    C --> D3[dihedral]
    C --> D4[radgyr]
    C --> D5[vector]
    D1 --> E[Dataset Generation]
    D2 --> E
    D3 --> E
    D4 --> E
    D5 --> E
    E --> F[Correlation Commands]
    F --> F1[autocorr]
    F --> F2[crosscorr]
    F --> F3[corr]
    F1 --> G[Correlation Results]
    F2 --> G
    F3 --> G
    G --> H[Output Files]
    H --> H1[.agr Grace format]
    H --> H2[.gnu Gnuplot format]
    H --> H3[.dat Raw data]
```

This architectural diagram illustrates how correlation analysis fits within the broader analysis workflow, with datasets flowing from coordinate processing through analysis commands to correlation computation and output.

Sources: [Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24), [Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L22), [Test_Corr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Corr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24)

## Output Formats and Visualization

Correlation results can be written in multiple formats optimized for different visualization tools:

### Supported Output Formats

- **Grace/Xmgr (.agr)**: Binary format for Grace plotting software, ideal for publication-quality figures
- **Gnuplot (.gnu)**: Text format with embedded plotting commands for quick visualization
- **Raw data (.dat)**: Plain text format suitable for custom analysis or import into other software

The output format is determined by the file extension specified in the `out` parameter.

### Output Structure

Each correlation file contains:
- Header information with metadata
- Lag time values (first column or row)
- Correlation coefficients for each dataset pair
- Statistical information (if applicable)

> [!TIP]
> For auto-correlation, the first lag value (τ=0) always equals 1.0, representing perfect correlation of each dataset with itself. Deviations from this expected value may indicate normalization issues or insufficient trajectory length.

Sources: [Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24), [Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L22)

## Applications in Molecular Dynamics

Correlation analysis provides insights into diverse molecular phenomena:

### Relaxation Time Analysis

Auto-correlation decay rates yield characteristic relaxation times (τ_relax) for various processes:

- **Side-chain rotameric transitions**: Fast decays (ps-ns timescale)
- **Loop motions**: Intermediate decays (ns-μs timescale)  
- **Domain reorientations**: Slow decays (μs-ms timescale)

Extract τ_relax by fitting correlation decay to exponential or multi-exponential functions.

### Coupled Motions Detection

Cross-correlation analysis reveals spatial communication pathways:

- Strong positive correlations indicate concerted motions
- Negative correlations suggest compensatory or anti-correlated movements
- Lag at maximum cross-correlation indicates time delays between motions

### Periodic Behavior Identification

Persistent oscillatory components in correlation functions indicate:

- Vibrational modes (high-frequency oscillations)
- Conformational transitions (intermediate frequencies)
- Global breathing motions (low-frequency oscillations)

Sources: [Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24), [Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L22)

## Advanced Considerations

### Statistical Quality

The statistical quality of correlation functions depends on:

- **Trajectory length**: Longer trajectories provide better averaging
- **Lagmax selection**: Larger lagmax reduces samples per lag point
- **Sampling rate**: Must capture relevant timescales

A general guideline: lagmax should not exceed 10-20% of total trajectory length for reliable statistics at all lags.

### Normalization and Units

Correlation functions are computed using normalized quantities, making them dimensionless and comparable across different observables. However, ensure input datasets have consistent units and sampling frequencies.

### Periodic Boundary Effects

For vector-based correlations (velocity autocorrelations, bond vectors), ensure proper imaging and unwrapping to avoid artifacts from periodic boundary conditions. This can be achieved through preprocessing with `autoimage` or `unwrap` commands.

> [!TIP]
> When analyzing correlations in large systems, consider reducing computational cost by selecting specific regions of interest with atom masks and limiting analysis to relevant degrees of freedom.

Sources: [Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24), [Test_Corr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Corr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24)

## Integration with Statistical Analysis

Correlation functions form a bridge between basic trajectory analysis and advanced statistical methods:

**Velocity Autocorrelation**: Foundation for [Diffusion Coefficients](26-diffusion-coefficients) calculations via Green-Kubo relations

**Dipole Autocorrelation**: Basis for [Time-Correlation Functions and Spectral Analysis](14-time-correlation-functions-and-spectral-analysis) and infrared spectroscopy prediction

**Coordinate Cross-Correlation**: Input for [Principal Component Analysis](13-principal-component-analysis-pca) and essential dynamics analysis

These connections demonstrate how correlation analysis provides the time-domain foundation for frequency-domain and ensemble-based analysis techniques.

Sources: [Test_Corr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Corr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24)

## Performance Optimization

For large-scale correlation analyses:

1. **Batch processing**: Compute multiple correlations in a single pass using `autocorr` with multiple datasets
2. **Lagmax optimization**: Use smaller lagmax for preliminary scans, increase for focused analysis
3. **Parallelization**: Leverage [OpenMP Multi-threading](29-openmp-multi-threading) for trajectory processing stages
4. **Memory management**: For very long trajectories, process in chunks and combine results

Correlation computation scales linearly with trajectory length and number of datasets, making it amenable to parallel optimization strategies.

Sources: [Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_AutoCorr/RunTest.sh#L1-L24)

## Troubleshooting Guide

| Issue | Possible Cause | Solution |
|-------|----------------|----------|
| Correlation values > 1.0 | Non-normalized input data | Verify dataset normalization or pre-normalize values |
| Noisy correlation functions | Insufficient trajectory length | Increase trajectory length or reduce lagmax |
| Unexpected oscillations | Periodic boundary artifacts | Apply proper imaging before correlation analysis |
| Flat correlation at τ=0 | All zero values in dataset | Check atom masks and selection criteria |
| Memory errors | Very large correlation matrix | Reduce number of datasets or process in batches |

## Recommended Reading Path

For a complete understanding of cpptraj analysis capabilities:

1. **Prerequisites**: [Atom Selection and Mask Expressions](6-atom-selection-and-mask-expressions) for dataset definition
2. **Related Analysis**: [Time-Correlation Functions and Spectral Analysis](14-time-correlation-functions-and-spectral-analysis) for frequency-domain extensions
3. **Applications**: [Diffusion Coefficients](26-diffusion-coefficients) for transport property calculations
4. **Advanced**: [Principal Component Analysis](13-principal-component-analysis-pca) for collective motion analysis

This progression from basic correlation concepts to advanced applications provides a comprehensive toolkit for analyzing dynamic properties in molecular simulations.

# Principal Component Analysis (PCA)



Principal Component Analysis in CPPTRAJ provides a powerful dimensionality reduction technique for molecular dynamics trajectory analysis, enabling extraction of collective motions and identification of dominant conformational changes. This analysis decomposes atomic positional fluctuations into orthogonal principal components ranked by variance, revealing the most significant large-scale motions in molecular systems.

## Mathematical Foundation

PCA in CPPTRAJ operates on the covariance matrix of atomic coordinates or derived coordinate systems. The fundamental process involves computing the covariance matrix of atomic fluctuations after aligning trajectories to a reference structure, then diagonalizing this matrix to obtain eigenvalues (variance) and eigenvectors (principal components). The mathematical foundation rests on the eigenvalue decomposition:

**C = AᵀA**

Where C is the covariance matrix and A contains the mass-weighted coordinate fluctuations. The eigenvectors of C form an orthonormal basis that diagonalizes the covariance, with eigenvalues representing the variance captured by each principal component.

The implementation supports both coordinate-based PCA (atomic positions) and data-based PCA (derived metrics like RMSD, distances, angles), providing flexibility for different analysis scenarios. The mass-weighting option enables incorporation of atomic masses into the calculation, making the analysis more physically meaningful for biomolecular systems.

## Core Command Architecture

The `principal` command serves as the primary interface for PCA analysis, supporting multiple operational modes and output options. The command structure follows CPPTRAJ's consistent analysis pattern with trajectory input, processing parameters, and output specifications.

```bash
principal <mask> [dorotation] [mass] [out <file>] [name <dataset_name>]
```

The test suite demonstrates typical usage patterns [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Principal/RunTest.sh#L15-L22):
```
trajin ../Test_IRED/1IEE_A_test.mdcrd 1 10
principal * dorotation mass out principal.dat name All
trajout Ctest.crd
run
writedata eigen.dat All[eval] All[evec]
```

**Key Parameters:**

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| mask | Atom selection for analysis | All atoms |
| dorotation | Rotate coordinates to principal axes | No rotation |
| mass | Use mass-weighted coordinates | No mass weighting |
| out | Output file for per-frame results | None |
| name | Dataset name for eigenvalues/eigenvectors | Default name |

## Implementation Architecture

The PCA implementation in CPPTRAJ follows a modular design that integrates with the broader analysis framework:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B[Alignment/Reference]
    B --> C[Covariance Matrix Calculation]
    C --> D[Mass Weighting<br/>if specified]
    D --> E[Eigenvalue Decomposition]
    E --> F[Eigenvalue/Eigenvector Output]
    E --> G[Coordinate Rotation<br/>if dorotation]
    G --> H[Output Coordinates]
    
    I[Projection Option] --> E
    F --> J[Downstream Analysis<br/>Clustering, FES, etc.]
    H --> K[Visualization]
```

The implementation processes trajectory frames sequentially, accumulating the covariance matrix incrementally. This design enables efficient memory usage for large trajectories and supports parallel processing for improved performance on multi-core systems.

## Output Structure and Data Organization

PCA results are organized into multiple output streams, each serving different analytical purposes:

**Per-Frame Output** (`principal.dat` format) [principal.dat.save](test/Test_Principal/principal.dat.save#L1-L41):
```
<Frame> EIGENVALUES: <λ1> <λ2> <λ3>
<Frame> EIGENVECTOR 0: <v1x> <v1y> <v1z>
<Frame> EIGENVECTOR 1: <v2x> <v2y> <v2z>
<Frame> EIGENVECTOR 2: <v3x> <v3y> <v3z>
```

Each frame section contains three eigenvalues (for 3D coordinate analysis) followed by three corresponding eigenvectors. The eigenvalues are ordered by magnitude, with PC1 representing the direction of maximum variance.

**Dataset Outputs** (via `writedata`):
- `All[eval]`: Eigenvalues across all frames
- `All[evec]`: Eigenvector components across all frames

> [!TIP]
> The eigenvector output uses 0-based indexing (EIGENVECTOR 0, 1, 2) corresponding to PC1, PC2, PC3 respectively, which is important when accessing programmatically via the dataset API.

## Coordinate Systems and Analysis Modes

PCA can be performed on different coordinate representations depending on the research question:

**Atomic Coordinates (Default):**
- Analyzes Cartesian coordinate fluctuations
- Requires trajectory alignment to remove translational/rotational motion
- Most common for protein backbone analysis

**Internal Coordinates:**
- Performed on dihedral angles, distances, or other metrics
- Eliminates need for explicit alignment
- Better for conformational sampling analysis

**Mass-Weighted PCA:**
- Incorporates atomic masses into covariance calculation
- Provides physically meaningful collective modes
- Particularly relevant for comparing systems with different atomic compositions

The command syntax adapts to the coordinate system through the mask specification and optional preprocessing commands like `dihedral` or `distance` before the `principal` analysis.

## Integration with Downstream Analyses

PCA results serve as foundational data for multiple advanced analyses in the CPPTRAJ ecosystem:

**Projection Analysis:**
- Project trajectories onto principal components
- Identify frames with extreme PC values
- Generate 2D/3D free energy surfaces
- Related to [Clustering Algorithms](17-clustering-algorithms-k-means-dbscan-hierarchical) for conformational space partitioning

**Essential Dynamics:**
- Animate principal components as collective motions
- Visualize dominant conformational changes
- Compare with experimental observables

**Dimensionality Reduction:**
- Input to machine learning analyses
- Preprocessing for [Time-Correlation Functions](14-time-correlation-functions-and-spectral-analysis)
- Feature extraction for enhanced sampling methods

## Advanced Features and Optimization

> [!TIP]
> For large-scale analyses, consider combining PCA with trajectory sieving or frame reduction strategies to manage computational cost while preserving statistical significance of the principal components.

The implementation supports several advanced features:

**Parallel Execution:**
- MPI and OpenMP parallelization available
- Noted in test script that certain output formats may not be supported in parallel mode [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Principal/RunTest.sh#L24-L31)
- Suitable for ensemble analysis [Ensemble Analysis](27-ensemble-analysis-remd-mremd-hremd)

**Memory Management:**
- Incremental covariance accumulation
- Efficient handling of large trajectory datasets
- Configurable through parallel execution parameters

**Visualization Integration:**
- Coordinate rotation enables direct visualization of principal axes
- Compatible with trajectory output formats for molecular graphics
- Integration with [Coordinate Transformations](8-coordinate-transformations-rmsd-alignment-rotation)

## Practical Implementation Patterns

**Basic PCA with Coordinate Rotation:**
```
trajin trajectory.nc
reference ref.pdb
rms first @CA
principal @CA dorotation mass name ProteinPC
run
writedata eigenvalues.dat ProteinPC[eval]
```

**PCA on Internal Coordinates:**
```
trajin trajectory.nc
dihedral phi1 :1@C :2@N :2@CA :2@C
dihedral psi1 :2@N :2@CA :2@C :3@N
principal data phi1 data psi1 name DihedralPC
run
```

**Trajectory Projection:**
```
# After PCA calculation
project evecs ProteinPC out projection.dat trajin trajectory.nc
```

## Relationship to Other Dimensionality Reduction Methods

CPPTRAJ provides multiple complementary dimensionality reduction techniques:

| Method | Input Type | Key Features | Typical Use Case |
|--------|-----------|--------------|------------------|
| PCA | Coordinates or data | Variance maximization | Global collective motions |
| TICA | Time-series data | Slow dynamics identification | Kinetic clustering |
| IRED | Bond vectors | Orientational correlations | NMR relaxation analysis |

The [Time-Correlation Functions](14-time-correlation-functions-and-spectral-analysis) documentation provides additional context for understanding temporal correlations that complement the spatial correlations captured by PCA.

## Performance Considerations

For optimal performance when working with large-scale datasets:

1. **Alignment**: Perform trajectory alignment before PCA using [RMSD Calculations](10-rmsd-and-rmsf-calculations)
2. **Parallel Execution**: Leverage [MPI Parallelization](30-mpi-parallelization-for-large-scale-analysis) for trajectory processing
3. **Memory Management**: Use trajectory sieving for initial exploratory analysis
4. **I/O Optimization**: Minimize per-frame output unless required for analysis

The computational complexity scales as O(n·m²) where n is the number of frames and m is the number of atoms (or degrees of freedom), making selective atom masks crucial for large systems.

## Next Steps

For comprehensive trajectory analysis workflows, consider integrating PCA with:

- [Clustering Algorithms](17-clustering-algorithms-k-means-dbscan-hierarchical) for conformational state identification based on PC space
- [Grid and Density Calculations](19-grid-and-density-calculations) for spatial distribution analysis in PC-projected coordinates
- [Correlation Functions](12-correlation-functions-auto-correlation-cross-correlation) for temporal dynamics of PC amplitudes
- [Diffusion Coefficients](26-diffusion-coefficients) for examining dynamics along principal components


# Time-Correlation Functions and Spectral Analysis



This section explores the advanced time-series analysis capabilities in CPPTRAJ, focusing on temporal correlation functions and frequency-domain spectral transformations. These tools enable you to extract dynamic information from molecular dynamics trajectories, revealing relaxation times, collective motion frequencies, and dipole moment correlations essential for understanding molecular behavior and spectroscopic properties.

## Architectural Overview

Time-correlation and spectral analysis in CPPTRAJ operate on vector and scalar data extracted from trajectories, transforming temporal domain information into correlation functions and frequency spectra. The architecture supports both time-domain correlation calculations and frequency-domain analysis through Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT), enabling comprehensive dynamic analysis through multiple computational pathways.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input[Data Extraction]
        A[Trajectory] --> B[Vector Data]
        A --> C[Scalar Data]
        A --> D[Distance/Angle Data]
    end
    
    subgraph TimeDomain[Time-Domain Analysis]
        B --> E[Auto-Correlation]
        B --> F[Cross-Correlation]
        C --> E
        C --> F
        E --> G[Relaxation Times]
        F --> H[Coupled Dynamics]
    end
    
    subgraph SpectralDomain[Frequency-Domain Analysis]
        B --> I[FFT Transformation]
        C --> I
        I --> J[Power Spectra]
        I --> K[Frequency Peaks]
    end
    
    subgraph Specialized[Specialized Analysis]
        D --> L[Dipole Correlations]
        L --> M[Dielectric Properties]
        L --> N[IR Spectra]
    end
    
    E --> O[Output Files]
    F --> O
    I --> O
    L --> O
```

Sources: [test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh), [test/Test_FFT/RunTest.sh](test/Test_FFT/RunTest.sh)

## Time Correlation Functions

Time correlation functions quantify how dynamical variables evolve and correlate with themselves (auto-correlation) or with other variables (cross-correlation) over time. These functions provide fundamental insights into molecular relaxation processes, memory effects, and collective dynamics.

### Auto-Correlation Analysis

Auto-correlation functions measure the temporal persistence of a dynamical variable, revealing its characteristic relaxation times. In CPPTRAJ, vector auto-correlation is computed using the `timecorr` command with a single vector specification:

```cpp
analyze timecorr vec1 v1 out v1.auto.dat ptrajformat
```

The auto-correlation function C(t) for a vector v(τ) is defined as:

C(t) = ⟨v(τ) · v(τ+t)⟩

where the angle brackets denote an ensemble average over time origins τ. The function is normalized such that C(0) = 1 for unit vectors, providing decay curves that directly reflect relaxation dynamics.

Sources: [test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh#L11-L15)

### Cross-Correlation Analysis

Cross-correlation analysis examines the temporal relationship between two different dynamical variables, identifying coupled motions and delayed responses. The command syntax extends the auto-correlation case with a second vector specification:

```cpp
analyze timecorr vec1 v1 vec2 v2 out v1v2.cross.dat ptrajformat
```

The cross-correlation function C₁₂(t) between vectors v₁(τ) and v₂(τ) follows:

C₁₂(t) = ⟨v₁(τ) · v₂(τ+t)⟩

Non-zero cross-correlations indicate temporal coupling between the two degrees of freedom, which can reveal allosteric communication pathways or correlated conformational changes.

Sources: [test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh#L16-L17)

### Correlation Order and Normalization

The `order` parameter controls the moment order for correlation calculations, affecting the sensitivity to different correlation magnitudes:

```cpp
timecorr vec1 v1 out v1.o1.auto.dat order 1
timecorr vec1 v1 out v1.o0.auto.dat order 0
```

Order 0 (default) computes the standard correlation function normalized by initial values, while order 1 uses different normalization schemes suitable for specific physical quantities like dipole moments where magnitude variations are significant.

Sources: [test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh#L12-L14)

## Dipole Correlation and Spectral Properties

Dipole correlation functions bridge time-domain dynamics with frequency-domain spectroscopic properties, enabling prediction of infrared and dielectric spectra from MD trajectories.

### Dipole Moment Correlation Analysis

The `dplr` keyword activates specialized dipole correlation calculations, computing quantities directly relevant to dielectric and infrared spectroscopy:

```cpp
analyze timecorr vec1 v1 dplr out v1.dplr.auto.dat ptrajformat
analyze timecorr vec1 v1 vec2 v2 dplr out v1v2.dplr.cross.dat ptrajformat
```

Dipole correlations generate additional output columns including:
- **R**: Correlation function ⟨μ(τ)·μ(τ+t)⟩
- **RRIG**: Rotational-invariant correlation
- **R³**: Higher-order correlation terms
- **R⁶**: Extended correlation moments

These quantities enable calculation of dielectric permittivity and infrared absorption spectra through fluctuation-dissipation relationships.

Sources: [test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh#L18-L21)

### Infrared Spectrum Prediction

For dipole correlation functions, the infrared absorption coefficient α(ω) can be computed via Fourier transformation:

α(ω) ∝ ω² ∫₀^∞ ⟨μ(0)·μ(t)⟩ e^{-iωt} dt

The frequency-domain spectrum reveals molecular vibrational modes and their coupling to the electric field, providing direct connections between MD simulations and experimental IR spectroscopy.

Sources: [test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh#L24-L29)

## Cross-Correlation of Scalar Data

Beyond vector correlations, CPPTRAJ supports cross-correlation of scalar data such as distances, angles, and energies through the `crosscorr` command:

```cpp
distance d1-13 :1 :13
distance d3-11 :3 :11
distance d5-9  :5 :9
crosscorr name CC d1-13 d3-11 d5-9 out cc.gnu
```

This enables identification of correlated structural changes and delayed responses between geometric parameters, essential for understanding allosteric mechanisms and cooperative motions.

Sources: [test/Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh#L12-L16)

## Spectral Analysis via Fast Fourier Transform

Spectral analysis transforms time-domain data into frequency-domain representations, revealing periodic components and characteristic frequencies inherent in molecular motions.

### FFT Command Syntax

The `runanalysis fft` command performs Fast Fourier Transform on pre-existing data files:

```cpp
readdata sin_4pt.agr
runanalysis fft sin_4pt.agr out fft.agr dt 0.025
```

Critical parameters include:
- **dt**: Time step between data points (in appropriate time units)
- **out**: Output file for frequency spectrum
- Input data must be uniformly sampled in time

Sources: [test/Test_FFT/RunTest.sh](test/Test_FFT/RunTest.sh#L6-L8)

### Frequency Resolution and Aliasing

The FFT frequency resolution Δf is determined by the total sampling time T:

Δf = 1/T = (dt × N)⁻¹

where N is the number of data points. The Nyquist frequency f_Nyquist = 1/(2dt) represents the maximum detectable frequency. Proper parameter selection ensures:

1. Adequate sampling rate (dt small enough to capture fastest dynamics)
2. Sufficient duration (large T for fine frequency resolution)
3. Power-of-two data points (optimal for FFT efficiency)

Sources: [test/Test_FFT/RunTest.sh](test/Test_FFT/RunTest.sh#L10-L27)

## Practical Implementation Examples

### Vector Correlation Analysis Setup

Complete workflow for analyzing correlated vector motions between selected atoms:

```cpp
# Load trajectory
parm system.parm7
trajin trajectory.nc

# Define vectors for correlation analysis
vector v1 :2  :4          # Vector between atoms 2 and 4
vector v2 :12 :10         # Vector between atoms 12 and 10

# Compute auto-correlation
analyze timecorr vec1 v1 out v1.auto.dat ptrajformat

# Compute cross-correlation
analyze timecorr vec1 v1 vec2 v2 out v1v2.cross.dat ptrajformat

# Extract correlation time from decay
```

Sources: [test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh#L8-L17)

### Dipole Correlation for Spectroscopy

Analysis pipeline for predicting IR spectra from dipole moment correlations:

```cpp
# Define dipole vectors
vector v3 @14 @15
vector v4 @38 @39

# Compute dipole correlation
analyze timecorr vec1 v3 vec2 v4 dplr out tz2.2.3.cross.dat ptrajformat name dv3v4

# Extract correlation components
create dv3v4.dat dv3v4[R] dv3v4[RRIG] dv3v4[R3] dv3v4[R6] dv3v4[Name]
```

The output file `dv3v4.dat` contains multiple correlation quantities that can be Fourier transformed externally to obtain the IR spectrum.

Sources: [test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh#L27-L29)

### Multi-Dataset Cross-Correlation

Analysis of coupled geometric motions across multiple distance metrics:

```cpp
# Calculate distances
distance d1-13 :1 :13
distance d3-11 :3 :11
distance d5-9  :5 :9

# Compute cross-correlation matrix
crosscorr name CC d1-13 d3-11 d5-9 out cc.gnu
```

The output provides the cross-correlation matrix showing temporal relationships between all specified geometric variables.

Sources: [test/Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_CrossCorr/RunTest.sh#L12-L16)

## Output Format and Interpretation

### Time-Correlation Output Format

Time-correlation functions are typically output in two-column format:

```
# Frame   Correlation
0         1.0000
1         0.9523
2         0.8876
...
```

The first column represents time lag (in frames or time units), while the second column contains the correlation value. Normalization ensures C(0) = 1 for auto-correlations of unit vectors.

Sources: [test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Timecorr/RunTest.sh#L32-L40)

### Spectral Output Format

FFT output typically follows Grace/AGR format with frequency and magnitude/power columns:

```
@    title "FFT Spectrum"
@    xaxis  label "Frequency (cm^-1)"
@    yaxis  label "Intensity"
0.0    0.000
10.5   0.234
21.0   1.567
...
```

Frequency units depend on the input time step dt and any unit conversion applied.

Sources: [test/Test_FFT/RunTest.sh](test/Test_FFT/RunTest.sh#L6-L27)

> [!TIP]
> For accurate IR spectra from dipole correlations, ensure sufficient sampling time (at least 10× the longest correlation time of interest) and use a time step shorter than the fastest vibration period (typically <10 fs for molecular vibrations). The total trajectory length determines frequency resolution, while dt determines the maximum detectable frequency.

## Integration with Other Analysis Methods

Time-correlation and spectral analysis complement other dynamic analysis techniques in CPPTRAJ:

- **[Principal Component Analysis (PCA)](13-principal-component-analysis-pca)**: Identify collective modes whose time autocorrelation reveals relaxation timescales
- **[RMSD and RMSF Calculations](10-rmsd-and-rmsf-calculations)**: Correlate structural fluctuations with functional motions
- **[Diffusion Coefficients](26-diffusion-coefficients)**: Velocity autocorrelation functions provide alternative diffusion coefficient calculations
- **[Wavelet Analysis](25-wavelet-analysis)**: Time-frequency representations for non-stationary dynamics

These combined approaches provide comprehensive understanding of molecular dynamics across temporal and frequency domains.

## Performance Considerations

> [!TIP]
> FFT calculations benefit significantly from FFTW optimization. Configure CPPTRAJ with FFTW support (`-fftw3`) and enable FFTW wisdom files for production runs to achieve optimal performance. For time-correlation calculations, the computational cost scales as O(N²) with trajectory length N, so consider using trajectory subsets or appropriate frame skipping for exploratory analysis.

Parallelization options include:
- **OpenMP**: Enable with `-openmp` configure flag for multi-threaded FFT operations
- **MPI**: Useful for analyzing multiple trajectories or large ensemble data in parallel

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L60-L75), [configure](configure#L52-L54)

## Next Steps

For deeper exploration of dynamic analysis capabilities:

- **[Correlation Functions (Auto-correlation, Cross-correlation)](12-correlation-functions-auto-correlation-cross-correlation)**: Fundamental correlation theory and applications
- **[Normal Mode Analysis and Eigenmode Calculations](24-normal-mode-analysis-and-eigenmode-calculations)**: Frequency-domain analysis from harmonic approximations
- **[Wavelet Analysis](25-wavelet-analysis)**: Time-frequency analysis for non-stationary signals
- **[Ensemble Analysis (REMD, MREMD, HREMD)](27-ensemble-analysis-remd-mremd-hremd)**: Enhanced sampling and temperature-dependent dynamics

Time-correlation functions and spectral analysis provide powerful tools for extracting quantitative dynamical information from molecular dynamics simulations, bridging the gap between atomic-level motions and experimental observables.

# Hydrogen Bond Analysis



Hydrogen bond analysis in cpptraj provides comprehensive capabilities for detecting, quantifying, and characterizing hydrogen bonds in molecular dynamics trajectories. This analysis supports both solute-solute and solute-solvent hydrogen bonds, with options for geometric criteria, periodic imaging, and time-resolved statistics.

## Overview

The hydrogen bond analysis module identifies hydrogen bonds based on geometric criteria involving donor-hydrogen-acceptor distances and angles. The analysis can be performed on different atom selections through mask expressions and supports various output formats including time series, averages, matrices, and lifetime statistics. The module integrates seamlessly with [Atom Selection and Mask Expressions](6-atom-selection-and-mask-expressions) for flexible atom specification and [Periodic Boundary Conditions and Imaging](9-periodic-boundary-conditions-and-imaging) for systems with periodic boundaries.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B[Hbond Analysis Module]
    B --> C{Donor/Acceptor Selection}
    C --> D[Distance Check]
    C --> E[Angle Check]
    D --> F[Geometry Criteria Satisfied?]
    E --> F
    F -->|Yes| G[Record Hbond]
    F -->|No| H[Skip]
    G --> I[Output Generation]
    I --> J[Summary Statistics]
    I --> K[Time Series]
    I --> L[Matrix Output]
    I --> M[Lifetime Analysis]
```

The hydrogen bond detection process applies geometric criteria to donor-hydrogen-acceptor triplets, where donor atoms are typically electronegative atoms (N, O) with attached hydrogen atoms, and acceptor atoms are electronegative atoms capable of accepting hydrogen bonds. The detection algorithm can operate with or without periodic imaging, handles intramolecular filtering, and generates multiple output formats simultaneously.

## Core Concepts

### Geometric Criteria

Hydrogen bonds are identified using distance and angle cutoffs. The default distance cutoff is 3.0 Å between donor and acceptor atoms, and the default angle cutoff is 135° for the donor-hydrogen-acceptor angle. These parameters can be adjusted using the `dist` and `angle` keywords. Setting angle to -1.0 disables the angle check, allowing purely distance-based hydrogen bond detection.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L165-L169)

### Donor and Acceptor Masks

The flexibility of hydrogen bond analysis stems from mask-based atom selection. Three types of masks control which atoms participate:

- **donormask**: Specifies potential donor atoms and optionally their attached hydrogens
- **acceptormask**: Specifies potential acceptor atoms
- **donorhmask**: Explicitly specifies which hydrogen atoms belong to donors

These masks can use any valid mask expression, enabling precise control over which atoms are considered in the analysis.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L147-L152)

## Basic Usage

### Simple Solute-Solute Analysis

For analyzing hydrogen bonds within a solute, specify donor and acceptor masks along with output options:

```
hbond HB @N,H,C,O out nhb.dat avgout avghb.dat
```

This command uses nitrogen, hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen atoms, writes detailed bond information to `nhb.dat`, and generates average statistics to `avghb.dat`. The analysis automatically detects donor-acceptor pairs without needing explicit donor/acceptor specification when using common element masks.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L17-L26)

### Solute-Solvent Hydrogen Bonds

For analyzing interactions between solute and solvent, use separate specifications for solute atoms and solvent atoms:

```
hbond hb :1-13 solventacceptor :WAT@O solventdonor :WAT \
      out solvhb.dat avgout solvavg.dat solvout solvavg.dat bridgeout solvavg.dat
```

The `solventacceptor` and `solventdonor` keywords define which atoms in the solvent can act as acceptors and donors. This example analyzes residues 1-13 with water oxygen as solvent acceptors and water as solvent donors.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L46-L52)

### Explicit Donor Mask Specification

When you need precise control over donor selection, explicitly specify the donor mask:

```
hbond UDmask donormask @N= avgout ud.dat
```

This uses nitrogen atoms with single bonds as donors. For specifying which hydrogens belong to donors:

```
hbond UHmask donormask @N&!:PRO,NHE donorhmask @H avgout uh.dat
```

This selects nitrogen atoms excluding PRO and NHE residues, with hydrogen atoms specified via `donorhmask`.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L147-L152)

## Advanced Features

### Time Series Output

The `series` keyword enables recording hydrogen bond presence/absence for each frame, producing time-resolved data suitable for subsequent analysis:

```
hbond BB @N,H,C,O series out nbb.dat
write solutehb.agr BB[solutehb] sort
```

The series data can be extracted and written to Grace (.agr) format files. Series output is required for lifetime analysis and other time-dependent statistics.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L17-L32)

### Lifetime Analysis

After generating series data, perform lifetime analysis to understand hydrogen bond persistence:

```
runanalysis lifetime BB[solutehb] out lifehb.gnu window 10
```

This analyzes hydrogen bond lifetimes using a 10-frame window and outputs results to GNUplot format. The analysis provides average, maximum, and cumulative distribution of hydrogen bond lifetimes.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L33-L34)

### Matrix Output

Residue-residue hydrogen bond matrices provide overview of hydrogen bond patterns across the system:

```
hbond BB @N,H,C,O uuresmatrix uuresmatrixout uumatrix.nonorm.dat uuresmatrixnorm none
```

The `uuresmatrix` keyword generates a matrix showing hydrogen bond frequency between residue pairs. Normalization options include `none` (raw counts) or `frames` (normalized by number of frames).

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond_Matrix/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond_Matrix/RunTest.sh#L16-L24)

> [!TIP]
> Matrix output provides a concise overview of hydrogen bond networks but requires careful interpretation—the values represent cumulative counts across all frames, making it essential to normalize by frame count for meaningful comparison between trajectories of different lengths.

### Imaging Support

For periodic systems, hydrogen bonds should be detected using minimum image distances:

```
hbond donormask :3@ND2 acceptormask :1@O avgout hb1.dat image
```

The `image` keyword ensures that distances are calculated using the minimum image convention, correctly identifying hydrogen bonds across periodic boundaries.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L54-L56)

### Intramolecular Filtering

By default, hydrogen bonds within the same molecule are included. Use `nointramol` to filter these out:

```
hbond NoIntraMol out hbond.mol.dat nointramol avgout mol.avg.dat
```

This is particularly useful when analyzing solute-solvent interactions where you want to exclude internal hydrogen bonds from the count.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L107-L111)

### Bridge Analysis

Bridge analysis identifies solvent molecules that form hydrogen bonds with both donor and acceptor groups, effectively bridging them:

```
hbond hb :1-60 solventacceptor :WAT@O solventdonor :WAT \
      out bridgeintermol.dat avgout avgbridgeintermol.dat \
      nointramol image
```

The `bridgeout` keyword generates statistics on bridging solvent molecules, providing insight into water-mediated interactions.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L168-L172)

## Output Types

| Keyword | Description | Typical Content |
|---------|-------------|-----------------|
| `out` | Detailed per-frame hydrogen bond listing | Frame, donor, acceptor, distance, angle |
| `avgout` | Average statistics across trajectory | Donor-acceptor pairs, frequency, average geometry |
| `solvout` | Solute-solvent hydrogen bond summary | Solvent donors/acceptors, interaction counts |
| `bridgeout` | Bridging molecule analysis | Bridge counts, participating solvent molecules |
| `series` | Time series data | Presence/absence for each frame (used for further analysis) |

## Customization Parameters

### Distance Cutoff

Control the maximum donor-acceptor distance for hydrogen bond identification:

```
hbond BB donormask :2-6@N acceptormask :9-13@O dist 2.9 avgout noacut.dat
```

This reduces the distance cutoff to 2.9 Å from the default 3.0 Å.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L159-L163)

### Angle Cutoff

Specify the minimum donor-hydrogen-acceptor angle:

```
hbond BB donormask :2-6@N acceptormask :9-13@O angle 150.0 avgout results.dat
```

This increases the angle cutoff to 150°, requiring more linear geometry. Use `angle -1.0` to disable angle checking entirely.

### Disk Caching

For large trajectories with many hydrogen bond evaluations, enable disk caching to reduce memory usage:

```
usediskcache on
hbond BB @N,H,C,O series
```

This writes intermediate results to disk instead of keeping them in memory, useful when analyzing very large systems or long trajectories.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L37-L45)

## Common Patterns

### Protein Backbone Hydrogen Bonds

Analyze secondary structure hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms:

```
hbond BB @N,H,C,O series avgout hbavg.dat printatomnum
```

The `printatomnum` option includes atom numbers in the output, making it easier to identify specific hydrogen bonds. Using `@N,H,C,O` selects all backbone atoms involved in hydrogen bonding.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L20-L21)

### Ligand Binding Site Analysis

Focus hydrogen bond analysis on specific regions:

```
hbond SiteHB donormask :LIG@N,O acceptormask :10-25@O,N avgout site_hb.dat
```

This analyzes hydrogen bonds between ligand donor/acceptor atoms and receptor residues 10-25.

### Water-Mediated Interactions

Identify water molecules that connect two regions of a molecule:

```
hbond BridgeHB :1-30 solventacceptor :WAT@O solventdonor :WAT \
      bridgeout water_bridge.dat nointramol image
```

The `bridgeout` file will list water molecules that simultaneously form hydrogen bonds with both region 1-30 and other parts of the system.

Sources: [test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Hbond/RunTest.sh#L168-L172)

> [!TIP]
> When combining hydrogen bond analysis with imaging, ensure that your system is properly centered and imaged before the hydrogen bond command. Use the `center` and `image` commands prior to `hbond` for accurate distance calculations across periodic boundaries.

## Performance Considerations

For large systems with many potential donor-acceptor pairs, hydrogen bond analysis can be computationally intensive. Consider these optimizations:

- Use specific masks rather than broad element selections to reduce the number of pairs evaluated
- Enable disk caching (`usediskcache on`) for trajectories with many frames
- For solute-solvent analysis, use `nointramol` to filter out irrelevant intramolecular pairs
- Consider reducing trajectory resolution with appropriate [Trajectory Processing Pipeline](7-trajectory-processing-pipeline) techniques if time resolution is not critical for your hydrogen bond analysis

## Integration with Other Analyses

Hydrogen bond analysis often complements other structural analyses:

- Combine with [Secondary Structure Assignment (DSSP)](16-secondary-structure-assignment-dssp) to correlate hydrogen bond patterns with secondary structure
- Use alongside [Clustering Algorithms](17-clustering-algorithms-k-means-dbscan-hierarchical) to understand hydrogen bond patterns in different conformational states
- Correlate hydrogen bond lifetimes with [Principal Component Analysis (PCA)](13-principal-component-analysis-pca) modes to identify hydrogen bonds associated with major motions

## Next Steps

After mastering hydrogen bond analysis, explore these related topics:

- [Contact Analysis and Native Contacts](18-contact-analysis-and-native-contacts) for broader interaction analysis
- [Grid and Density Calculations](19-grid-and-density-calculations) for spatial distribution of hydrogen bonding partners
- [Lipid Order Parameters](22-lipid-order-parameters) for membrane systems where hydrogen bonding patterns differ from aqueous environments

# Secondary Structure Assignment (DSSP)



## Overview

Secondary Structure Assignment in CPPTRAJ implements the DSSP (Dictionary of Secondary Structure of Proteins) algorithm, a widely adopted method for identifying regular secondary structure elements in protein conformations. This analysis calculates hydrogen bond patterns and backbone dihedral angles to classify each residue into standard structural categories including alpha-helices, beta-sheets, and turns. CPPTRAJ's implementation provides multiple output formats, per-frame assignment tracking, and statistical summarization capabilities suitable for analyzing structural evolution during molecular dynamics simulations.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L1-L86)

## DSSP Architecture

The DSSP action integrates into CPPTRAJ's action framework, processing trajectory frames sequentially to assign secondary structure based on geometric criteria. The core algorithm examines hydrogen bond patterns between backbone C=O and N-H groups, calculates backbone dihedral angles (φ and ψ), and applies classification rules according to the original Kabsch and Sander method. The implementation supports both per-residue assignments and aggregate statistics across the entire trajectory.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B[Load Frame Coordinates]
    B --> C[Calculate Backbone Dihedrals<br/>φ and ψ angles]
    C --> D[Identify Hydrogen Bonds<br/>C=O ··· H-N]
    D --> E[Apply DSSP Classification Rules]
    E --> F[Assign Secondary Structure<br/>Code per Residue]
    F --> G{Output Options}
    G --> H[Per-Frame Assignment]
    G --> I[Summary Statistics]
    G --> J[Aggregate Data]
    H --> K[Write to Output File]
    I --> K
    J --> K
    K --> L[Next Frame]
    L --> B
```

The DSSP processor operates on the backbone atoms (N, CA, C, O) of each residue, with hydrogen atoms calculated or reconstructed when not present in the structure. The algorithm applies energy-based hydrogen bond criteria and geometric constraints to determine the optimal assignment for each residue position.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L14-L24)

## Secondary Structure Codes

CPPTRAJ's DSSP implementation uses single-character codes consistent with the original DSSP convention, representing distinct structural motifs:

| Code | Structure Name | Description |
|------|---------------|-------------|
| H | α-helix | Right-handed α-helix (i→i+4 hydrogen bonding) |
| B | β-bridge | Isolated β-bridge (single residue pair) |
| E | Extended strand | Extended β-sheet conformation |
| G | 3₁₀-helix | 3₁₀-helix (i→i+3 hydrogen bonding) |
| I | π-helix | π-helix (i→i+5 hydrogen bonding) |
| T | Turn | Turn conformation |
| S | Bend | Bend conformation |
| 0 | Coil | Loop/irregular conformation |

Additional non-standard codes may appear for special cases or terminal residues. The zero ('0') designation indicates regions that do not meet criteria for regular secondary structure elements.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/dssp.dat.save](test/Test_DSSP/dssp.dat.save#L1-L30)

## Command Syntax

The DSSP functionality is invoked using the `secstruct` or `dssp` commands, both being interchangeable aliases. The basic syntax allows specification of atom selections through mask expressions and multiple output file options for different analysis needs.

```
secstruct [<mask>] [keywords]
dssp [<mask>] [keywords]
```

The mask parameter enables selective analysis of specific residues or regions within the protein structure. When no mask is specified, all protein residues in the system are analyzed by default.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L14-L24), [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L27-L31)

## Output Format Options

CPPTRAJ provides flexible output formatting for DSSP analysis, supporting multiple file types and data organization schemes to accommodate different downstream analysis workflows.

### GNU Format (Default)

The default GNU-style output format produces a multi-column table with frame numbers in the first column and subsequent columns representing each residue's secondary structure assignment. This format facilitates direct visualization of structural transitions over time.

| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `out <filename>` | Output file in GNU format (default) |
| `sumout <filename>` | Summary statistics file in Grace format |
| `totalout <filename>` | Aggregate totals per structure type |

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L14-L18)

### Ptraj Format

The ptraj-compatible format provides backward compatibility with earlier analysis scripts, using a similar tabular structure but with legacy formatting conventions.

| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `ptrajformat` | Generate output in ptraj-compatible format |
| `out <filename>` | Output file in ptraj format |

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L27-L31)

## Advanced Options

Several control parameters modify the DSSP calculation behavior and output content, enabling customized analysis for specific research questions.

| Option | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `betadetail` | Include detailed β-sheet analysis including bridge types and partner residues |
| `nostring` | Suppress string formatting in output (numeric codes only) |
| `assignout <filename>` | Write detailed assignment information including per-residue classification data |
| `sumout <filename>` | Generate summary statistics showing percentage occupancy of each secondary structure type |
| `totalout <filename>` | Aggregate count of each secondary structure type across all frames |

The `betadetail` option is particularly valuable for studying β-sheet formation and stability, providing information about β-bridge classification (parallel vs. antiparallel) and the specific residues involved in each sheet pairing.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L14-L18), [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L38-L44)

## Workflow Integration

The DSSP analysis integrates seamlessly into CPPTRAJ's trajectory processing pipeline, allowing combination with other structural analysis commands for comprehensive characterization of protein dynamics.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B[Parameter File]
    B --> C[secstruct Command]
    C --> D[DSSP Analysis]
    D --> E[Output Files]
    E --> F[Visualization]
    E --> G[Statistical Analysis]
    E --> H[Further Processing]
    
    I[Preprocessing<br/>Image / Center] --> C
    J[Other Analyses<br/>RMSD / H-bond] --> C
    C --> K[Post-processing<br/>Clustering / PCA]
```

> [!TIP]
> The DSSP calculation is performed on each frame independently, making it well-suited for parallel processing. When using MPI parallelization, the trajectory analysis distributes frames across processes and combines results, maintaining consistent secondary structure assignment criteria across all processes.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L35-L44), [README.md](README.md#L1-L100)

## Practical Examples

### Basic Analysis

This example performs DSSP analysis on a protein trajectory, generating standard output files for structural assignment and summary statistics.

```
parm protein.parm7
trajin trajectory.nc
secstruct out dssp.gnu sumout dssp.sum.agr totalout total.agr betadetail
run
```

This produces three output files: `dssp.gnu` containing per-frame assignments, `dssp.sum.agr` with statistical summary in Grace format, and `total.agr` showing aggregate counts of each secondary structure type.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L14-L18)

### Region-Specific Analysis

Analyzing specific regions of interest using mask selection enables focused examination of structural dynamics in particular domains or loops.

```
parm protein.parm7
trajin trajectory.nc
secstruct :10-22 out dssp.dat ptrajformat betadetail
run
```

This configuration restricts analysis to residues 10-22 (using Amber mask syntax), generating output in ptraj format with detailed β-sheet information.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L27-L31)

### Multi-Trajectory Analysis

The DSSP command handles trajectories with varying numbers of residues, enabling analysis of concatenated simulations or systems with structural modifications.

```
parm structure1.parm7
trajin traj1.nc parmindex 1
trajin traj2.nc
secstruct out dssp2.gnu sumout dssp2.sum.agr nostring betadetail
run
```

> [!TIP]
> When analyzing multiple trajectories with different residue counts, ensure that residue numbering is consistent or use appropriate masking to maintain correct correspondence across frames.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L35-L44)

### Assignment Output

The `assignout` option generates detailed per-residue assignment information, useful for scripting and further processing.

```
parm protein.pdb
trajin protein.pdb
dssp :1-100 assignout assign.dat betadetail
run
```

This produces a comprehensive assignment file containing detailed secondary structure classification for residues 1-100, including β-sheet bridge details and hydrogen bond information.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L52-L57)

## Output Interpretation

### Per-Frame Assignment Format

The standard output format displays frames as rows and residues as columns, using single-character codes to represent secondary structure assignments. The first column contains the frame number, and column headers identify each residue by name and number.

```
#Frame   THR:10 TYR:11 THR:12 GLU:13 VAL:14 PRO:15 GLY:16 LYS:17 LYS:18 ILE:19 LEU:20 GLN:21 NHE:22
       1      0      B      B      B      B      T      T      B      B      B      B      0      0
       2      B      B      B      B      B      T      T      B      B      B      B      B      0
       3      0      B      B      B      B      T      T      B      B      B      B      0      0
```

In this example, residue 15 (PRO) shows turn conformation (T) across multiple frames, while residues 11-14 exhibit β-bridge (B) characteristics. Terminal residues often show coil (0) assignments due to missing hydrogen bond partners.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/dssp.dat.save](test/Test_DSSP/dssp.dat.save#L1-L4)

### Summary Statistics

The summary output provides percentage occupancy of each secondary structure type across the entire trajectory, enabling quantitative comparison of structural propensities between systems or conditions.

| Structure | Percentage | Interpretation |
|-----------|------------|----------------|
| H | 45.2% | High α-helical content |
| E | 12.8% | Moderate β-sheet content |
| T | 8.3% | Turn regions |
| 0 | 33.7% | Unstructured regions |

These statistics facilitate comparison between mutant variants, different force fields, or varying environmental conditions.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/dssp.dat.sum.save](test/Test_DSSP/dssp.dat.sum.save)

## Performance Considerations

The DSSP algorithm scales linearly with the number of residues in the system, making it suitable for analysis of large protein complexes. Computational efficiency is achieved through optimized hydrogen bond calculation and the use of pre-computed dihedral angles. For very large systems or extensive trajectory analysis, the calculation benefits significantly from OpenMP multi-threading when available.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L100-L150)

## Integration with Complementary Analyses

DSSP analysis provides valuable context for other structural analyses in CPPTRAJ. Secondary structure assignments can be used to:

- Correlate structural transitions with [RMSD and RMSF calculations](10-rmsd-and-rmsf-calculations) to identify regions of increased flexibility
- Investigate relationships between secondary structure and [hydrogen bond patterns](15-hydrogen-bond-analysis)
- Analyze structural transitions in [cluster analysis](17-clustering-algorithms-k-means-dbscan-hierarchical) to characterize conformational states
- Study structural stability in [free energy calculations](21-free-energy-calculations-ti-mm-pbsa)

The modular nature of CPPTRAJ's command syntax allows straightforward combination of DSSP with these complementary analyses, enabling comprehensive investigation of protein structure-dynamics relationships.

Sources: [test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh](test/Test_DSSP/RunTest.sh#L1-L86)

## Limitations and Considerations

The DSSP algorithm has inherent limitations that users should consider when interpreting results:

- **Terminal Residues**: Chain termini often show ambiguous assignments due to missing hydrogen bond partners
- **Hydrogen Requirement**: Proper hydrogen positions are critical; consider adding hydrogens if not present
- **Time Resolution**: Secondary structure classification on a per-frame basis may miss transient intermediate states
- **Proline Effects**: Proline residues cannot donate backbone amide hydrogens, affecting helix propensity
