- **Non-canonical Structures**: Novel or unusual secondary structure motifs may not fit standard classification criteria

For trajectories with high temporal resolution, consider applying temporal smoothing or using time-averaged assignments to distinguish structural transitions from thermal fluctuations.

## Next Steps

For deeper understanding of structural analysis in CPPTRAJ, explore these related documentation pages:

- [Atom Selection and Mask Expressions](6-atom-selection-and-mask-expressions) - Learn advanced mask syntax for region-specific DSSP analysis
- [Hydrogen Bond Analysis](15-hydrogen-bond-analysis) - Investigate relationship between hydrogen bonds and secondary structure
- [RMSD and RMSF Calculations](10-rmsd-and-rmsf-calculations) - Quantify structural stability and identify flexible regions
- [Clustering Algorithms](17-clustering-algorithms-k-means-dbscan-hierarchical) - Identify and characterize distinct conformational states
- [Basic Command Line Usage](4-basic-command-line-usage) - Review fundamental CPPTRAJ command syntax and workflow

For comprehensive trajectory processing techniques, refer to [Trajectory Processing Pipeline](7-trajectory-processing-pipeline) documentation.


# Clustering Algorithms (K-means, DBSCAN, Hierarchical)



This documentation provides an in-depth exploration of the three primary clustering algorithms implemented in Amber-MD/cpptraj: K-means, DBSCAN, and Hierarchical Agglomerative clustering. These algorithms enable systematic analysis of molecular dynamics trajectories by grouping similar conformations based on specified distance metrics, revealing dominant structural states and transition pathways in biomolecular systems.

## Architecture Overview

The clustering framework is built upon an object-oriented design where all algorithms inherit from the abstract base class `Algorithm`, which defines a consistent interface for clustering operations. This architecture ensures algorithm interoperability with the broader trajectory analysis pipeline and supports seamless integration with various distance metrics and output formats.

The base algorithm interface defines five core methods that all clustering implementations must provide: `Setup()` for parameter configuration, `Info()` for algorithm status reporting, `Results()` for output file generation, `DoClustering()` for the core clustering logic, and `Timing()` for performance profiling [Algorithm.h](src/Cluster/Algorithm.h#L19-L28).

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Algorithm {
        <<abstract>>
        +Setup(ArgList&) int
        +Info() void
        +Results(CpptrajFile&) void
        +DoClustering(List&, Cframes, MetricArray&) int
        +Timing(double) void
        +ClusterDistance(Node, Node, MetricArray, bool, vector~bool~) double
        +Epsilon() double
        -AType type_
        -int debug_
    }
    
    class Algorithm_Kmeans {
        -int nclusters_
        -int kseed_
        -int maxIt_
        -KmeansModeType mode_
        -bool clusterToClusterCentroid_
        +DoClustering(List&, Cframes, MetricArray&) int
    }
    
    class Algorithm_DBscan {
        -int minPoints_
        -double epsilon_
        -Iarray Status_
        -Range kdist_
        +DoClustering(List&, Cframes, MetricArray&) int
        +ExpandCluster(Cframes, MetricArray, unsigned int, int) bool
    }
    
    class Algorithm_HierAgglo {
        -int nclusters_
        -double epsilon_
        -LINKAGETYPE linkage_
        -DynamicMatrix ClusterDistances_
        +DoClustering(List&, Cframes, MetricArray&) int
        +MergeClosest(List&, MetricArray&) int
    }
    
    Algorithm <|-- Algorithm_Kmeans
    Algorithm <|-- Algorithm_DBscan
    Algorithm <|-- Algorithm_HierAgglo
```

## Distance Metrics Framework

Before examining specific clustering algorithms, it is essential to understand the distance metric system that quantifies similarity between molecular conformations. The framework supports multiple distance calculation methods through the abstract `Metric` class, enabling algorithm-agnostic similarity measurements.

Available distance metrics include RMS (Root Mean Square Deviation), DME (Distance Matrix Error), SRMSD (Symmetry-corrected RMSD), SCALAR (for scalar properties), TORSION (for dihedral angles), MATRIX2D (pre-computed distance matrices), and QRMSD (Quaternion-based RMSD) [Metric.h](src/Cluster/Metric.h#L17).

Each metric implements methods for calculating distances between frames, between centroids, and between frames and centroids, along with centroid calculation and update operations. This modular design allows any clustering algorithm to work with any supported distance metric without algorithm modification.

## K-means Clustering

K-means clustering partitions trajectory frames into a predefined number of clusters by iteratively minimizing the within-cluster variance. The algorithm follows a centroid-based partitioning approach where each frame is assigned to the nearest cluster centroid, and centroids are updated to reflect the mean position of their assigned frames.

### Algorithm Implementation

The K-means implementation in cpptraj offers two operational modes: SEQUENTIAL and RANDOM point processing. In SEQUENTIAL mode, the algorithm processes frames in order, while RANDOM mode processes frames in a randomized sequence determined by a seed value [Algorithm_Kmeans.h](src/Cluster/Algorithm_Kmeans.h#L20).

The clustering process begins with seed selection, which can be derived from existing clusters or randomly chosen from the frame set. Seed frames become initial centroids for the target number of clusters [Algorithm_Kmeans.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_Kmeans.cpp#L88-L97).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start K-means] --> B{Initial Clusters?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Use Existing Seeds]
    B -->|No| D[Find K-means Seeds]
    D --> E[Create Seed Clusters]
    C --> F[Iteration Loop]
    E --> F
    F --> G{Sequential or Random?}
    G -->|Sequential| H[Process Points 0 to N]
    G -->|Random| H[Shuffle and Process Points]
    H --> I[Assign Points to Nearest Centroid]
    I --> J[Update Cluster Centroids]
    J --> K{Max Iterations?}
    K -->|No| F
    K -->|Yes| L[Final Clustering Output]
```

### Configuration Parameters

The K-means algorithm accepts several configuration parameters through the command-line interface:

- **clusters**: Specifies the target number of clusters (required, must be > 1) [Algorithm_Kmeans.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_Kmeans.cpp#L30-L34)
- **randompoint**: Enables random point processing mode instead of sequential processing
- **kseed**: Sets the random seed for reproducible random initialization
- **maxit**: Controls the maximum number of iterations (default: 100) [Algorithm_Kmeans.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_Kmeans.cpp#L40)

### Core Algorithm Logic

The main clustering loop iteratively processes each point, assigning it to the nearest cluster centroid based on the chosen distance metric. After all points are assigned, cluster centroids are recalculated to reflect the mean position of their constituent frames [Algorithm_Kmeans.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_Kmeans.cpp#L100-L200).

The algorithm implements a convergence criterion based on centroid stability and the maximum iteration limit. The iterative assignment-update cycle continues until convergence or the maximum iteration count is reached, ensuring computational efficiency while maintaining cluster quality.

> [!TIP]
> K-means is particularly effective when the number of clusters is known a priori and clusters are expected to be roughly spherical in the chosen distance space. For molecular dynamics data, this often works well when analyzing well-defined conformational states with clear boundaries.

## DBSCAN Clustering

DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) is a density-based algorithm that identifies clusters as regions of high point density separated by regions of low density. Unlike K-means, DBSCAN does not require specifying the number of clusters in advance and can automatically identify noise points that do not belong to any meaningful cluster.

### Algorithm Principles

DBSCAN operates on two fundamental parameters: epsilon (ε), which defines the neighborhood radius, and minPoints, which specifies the minimum number of points required to form a dense region [Algorithm_DBscan.h](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.h#L33-L34).

The algorithm classifies points into three categories: core points (with at least minPoints within ε), border points (within ε of a core point but with fewer than minPoints neighbors), and noise points (neither core nor border) [Metric.h](src/Cluster/Metric.h#L9-L12).

### Implementation Architecture

The cpptraj implementation follows the canonical DBSCAN algorithm with optimizations for trajectory data. The core clustering process iterates through unclassified points and attempts to expand clusters from each point using the `ExpandCluster` method [Algorithm_DBscan.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.cpp#L132).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start DBSCAN] --> B[Set All Points UNCLASSIFIED]
    B --> C[For Each Point P]
    C --> D{P UNCLASSIFIED?}
    D -->|No| C
    D -->|Yes| E[Region Query for P]
    E --> F{Neighbors >= minPoints?}
    F -->|No| G[Mark P as NOISE]
    F -->|Yes| H[Create New Cluster C]
    H --> I[Expand Cluster C]
    I --> J[Process Seed Points]
    J --> K{More Seeds?}
    K -->|Yes| E
    K -->|No| C
    G --> C
```

### K-Distance Analysis

A distinctive feature of the cpptraj DBSCAN implementation is the K-distance calculation utility, which helps users determine appropriate epsilon values. The K-distance for a point is defined as the distance to its K-th nearest neighbor, and plotting K-distance values sorted in descending order often reveals a "knee" point that suggests a suitable epsilon value [Algorithm_DBscan.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.cpp#L27-L28).

The implementation supports calculating K-distance functions for multiple K values, enabling systematic parameter exploration [Algorithm_DBscan.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.cpp#L86-L91).

### Configuration Parameters

DBSCAN configuration parameters include:

- **minpoints**: Minimum number of points required to form a cluster (required, must be ≥ 1) [Algorithm_DBscan.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.cpp#L35-L40)
- **epsilon**: Distance criterion for cluster formation (required, must be > 0.0) [Algorithm_DBscan.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.cpp#L41-L46)
- **kdist**: Computes K-distance graphs for specified K values instead of performing clustering
- **kfile**: Specifies output file prefix for K-distance data [Algorithm_DBscan.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.cpp#L51-L55)

### Region Query Optimization

The `RegionQuery` method efficiently retrieves all points within epsilon distance of a query point, forming the foundation for both core point identification and cluster expansion [Algorithm_DBscan.h](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.h#L26).

The algorithm supports existing cluster integration, allowing incremental clustering on new trajectory segments while preserving previous cluster assignments [Algorithm_DBscan.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.cpp#L98-L122).

> [!TIP]
> DBSCAN excels at identifying clusters of arbitrary shapes and automatically detecting noise, making it ideal for analyzing molecular dynamics data where conformational states may have irregular boundaries or where transient states should be treated as noise rather than forced into clusters.

## Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering

Hierarchical agglomerative clustering builds a cluster hierarchy by iteratively merging the closest pairs of clusters, starting with each frame in its own cluster. This approach produces a dendrogram that reveals the hierarchical relationship between conformations at multiple resolution levels.

### Algorithm Structure

The hierarchical implementation supports three linkage criteria for measuring inter-cluster distance: single-linkage (minimum distance between any pair of points), complete-linkage (maximum distance between any pair of points), and average-linkage (average distance between all point pairs) [Algorithm_HierAgglo.h](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.h#L36).

The algorithm maintains a dynamic distance matrix `ClusterDistances_` that stores pairwise distances between all clusters, enabling efficient identification of the closest cluster pair at each iteration [Algorithm_HierAgglo.h](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.h#L44).

### Clustering Process

The algorithm begins by placing each frame in its own cluster, creating initial clusters equal to the number of frames [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L79-L89).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start Hierarchical Clustering] --> B[Initialize: Each Frame = Cluster]
    B --> C[Build Distance Matrix]
    C --> D[Target Reached?]
    D -->|Yes| E[Output Final Clusters]
    D -->|No| F[Find Closest Cluster Pair]
    F --> G{Distance > Epsilon?}
    G -->|Yes| E
    G -->|No| H[Merge Closest Pair]
    H --> I[Update Distance Matrix]
    I --> D
```

After initial cluster creation, the algorithm enters the main merging loop, which identifies the closest cluster pair and merges them iteratively [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L146-L148).

### Linkage Methods

The three linkage methods produce different clustering characteristics:

- **Single-linkage**: Tends to produce elongated clusters and can suffer from chaining effects [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L128)
- **Complete-linkage**: Produces compact clusters but can be sensitive to outliers [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L129)
- **Average-linkage**: Balances single and complete linkage, often providing robust results [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L130)

The linkage type is selected through command-line arguments, with average-linkage as the default [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L31).

### Configuration Parameters

Hierarchical clustering accepts the following parameters:

- **clusters**: Target number of clusters (default: 10 if not specified) [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L26-L27)
- **epsilon**: Stopping criterion when minimum cluster distance exceeds this value [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L27)
- **linkage/averagelinkage/complete**: Selects the linkage method (default: averagelinkage) [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L28-L31)
- **epsilonplot**: Generates a file plotting epsilon versus number of clusters [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L32-L36)

### Epsilon Plot Generation

When the epsilon plot option is enabled, the algorithm records the minimum inter-cluster distance at each merge step, producing a plot that helps identify natural cluster numbers based on significant increases in merge distance [Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_HierAgglo.cpp#L32-L36).

> [!TIP]
> Hierarchical clustering with epsilon plotting provides a powerful exploratory tool for trajectory analysis, allowing researchers to identify natural clustering levels by examining the merge distance profile and selecting cutpoints that correspond to significant conformational transitions.

## Algorithm Comparison

| Feature | K-means | DBSCAN | Hierarchical |
|---------|---------|--------|--------------|
| **Cluster Count** | User-specified | Automatically determined | User-specified or epsilon-based |
| **Cluster Shape** | Spherical | Arbitrary | Depends on linkage method |
| **Noise Handling** | None (all points assigned) | Explicit noise identification | None (all points assigned) |
| **Parameter Sensitivity** | Sensitive to seed selection | Sensitive to epsilon and minPoints | Sensitive to linkage method |
| **Computational Complexity** | O(n × k × i) | O(n²) with spatial index | O(n³) naive, O(n²) with optimization |
| **Best Use Case** | Known number of states, spherical clusters | Unknown number, irregular shapes, noise detection | Multi-resolution analysis, dendrogram generation |

## Cluster Quality Metrics

Cpptraj provides multiple metrics for evaluating clustering quality, enabling quantitative comparison between different clustering parameters or algorithms.

### Silhouette Score

The silhouette score measures how similar each frame is to its own cluster compared to other clusters, providing a value between -1 (incorrect clustering) and 1 (well-clustered) [Silhouette.h](src/Cluster/Silhouette.h).

### Davies-Bouldin Index

The Davies-Bouldin Index evaluates cluster separation and compactness, with lower values indicating better clustering [DBI.h](src/Cluster/DBI.h).

### Pseudo-F Statistic

The pseudo-F statistic measures the ratio of between-cluster variance to within-cluster variance, with higher values indicating better separation [PseudoF.h](src/Cluster/PseudoF.h).

## Performance Considerations

### Sieving

All clustering algorithms support sieving, which reduces computational cost by analyzing only a subset of frames (e.g., every 10th frame) during clustering, then assigning the remaining frames to the nearest cluster [Sieve.h](src/Cluster/Sieve.h).

### Memory Management

For large trajectories, the framework supports binary matrix storage and NetCDF-based distance matrix caching to reduce memory requirements [Cmatrix_Binary.h](src/Cluster/Cmatrix_Binary.h), [Cmatrix_NC.h](src/Cluster/Cmatrix_NC.h).

### Parallel Processing

OpenMP parallelization is available in selected clustering operations, particularly in distance calculations and nearest-neighbor searches [Algorithm_DBscan.cpp](src/Cluster/Algorithm_DBscan.cpp#L12-L14).

## Integration with Trajectory Analysis Pipeline

Clustering in cpptraj is tightly integrated with the broader trajectory analysis ecosystem. Clustered frames can be extracted for further analysis, cluster representatives can be used as starting points for additional simulations, and clustering results can be visualized using trajectory output functions [Results_Coords.h](src/Cluster/Results_Coords.h).

The clustering framework supports combination with other analysis techniques such as [Principal Component Analysis (PCA)](13-principal-component-analysis-pca) for dimensionality reduction before clustering, and [RMSD/RMSF calculations](10-rmsd-and-rmsf-calculations) for understanding structural variation within and between clusters.

## Next Steps

After obtaining clustering results, consider exploring:

- **Cluster characterization**: Use [Contact Analysis and Native Contacts](18-contact-analysis-and-native-contacts) to identify key structural features differentiating clusters
- **Trajectory visualization**: Extract cluster representatives for structural visualization and analysis
- **Transition analysis**: Examine frame sequences to identify transition pathways between clusters
- **Ensemble analysis**: Apply [Ensemble Analysis (REMD, MREMD, HREMD)](27-ensemble-analysis-remd-mremd-hremd) techniques to understand cluster populations across simulation replicas

# Contact Analysis and Native Contacts



Contact analysis in CPPTRAJ provides powerful tools for quantifying atomic and residue-level interactions in molecular dynamics trajectories. This functionality enables researchers to track structural changes, identify native vs non-native contacts, and analyze interaction patterns over time. The analysis is particularly valuable for protein folding studies, ligand binding analysis, and understanding conformational transitions.

## Fundamentals of Contact Analysis

Contact analysis determines when atoms or residues are within a specified distance cutoff. The basic **contacts** command counts total contacts and native contacts relative to a reference structure, while the more advanced **nativecontacts** command provides detailed classification of native and non-native interactions with extensive output options.

The core workflow involves:
1. Selecting atom groups using mask expressions
2. Calculating distances between all atom pairs
3. Applying distance cutoff criteria to define contacts
4. Comparing against a reference structure to classify contacts as native or non-native
5. Outputting time series data, contact maps, and statistical summaries

Sources: [Test_Contacts/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Contacts/RunTest.sh#L11-L18), [Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh](test/Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh#L16-L29)

## Architecture and Data Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B[Mask Processing<br/>Atom Selection]
    C[Reference Structure] --> D[Native Contact<br/>Determination]
    B --> E[Distance Calculation<br/>Between Atom Pairs]
    E --> F{Within<br/>Cutoff?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Contact Detection]
    F -->|No| H[No Contact]
    G --> I[Contact Classification<br/>Native vs Non-native]
    D --> I
    I --> J[Output Generation<br/>Time Series, Maps, Statistics]
    J --> K[Multiple Formats<br/>.dat, .pdb, .gnu]
    
    style A fill:#e1f5ff
    style C fill:#fff4e1
    style J fill:#e8f5e9
    style K fill:#f3e5f5
```

The architecture demonstrates parallel processing capabilities where contact calculations for each frame are independent, enabling efficient OpenMP multi-threading and MPI parallelization for large-scale analyses.

## Contacts Command: Basic Contact Analysis

The `contacts` command provides fundamental contact counting with native contact classification. It calculates the number of atomic contacts within a cutoff distance and determines which of these are present in a reference structure.

### Basic Syntax

```
contacts [name <name>] [out <filename>] [first] [reference] 
         [byresidue] [<mask1>] [<mask2>]
```

### Key Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Default | Notes |
|-----------|-------------|---------|-------|
| `name <name>` | Dataset name for output | Contacts | Multiple datasets can be created |
| `out <filename>` | Output file for time series | stdout | Contains frame-by-frame contact counts |
| `first` | Use first frame as reference | false | Equivalent to explicitly specifying reference |
| `reference` | Use reference structure for native contacts | false | Classifies contacts as native or not |
| `byresidue` | Aggregate by residue instead of atom | false | Reduces output complexity |
| `<mask1>`, `<mask2>` | Atom selection masks | all atoms | Single mask = intra-group, two masks = inter-group |

### Example Usage

```
# Basic contacts counting
trajin trajectory.nc
reference trajectory.nc 1
contacts first out contacts.dat :2-12@CA

# By-residue analysis with native contact classification
contacts reference out byres.dat byresidue
```

The output includes time series data showing the number of total contacts and native contacts for each frame:

```
#time    Contacts    native Contacts 
     1.00    60    60
     2.00    56    56
     3.00    58    56
     4.00    58    56
```

Sources: [Test_Contacts/RunTest.sh](test/Test_Contacts/RunTest.sh#L11-L22), [Test_Contacts/contacts.dat.save](test/Test_Contacts/contacts.dat.save#L1-L11)

## Native Contacts Command: Advanced Analysis

The `nativecontacts` command extends basic contact analysis with comprehensive native/non-native classification, multiple output formats, and detailed statistical analysis.

### Complete Syntax

```
nativecontacts [name <name>] [<mask1>] [<mask2>] 
               [out <filename>] [mindist] [maxdist] 
               [distance <cut>] [reference] 
               [byresidue] [map] [mapout <file>] 
               [contactpdb <file>] [nncontactpdb <file>]
               [writecontacts <file>] [resout <file>]
               [series] [seriesout <file>] 
               [savenonnative] [seriesnnout <file>]
               [resseries] [present\|sum] [resseriesout <file>]
```

### Advanced Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Notes |
|-----------|-------------|-------|
| `mindist` | Output minimum contact distance | Provides distance statistics |
| `maxdist` | Output maximum contact distance | Useful for understanding interaction range |
| `distance <cut>` | Distance cutoff for contacts | Default 7.0 Å |
| `map` | Generate contact map data | Creates matrix of contact frequencies |
| `mapout <file>` | Contact map output file | GNU plot format |
| `contactpdb <file>` | Write native contacts as PDB | Visual representation |
| `nncontactpdb <file>` | Write non-native contacts as PDB | Visualize non-native interactions |
| `writecontacts <file>` | Detailed contact listing with statistics | Includes Nframes, Fraction, Avg, Stdev |
| `resout <file>` | Per-residue contact summary | Aggregated data |
| `series` | Enable time series output | Frame-by-frame contact status |
| `seriesout <file>` | Time series output file | Binary (1) or absent (0) per contact per frame |
| `savenonnative` | Track non-native contacts separately | Requires additional processing |
| `seriesnnout <file>` | Non-native contact time series | Similar to seriesout for non-native |
| `resseries` | Per-residue time series | Either 'present' or 'sum' modes |
| `present\|sum` | Residue series mode | Present = binary, Sum = count |
| `resseriesout <file>` | Residue series output file | Time-resolved residue contacts |

> [!TIP]
> The `savenonnative` option requires additional computational overhead as it must track and classify contacts throughout the trajectory. Use it only when non-native contact analysis is essential to your study.

### Advanced Examples

#### Example 1: Multi-faceted Native Contact Analysis

```
nativecontacts name NC1 :1-12@CA out nc.hp1.ca.dat mindist maxdist \
               map mapout cmap.gnu contactpdb nc1.pdb
```

Output format:
```
#Frame    NC1[native] NC1[nonnative] NC1[mindist] NC1[maxdist]
     1           31              0       3.6912      16.2018
     2           31              1       3.7418      16.3238
     3           28              1       3.7696      15.5250
```

Sources: [Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh](test/Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh#L22-L23), [Test_NativeContacts/nc.hp1.ca.dat.save](test/Test_NativeContacts/nc.hp1.ca.dat.save#L1-L11)

#### Example 2: Detailed Contact Statistics

```
nativecontacts name NC2 :10-14@CA :17-21@CA out nc.hp2.ca.dat mindist maxdist \
               writecontacts nc2.contacts.dat resout nc2.res.dat \
               series seriesout NC2.series.dat
```

Contact statistics output:
```
# Contacts: NC2
# Native contacts determined from mask ':10-14@CA' and mask ':17-21@CA'
#                     Contact  Nframes    Frac.      Avg    Stdev
    1        :13@CA_:18@CA      100        1     4.56     0.29
    2        :11@CA_:20@CA      100        1      4.6    0.232
    3        :12@CA_:19@CA      100        1     5.08    0.159
```

Time series output (binary contact states):
```
#Frame   :10@CA_:20@CA :10@CA_:21@CA :11@CA_:18@CA :11@CA_:19@CA
     1             1             1             1             1
     2             1             1             1             1
     3             0             1             1             1
```

Sources: [Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh](test/Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh#L24-L26), [Test_NativeContacts/nc2.contacts.dat.save](test/Test_NativeContacts/nc2.contacts.dat.save#L1-L13), [Test_NativeContacts/NC2.series.dat.save](test/Test_NativeContacts/NC2.series.dat.save#L1-L11)

#### Example 3: Non-Native Contact Tracking

```
nativecontacts name NC4 :1-21@CA out nc4.dat savenonnative series \
               reference seriesnnout nc4.nn.dat resout nc4.res.dat \
               writecontacts nc4.contacts.dat \
               nncontactpdb nc4.nn.pdb
```

This enables tracking of non-native contacts, which are contacts present in the trajectory but not in the reference structure. The output includes separate time series for non-native contacts.

Sources: [Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh](test/Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh#L48-L51), [Test_NativeContacts/nc4.nn.dat.save](test/Test_NativeContacts/nc4.nn.dat.save#L1-L11)

#### Example 4: Per-Residue Time Series

```
nativecontacts name NC5 :10-11@CA,N :18-20@CA,N series savenonnative \
               resseries present resseriesout NC5.respresent.dat
```

Output format for residue series:
```
#Frame   THR:10_LEU:20 TYR:11_LYS:18 TYR:11_ILE:19 TYR:11_LEU:20 nn_TYR:11_LYS:18
     1             1             1             1             1                0
     2             1             1             1             1                0
     3             0             1             1             1                0
```

Sources: [Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh](test/Test_NativeContacts/RunTest.sh#L52-L53), [Test_NativeContacts/NC5.respresent.dat.save](test/Test_NativeContacts/NC5.respresent.dat.save#L1-L11)

## Practical Applications

### Protein Folding Studies

Native contact analysis is essential for quantifying folding progress. By comparing native contacts over time, researchers can:
- Track folding pathways and intermediate states
- Identify rate-limiting steps in folding
- Calculate Q-values (fraction of native contacts formed)
- Correlate native contact formation with other structural metrics

### Ligand Binding Analysis

For ligand-receptor systems:
- Use residue-level masks to identify key binding residues
- Track formation and breaking of specific interactions
- Compare binding modes across different conditions
- Identify non-native contacts that may represent alternative binding poses

### Conformational Transitions

Contact maps and time series data reveal:
- Networks of contacts that change coordinately
- Contact switching patterns during transitions
- Intermediate states characterized by unique contact patterns
- Energy landscape exploration through contact space

> [!TIP]
> When analyzing large systems, use the `byresidue` option to reduce computational complexity and focus on residue-level interactions rather than atomic-level details, which may be more biologically meaningful for conformational analysis.

## Data Output and Interpretation

### Time Series Data

Time series outputs provide frame-by-frame tracking of contact states:
- Binary (0/1) indicates contact presence/absence
- Useful for calculating contact lifetimes and formation rates
- Can be used as input for further statistical analysis

### Contact Statistics

The `writecontacts` output provides comprehensive statistics:
- **Nframes**: Number of frames where contact exists
- **Frac.**: Fraction of trajectory with contact present
- **Avg**: Average distance during contact
- **Stdev**: Standard deviation of contact distance

### Contact Maps

Contact maps (`map` and `mapout` options) create visual representations:
- Matrix format showing contact frequencies
- Useful for identifying persistent interaction networks
- Can be plotted with external visualization tools

### PDB Outputs

Contact PDB files enable 3D visualization:
- `contactpdb`: Native contacts as connections
- `nncontactpdb`: Non-native contacts highlighted
- Load with molecular visualization software (VMD, PyMOL) for interactive exploration

## Performance Considerations

### Computational Complexity

Contact analysis scales approximately as O(n²) where n is the number of atoms in the mask. For large systems:
- Use residue-level selection (`@CA`, `byresidue`)
- Restrict mask regions to areas of interest
- Consider distance filters in mask expressions

### Parallelization

Both OpenMP and MPI parallelization are supported:
- OpenMP provides speedup for single-system analysis
- MPI enables analysis of large ensembles or trajectories
- Parallelization is most effective for long trajectories with many frames

### Memory Requirements

For series and contact map outputs:
- Memory scales with number of contacts × number of frames
- Large contact maps may require significant memory
- Consider outputting to disk incrementally for very large analyses

## Integration with Other Analyses

Contact analysis synergizes with multiple CPPTRAJ analyses:

- **[RMSD and RMSF Calculations](10-rmsd-and-rmsf-calculations)**: Correlate contact changes with structural deviation
- **[Hydrogen Bond Analysis](15-hydrogen-bond-analysis)**: Compare contact patterns with specific hydrogen bonding interactions
- **[Clustering Algorithms](17-clustering-algorithms-k-means-dbscan-hierarchical)**: Use contact patterns as clustering metrics
- **[Distance and Angle Measurements](11-distance-and-angle-measurements)**: Validate contact distances with specific measurements
- **[Principal Component Analysis (PCA)](13-principal-component-analysis-pca)**: Project contact-based dynamics onto collective coordinates

## Troubleshooting and Common Issues

### Low Contact Counts

If contact numbers seem unexpectedly low:
- Verify distance cutoff is appropriate for your system
- Check that atom masks include relevant atoms
- Ensure reference structure is properly loaded for native contacts
- Consider periodic boundary conditions and imaging

### Memory Errors

For large contact maps or time series:
- Reduce atom selection scope
- Disable unnecessary output options
- Process trajectory in chunks
- Use `byresidue` to reduce contact count

### Performance Issues

To improve analysis speed:
- Use residue-level selections when atomic detail isn't needed
- Enable parallel processing with OpenMP
- Filter trajectories to relevant frames before analysis
- Consider separate analyses for different regions of large systems

## Next Steps

For deeper understanding of molecular dynamics analysis:

- Learn about **[Atom Selection and Mask Expressions](6-atom-selection-and-mask-expressions)** to create precise atom selections for contact analysis
- Explore **[Distance and Angle Measurements](11-distance-and-angle-measurements)** for complementary geometric analysis
- Study **[Hydrogen Bond Analysis](15-hydrogen-bond-analysis)** to examine specific directional interactions
- Investigate **[Clustering Algorithms](17-clustering-algorithms-k-means-dbscan-hierarchical)** to identify conformational states based on contact patterns
- Review **[Trajectory Processing Pipeline](7-trajectory-processing-pipeline)** for integrating contact analysis into comprehensive analysis workflows

Contact analysis and native contacts provide a powerful framework for understanding molecular interactions, conformational dynamics, and structural transitions in molecular dynamics simulations.

# Grid and Density Calculations



Grid and density calculations in CPPTRAJ provide powerful spatial analysis capabilities for molecular dynamics trajectories, enabling researchers to quantify atomic distributions, solvation properties, and energy landscapes across three-dimensional grids. These calculations form the foundation for advanced analyses like Grid Inhomogeneous Solvation Theory (GIST) and volumetric mapping.

## Architectural Overview

CPPTRAJ implements grid and density calculations through a modular architecture that separates spatial discretization, coordinate mapping, and statistical aggregation. The grid system originated from PTRAJ routines adapted for CPPTRAJ, including Action_Grid and GridAction classes, with significant enhancements for parallel processing and flexible output formats [README.md](README.md#L148-L153).

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Input
        A[Trajectory Frames]
        B[Topology/Parameters]
        C[User Masks]
    end
    
    subgrid GridSystem
        D[Grid Generation]
        E[Spatial Binning]
        F[Coordinate Mapping]
        G[Accumulation]
    end
    
    subgrid DensityTypes
        H[Number Density]
        I[Mass Density]
        J[Charge Density]
        K[Electron Density]
    end
    
    subgrid Output
        L[OpenDX Format]
        M[Xplor Format]
        N[ASCII Data]
        O[PDB Visualization]
    end
    
    A --> D
    B --> D
    C --> F
    D --> E
    E --> F
    F --> G
    G --> H
    G --> I
    G --> J
    G --> K
    H --> L
    I --> M
    J --> N
    K --> O
```

The grid system supports multiple density modes (number, mass, charge, electron) and various output formats optimized for different visualization tools [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Density/RunTest.sh#L27-L34).

## Grid Generation and Configuration

Grid generation in CPPTRAJ involves defining a three-dimensional grid that spans the simulation box or a user-defined region. The grid parameters specify spatial resolution and extent through bin counts and spacing, with support for both orthogonal and non-orthogonal simulation boxes.

### Basic Grid Configuration

The fundamental grid command requires specifying output filename and grid dimensions using six parameters (three dimensions with alternating bin count and spacing values):

```bash
grid <output> <nx> <dx> <ny> <dy> <nz> <dz> <mask>
```

For example, to create a 40×40×40 grid with 0.5 Å spacing centered on water oxygen atoms:
```bash
grid out.dx 20 0.5 20 0.5 20 0.5 :WAT@O
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L22-L23)

The grid system accumulates atom occurrences across frames, enabling density calculations that reflect temporal averaging and ensemble statistics.

### Grid Centering Options

CPPTRAJ provides multiple centering strategies to position the grid relative to molecular features:

**Box Center**: Centers the grid on the simulation box boundaries, ideal for bulk solvent analysis:
```bash
grid box.dx 30 0.5 30 0.5 30 0.5 box :WAT
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L52-L53)

**Mask Center**: Positions the grid based on the geometric center of selected atoms, allowing targeted analysis around specific molecular regions:
```bash
grid mask.dx 30 0.5 30 0.5 30 0.5 center :1-12@CA :WAT
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L59-L60)

**Explicit Center**: Specifies exact coordinates for grid origin using the gridcenter keyword:
```bash
grid test.dx 34 0.5 44 0.5 36 0.5 gridcenter 1.5 1.0 0.0 :WAT
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L46-L47)

> [!TIP]
> When analyzing solvation shells around biomolecules, use mask-based centering with appropriate solute selection to ensure the grid captures the complete hydration layer without excessive empty space at boundaries.

### Aggregation Modes

The grid system supports different atomic aggregation strategies that affect how atoms contribute to grid bins:

**byres**: Aggregates atoms by residue, placing the entire residue contribution in the bin containing any residue atom. This is useful for mapping residue-level distributions:
```bash
grid out byres.dx 10 1 10 1 10 1 :WAT byres
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L27)

**bymol**: Aggregates by molecule, grouping all atoms within the same molecular entity. This is particularly valuable for solvent molecules where you want to treat each water molecule as a single unit:
```bash
grid out bymol.dx 10 1 10 1 10 1 :WAT bymol
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L28)

These aggregation modes significantly affect density interpretation—residue-level analysis reveals macromolecular features while molecular-level aggregation is more appropriate for solvent distributions.

### Non-Orthogonal Grid Support

CPPTRAJ handles non-orthogonal simulation boxes (truncated octahedra, rhombic dodecahedra) through the boxref parameter, which references a structure containing the appropriate box vectors:

```bash
grid nonortho.dx boxref [REF] 50 50 50 :WAT@O pdb nonortho.pdb
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L67-L68)

The grid wrapping option (gridwrap) ensures atoms near periodic boundaries are correctly mapped into their periodic images, maintaining consistent density across box edges:
```bash
grid nonortho_wrap.dx boxref [REF] 20 20 20 :WAT@O gridwrap name BC
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L76-L77)

> [!TIP]
> When working with non-orthogonal systems, always verify the box reference structure matches the trajectory geometry to prevent coordinate transformation errors that corrupt density distributions.

### Output Formats

CPPTRAJ generates grids in multiple formats optimized for different analysis workflows:

**OpenDX Format**: Default format for grid data, widely supported by visualization tools like VMD, PyMOL, and Chimera:
```bash
grid out.dx 20 0.5 20 0.5 20 0.5 :WAT@O
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L23)

**Xplor Format**: Alternative format compatible with Xplor-NIH and other structure analysis tools:
```bash
grid out.xplor 20 0.5 20 0.5 20 0.5 :WAT@O name XPLOR
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L22)

**PDB Format**: Generates atomic coordinates representing grid points for quick visualization and validation:
```bash
grid nonortho.dx boxref [REF] 50 50 50 :WAT@O pdb nonortho.pdb
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L67)

The grid system can also read previously generated grids for further processing or comparison:
```bash
readdata out.dx.save
grid out.dx.2 data out.dx.save @CA opendx
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L35-L38)

## Density Calculations Along Axes

While 3D grids provide complete volumetric distributions, density calculations along specific axes offer efficient analysis of directional properties, particularly for membrane systems and anisotropic environments.

### Density Types

CPPTRAJ implements four distinct density calculation modes, each emphasizing different physical properties:

| Density Type | Description | Typical Applications |
|--------------|-------------|---------------------|
| **Number** | Atom count per unit volume | Solvent distribution, occupancy analysis |
| **Mass** | Mass per unit volume | Mass transport, sedimentation studies |
| **Charge** | Charge per unit volume | Electrostatic potential analysis |
| **Electron** | Electron density per unit volume | X-ray scattering calculations |

These modes are specified as keywords in the density command:
```bash
density out number_density.dat number delta 0.25 ":PC@P31" ":PC@N31"
density out mass_density.dat mass delta 0.25 ":PC@P31" ":PC@N31"
density out charge_density.dat charge delta 0.25 ":PC@P31" ":PC@N31"
density out electron_density.dat electron delta 0.25 ":PC@P31" ":PC@N31"
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Density/RunTest.sh#L27-L34)

### Axis Configuration

The delta parameter specifies bin spacing along the calculation axis, determining the resolution of density profiles. For lipid bilayer analysis, finer resolution (0.25-0.5 Å) captures the detailed structure of headgroup regions:

```bash
density :WAT@O out tz2.wato.agr xydy
density :WAT@O out restrict.agr xydy delta 0.5 restrict cylinder cutoff 5.0
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Density/RunTest.sh#L45-L46)

The xydy output format produces Grace-compatible data files containing the axis position and density values suitable for direct plotting.

### Density Restrictions

CPPTRAJ supports spatial restrictions on density calculations, allowing analysis focused on specific regions. The cylinder restriction enables density profiling within a cylindrical volume defined by radius (cutoff) and axis:

```bash
density :WAT@O out restrict.agr xydy delta 0.5 restrict cylinder cutoff 5.0
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Density/RunTest.sh#L46)

This is particularly useful for analyzing water penetration into membrane pores or ion channel selectivity filters where the relevant density is confined to a cylindrical pathway.

### Multi-Frame and Ensemble Density

Density calculations automatically aggregate across multiple frames, providing ensemble-averaged profiles. For comparing different simulation conditions (different box shapes, temperatures, force fields), CPPTRAJ can calculate separate densities and combine them for comparative analysis:

```bash
parm ../tz2.truncoct.parm7 [OCT]
trajin ../tz2.truncoct.nc parm [OCT]
density D1
go
clear trajin

parm ../tz2.ortho.parm7 [ORTHO]
trajin ../tz2.ortho.nc parm [ORTHO]
density D2
go

writedata total.dat D1 D2
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Density/RunTest.sh#L51-L63)

This pattern enables systematic comparison of density profiles across simulation conditions while maintaining the underlying frame-by-frame data for detailed analysis.

## Bounds-Based Grid Generation

For analyses requiring precise spatial control, CPPTRAJ can generate grids based on molecular bounds rather than box dimensions. The bounds command calculates the minimum and maximum coordinates of selected atoms, defining a custom grid region that tightly encompasses the molecular structure:

```bash
bounds :1-13 dx 0.5 name MyGrid out bounds.dat
crdaction MyCoords grid bounds.xplor data MyGrid :WAT@O
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_Grid/RunTest.sh#L98-L101)

This two-step approach first defines the grid bounds and data, then applies it to a specific mask, enabling flexible analysis workflows where grid parameters can be defined independently from the density calculation.

## Grid Inhomogeneous Solvation Theory (GIST)

GIST represents the most sophisticated application of grid and density calculations in CPPTRAJ, providing a thermodynamic framework for analyzing solvation structure and energetics. The original Action_Gist implementation was contributed by Crystal N. Nguyen and Romelia F. Salomon from UC San Diego, with subsequent enhancements by Johannes Kraml, Franz Waibl, Klaus R. Liedl, and Steven Ramsey [README.md](README.md#L161-L166).

### GIST Output Components

GIST calculations produce multiple grid-based output files characterizing different aspects of solvation:

**Water Distributions**: Separate grids for water oxygen (gO) and hydrogen (gH) densities reveal spatial localization patterns:
```
Gist2-gO.dx.save
Gist2-gH.dx.save
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_GIST)

**Energy Densities**: Solvent-solute (Esw) and solvent-solvent (Eww) energy grids provide thermodynamic insights into local interactions:
```
Gist4-Esw-dens.dx.save
Gist4-Eww-dens.dx.save
Gist5-Solute-Etot-pme-dens.dx.save
Gist5-Water-Etot-pme-dens.dx.save
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_GIST)

**Entropic Contributions**: Translational, orientational, and six-component entropic densities decompose solvation entropy into physical components:
```
Gist2-dTStrans-dens.dx.save
Gist2-dTSorient-dens.dx.save
Gist2-dTSsix-dens.dx.save
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_GIST)

**Order Parameters**: Molecular orientation and neighbor-count densities quantify water structuring:
```
Gist2-neighbor-norm.dx.save
Gist2-order-norm.dx.save
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_GIST)

**Molecular Decomposition**: GIST can generate separate grids for different molecular species (ions, water molecules), enabling species-specific solvation analysis:
```
Gist8-Esw-mol-CL.dx.save
Gist8-Esw-mol-NA.dx.save
Gist8-Esw-mol-WAT.dx.save
```
[RunTest.sh](test/Test_GIST)

### GIST Integration with Grid System

GIST leverages the underlying grid infrastructure for spatial discretization and accumulation but adds specialized calculations for thermodynamic quantities. The multi-file output pattern reflects the complexity of solvation thermodynamics, with each grid representing a different contribution to the overall solvation free energy.

For researchers interested in detailed solvation analysis, the dedicated [GIST (Grid Inhomogeneous Solvation Theory)](23-gist-grid-inhomogeneous-solvation-theory) documentation provides complete coverage of GIST methodology, interpretation guidelines, and practical applications.

## Parallel Processing Considerations

Grid and density calculations in CPPTRAJ are designed for efficient parallelization using both OpenMP and MPI, enabling large-scale analysis of extensive trajectory data. The parallel strategy typically divides spatial domains or trajectory frames across processing elements, with careful handling of boundary conditions and accumulation to ensure correct results.

The grid system's design supports thread-safe accumulation, allowing multiple threads to increment grid bins simultaneously without race conditions when using appropriate synchronization mechanisms. This parallel capability is essential for production-level analysis of high-resolution grids from long trajectories.

## Common Analysis Patterns

### Hydration Shell Analysis

For analyzing water structure around proteins or nucleic acids:

```bash
# Center on solute and map water oxygen positions
autoimage origin
rms first :1-13
grid hydration.dx 40 0.5 40 0.5 40 0.5 center :1-13 :WAT@O
```

This generates a high-resolution density map suitable for identifying hydration sites and water-mediated interactions.

### Membrane Lipid Distributions

For analyzing lipid component distributions along membrane normal:

```bash
# Calculate number density for different lipid components
density PC_P31.dat number delta 0.25 :PC@P31
density PC_N31.dat number delta 0.25 :PC@N31
density OL_O16.dat number delta 0.25 :OL | :OL2
```

The overlapping density profiles reveal lipid component localization and tailgroup ordering.

### Ion Channel Penetration

For analyzing ion distributions in channel systems:

```bash
# Restrict density to cylindrical pathway along channel axis
density ion_density.dat xydy delta 0.5 restrict cylinder cutoff 3.0 :Na+ :Cl-
```

The cylindrical restriction focuses the calculation on the channel pore, avoiding bulk contributions that obscure permeation profiles.

## Integration with Other Analyses

Grid and density calculations often serve as preprocessing steps for more complex analyses:

**Contact Analysis**: Grid-based density maps identify high-probability contact regions that can be quantified using distance-based contact measurements, as detailed in [Contact Analysis and Native Contacts](18-contact-analysis-and-native-contacts).

**Hydrogen Bond Analysis**: Water density maps correlate with hydrogen bond networks, providing spatial context for bond formation and breaking patterns described in [Hydrogen Bond Analysis](15-hydrogen-bond-analysis).

**Energy Analysis**: GIST energy grids complement potential of mean force calculations and free energy methods documented in [Free Energy Calculations (TI, MM/PBSA)](21-free-energy-calculations-ti-mm-pbsa).

**Solvent Analysis**: Density-based solvation patterns provide context for general solvent behavior described in [Energy Extraction and Analysis](20-energy-extraction-and-analysis).

## Performance Optimization

For large-scale grid and density calculations, consider these optimization strategies:

1. **Resolution Balancing**: Use coarser grids for exploratory analysis, then refine around regions of interest identified from initial results.

2. **Mask Pruning**: Restrict density calculations to relevant atoms using precise mask expressions, avoiding unnecessary calculations on non-contributing species.

3. **Frame Subsampling**: For equilibrium properties, analyze representative subsets rather than full trajectories, reducing computational cost while maintaining statistical quality.

4. **Parallel Execution**: Leverage OpenMP or MPI parallelization for production analyses, particularly for high-resolution grids or long trajectories.

## Summary

CPPTRAJ's grid and density calculation capabilities provide a comprehensive toolkit for spatial analysis of molecular dynamics trajectories. The modular architecture supports a wide range of analyses from simple atomic density maps to sophisticated thermodynamic decomposition via GIST. By understanding the available options for grid generation, density types, and output formats, researchers can extract quantitative insights into solvation structure, molecular distributions, and energetic landscapes that complement other trajectory analysis methods.

For detailed information on related topics, refer to [GIST (Grid Inhomogeneous Solvation Theory)](23-gist-grid-inhomogeneous-solvation-theory) for advanced solvation thermodynamics, [Periodic Boundary Conditions and Imaging](9-periodic-boundary-conditions-and-imaging) for handling boundary effects in grid calculations, and [OpenMP Multi-threading](29-openmp-multi-threading) for parallel execution strategies.


# Energy Extraction and Analysis



Energy extraction and analysis in cpptraj provides comprehensive capabilities for calculating, decomposing, and comparing energetic properties from molecular dynamics simulations. This functionality enables researchers to extract potential energy components from trajectory files, calculate kinetic energy from velocities, decompose total energy into contributions, and perform comparative energy analysis between different coordinate sets.

## Overview of Energy Analysis Architecture

![cpptraj energy analysis workflow](https://github.com/Amber-MD/cpptraj/raw/master/doc/manual/energy_workflow.png)

The energy analysis system in cpptraj operates through multiple specialized commands that integrate seamlessly with the trajectory processing pipeline. The architecture supports both static energy extraction from stored trajectory data and dynamic energy calculations from atomic coordinates, velocities, and forces.

**Core Energy Commands**:

| Command | Purpose | Input Requirements | Output |
|---------|---------|-------------------|--------|
| `energy` | Extract potential energy components | Parameter file + trajectory | Time-series energy data |
| `energy kinetic` | Calculate kinetic energy | Coordinates + velocities | Kinetic energy values |
| `energy total` | Calculate total energy | Coordinates + velocities + forces | Total energy values |
| `compareenergy` | Compare energy between coordinate sets | Two coordinate sets | Energy differences |

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Energy/RunTest.sh#L1-L62), [RunTest.sh](test/Test_CompareEnergy/RunTest.sh#L1-L29)

## Basic Energy Extraction

The fundamental `energy` command extracts potential energy components stored in trajectory files, providing access to the energy values calculated during the simulation by the MD engine. This is particularly useful for analyzing energy fluctuations, convergence, and thermodynamic properties.

```bash
# Basic energy extraction from trajectory
parm system.parm7
trajin system.nc
energy SystemName out energy_data.agr
```

The extracted energy data can include multiple components depending on what was saved in the trajectory file. Common components include total potential energy, bond, angle, dihedral, electrostatic, and van der Waals energies.

**Key Features**:
- Supports NetCDF trajectory format with energy data
- Outputs data in various formats (agr, dat, etc.)
- Integrates with mask expressions for selective analysis
- Compatible with time-series analysis workflows

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Energy/RunTest.sh#L13-L20)

## Kinetic and Total Energy Calculation

For trajectories containing velocity and force information, cpptraj can calculate kinetic and total energy components dynamically. This capability extends energy analysis beyond what was originally computed and stored during simulation.

```bash
# Kinetic energy calculation with timestep specification
parm system.parm7
trajin system.crd mdvel system.vel mdfrc system.frc
energy kinetic Short out short.dat dt 0.002

# Total energy calculation
energy Tz2 out tz2.dat dt 0.002
```

The `dt` parameter specifies the timestep in picoseconds, which is essential for converting the kinetic energy calculation into proper units. This functionality requires trajectories that include velocity and force data, typically stored in separate files or NetCDF extensions.

**Implementation Details**:
- Kinetic energy: E_kin = 0.5 * Σ m_i * v_i²
- Total energy: E_total = E_kin + E_potential
- Requires atomic masses from parameter files
- Supports parallel processing for large systems

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Energy/RunTest.sh#L23-L41)

## Energy Decomposition by Atom Selection

Energy decomposition allows researchers to analyze contributions from specific subsets of atoms, residues, or regions within a molecular system. This is invaluable for understanding energy hotspots, binding interactions, and regional stability.

```bash
# Partial energy calculations with atom selection
parm system.parm7
trajin system.nc
energy out strip.dat :NDP ENE1
energy out elec.dat  :NDP ENE2 elec
energy out vdw.dat   :NDP ENE3 vdw
```

The mask syntax `:NDP` selects specific residues (in this case, nucleotides), and the output can be further specified to extract particular energy components. Multiple `energy` commands can be chained to analyze different selections and energy types in a single analysis run.

**Supported Energy Components**:
- `elec` - Electrostatic energy
- `vdw` - Van der Waals energy
- `bond` - Bond stretching energy
- `angle` - Angle bending energy
- `dihedral` - Dihedral torsion energy

> [!TIP]
> When performing energy decomposition with atom selections, ensure that the trajectory contains the complete energy information for the requested components. Some formats may store only total energy, limiting decomposition capabilities.

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_Energy/RunTest.sh#L44-L59)

## Energy Comparison Between Coordinate Sets

The `compareenergy` command enables comparative analysis of energy components between different structural conformations. This is particularly useful for analyzing energy differences along reaction pathways, comparing mutant vs. wild-type structures, or evaluating conformational changes.

```bash
# Energy comparison workflow
parm system.parm7
loadcrd system.nc 1 1 name CRD1
loadcrd system.nc 2 2 name CRD2

# Compare bond energies
compareenergy crd0 CRD1 crd1 CRD2 bondout compare.bonds.dat mask1 :2 mask2 :2

# Compare angle energies
compareenergy crd0 CRD1 crd1 CRD2 angleout compare.angles.dat mask1 :2 mask2 :2 mask3 :2

# Compare dihedral energies
compareenergy crd0 CRD1 crd1 CRD2 dihedralout compare.dih.dat mask1 :2 mask2 :2 mask3 :2 mask4 :2
```

The comparison requires defining two coordinate sets (crd0 and crd1) and applying appropriate masks to specify which atoms participate in the energy terms. The output provides energy differences between the two conformations.

**Mask Requirements by Energy Type**:
| Energy Type | Required Masks | Description |
|-------------|----------------|-------------|
| Bond | mask1, mask2 | Two atoms defining the bond |
| Angle | mask1, mask2, mask3 | Three atoms defining the angle |
| Dihedral | mask1, mask2, mask3, mask4 | Four atoms defining the dihedral |

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_CompareEnergy/RunTest.sh#L1-L29)

## Integration with Energy Decomposition Analysis

For more detailed energy breakdown, cpptraj supports the `enedecomp` functionality (available in Test_EneDecomp), which provides comprehensive energy decomposition into residue-by-residue and component-wise contributions. This extends the basic energy extraction with detailed analysis capabilities.

The energy decomposition analysis workflow typically involves:
1. Loading trajectory and topology files
2. Specifying energy decomposition parameters
3. Generating detailed component breakdowns
4. Outputting per-residue and per-type energy data

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Load Trajectory & Topology] --> B[Specify Energy Analysis Type]
    B --> C{Analysis Mode}
    C -->|Basic| D[energy Command]
    C -->|Decomposition| E[enedecomp Command]
    C -->|Comparison| F[compareenergy Command]
    D --> G[Extract Energy Components]
    E --> H[Generate Component Breakdown]
    F --> I[Calculate Energy Differences]
    G --> J[Output Time-Series Data]
    H --> J
    I --> J
    J --> K[Statistical Analysis]
```

## Output Formats and Data Handling

Energy analysis results can be output in multiple formats depending on downstream analysis needs:
- **.agr** - Grace/Xmgrace format for plotting
- **.dat** - Plain text format for spreadsheet analysis
- **.gnu** - Gnuplot format for data visualization
- **NetCDF** - Binary format for large datasets

The output files typically contain columns corresponding to frame number or time, followed by energy values for each requested component.

> [!TIP]
> For long trajectories or systems with many energy components, consider using NetCDF output format to reduce file size and improve I/O performance during subsequent analysis steps.

## Practical Applications

Energy extraction and analysis in cpptraj supports several key applications:

1. **Convergence Analysis**: Monitor energy fluctuations over time to assess simulation convergence and equilibration
2. **Binding Energy Analysis**: Decompose energies to understand contributions from specific residues or regions in protein-ligand complexes
3. **Pathway Analysis**: Compare energies along reaction coordinates or conformational pathways
4. **Validation**: Compare energy components between different simulation engines or parameter sets

## Advanced Integration

Energy analysis can be combined with other cpptraj capabilities for comprehensive analysis:

- Combine with [Time-Correlation Functions](14-time-correlation-functions-and-spectral-analysis) to analyze energy autocorrelation and fluctuation timescales
- Integrate with [Principal Component Analysis](13-principal-component-analysis-pca) to identify collective motions associated with energy changes
- Use with [Free Energy Calculations](21-free-energy-calculations-ti-mm-pbsa) for thermodynamic property calculation
- Apply [Statistical Analysis](12-correlation-functions-auto-correlation-cross-correlation) tools for energy distribution analysis


# Free Energy Calculations (TI, MM/PBSA)



This documentation covers cpptraj's advanced capabilities for free energy calculations through Thermodynamic Integration (TI) and energy decomposition methods used in MM/PBSA (Molecular Mechanics/Poisson-Boltzmann Surface Area) analysis. These tools enable rigorous computation of free energy changes and component-wise energy breakdown for molecular systems.

Sources: [test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh](test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh#L1-L32), [test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh](test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh#L1-L76)

## Architecture Overview

The free energy calculation framework in cpptraj operates on a modular architecture that separates data input, analysis algorithms, and statistical post-processing. The system is designed to handle multiple λ-windows simultaneously for TI calculations and provides flexible decomposition schemes for per-residue or per-atom energy analysis.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph DataInput
        A[∇H/∂λ Data Files]
        B[Trajectory Files]
        C[Topology Files]
    end
    
    subgraph AnalysisCore
        D[TI Analysis Engine]
        E[Energy Decomposer]
        F[Statistical Sampler]
    end
    
    subgraph OutputGeneration
        G[Curves & Plots]
        H[Bootstrap Samples]
        I[Decomposition Tables]
    end
    
    A --> D
    B --> E
    C --> E
    D --> F
    E --> F
    D --> G
    F --> H
    E --> I
```

The architecture supports two primary workflows: TI-based free energy integration from ∂H/∂λ data, and direct energy component decomposition from trajectory analysis using various electrostatic models including PME.

Sources: [test/Test_TI/dvdl.dat](test/Test_TI/dvdl.dat#L1-L5), [test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh](test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh#L12-L19)

## Thermodynamic Integration (TI) Implementation

### Data Format and Structure

TI analysis requires pre-computed ∂H/∂λ values across multiple λ windows. The input data format is structured as time-series data where each column represents a specific λ window. The dvdl.dat format contains ∂H/∂λ values for nine λ windows (TI_0 through TI_8) sampled across multiple time frames, enabling robust statistical analysis through ensemble averaging.

The integration framework supports flexible λ-sampling strategies through the `nq` parameter, which specifies the number of quadrature points for numerical integration. Skip-based analysis allows systematic evaluation of equilibration effects by excluding initial frames from the calculation.

Sources: [test/Test_TI/dvdl.dat](test/Test_TI/dvdl.dat#L1-L102)

### TI Analysis Command Syntax

The core TI analysis command implements numerical integration with multiple analysis modes:

```bash
ti <dataset_name> nq <num_points> name <analysis_name> \
  [out <output_file>] \
  [curveout <curve_file>] \
  [bsout <bootstrap_output>] \
  [nskip <skip_frames>] \
  [avgincrement <increment_size>] \
  [bs_samples <num_samples>] \
  [bs_seed <seed_value>] \
  [bs_pts <num_points>]
```

The `ti` command performs thermodynamic integration analysis on datasets containing ∂H/∂λ values. The integration is performed using numerical quadrature over λ-space, with the number of quadrature points specified by `nq`. This parameter determines the resolution of the integration grid, with typical values ranging from 5 to 20 points depending on the complexity of the λ-dependence.

Sources: [test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh](test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh#L13-L20)

### Statistical Methods and Bootstrapping

cpptraj implements sophisticated statistical analysis for TI calculations including bootstrap resampling for error estimation. The bootstrap analysis is controlled through three key parameters: `bs_samples` specifies the number of bootstrap replicates to generate, `bs_seed` sets the random number generator seed for reproducibility, and `bs_pts` determines the number of data points to include in each bootstrap sample.

The random number generation uses high-quality generators supported by the framework, with Marsaglia and Xoshiro128++ being available options. These generators have been validated against the Dieharder test suite, with Xoshiro128++ showing superior statistical properties compared to the C standard library generator.

Sources: [test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh](test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh#L21), [devtools/rngtest/README.md](devtools/rngtest/README.md#L36-L42)

> [!TIP]
> Set `bs_seed` explicitly when performing bootstrap analysis to ensure reproducible results. The seed controls the entire random sequence, which affects both the bootstrap resampling and any subsequent random-dependent calculations. For publication-quality results, use a fixed seed and document it in your methods section.

### Incremental and Skip-Based Analysis

The TI framework supports two complementary analysis strategies for evaluating equilibration and convergence. Incremental analysis divides the trajectory into segments specified by `avgincrement`, computing free energy estimates for each segment to assess time-series convergence. Skip-based analysis uses `nskip` to systematically exclude initial frames from calculation, allowing evaluation of equilibration effects.

For robust convergence assessment, combine both strategies: use skip-based analysis to identify the equilibration point, then apply incremental analysis on the equilibrated portion to verify stability.

Sources: [test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh](test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh#L13-L22)

## Energy Decomposition

### Command Interface and Options

The energy decomposition functionality is accessed through the `enedecomp` command, which performs per-atom or per-residue energy calculations using various electrostatic models. The command supports PME (Particle Mesh Ewald) calculations for long-range electrostatics, with fine-grained control over cutoff distances, tolerance parameters, and FFT grid dimensions.

```bash
enedecomp <dataset_name> <mask> [out <output_file>] \
  [savecomponents] \
  [pme] [cut <distance>] \
  [dsumtol <tolerance>] \
  [skinnb <skin_distance>] \
  [nfft <x>,<y>,<z>]
```

The `savecomponents` option enables output of individual energy components (electrostatic, van der Waals, etc.) rather than just the total energy per atom/residue. This is particularly useful for MM/PBSA workflows where separate treatment of different energy terms is required.

Sources: [test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh](test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh#L17-L25)

### PME Configuration Parameters

The PME implementation in cpptraj provides several configuration options for optimizing accuracy vs. computational cost:

| Parameter | Description | Typical Values | Impact |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|--------|
| `cut` | Real-space cutoff distance | 5.6-10.0 Å | Shorter cutoffs are faster but may require larger FFT grids |
| `dsumtol` | Direct sum tolerance | 0.0000001 | Lower values improve accuracy but increase computation |
| `skinnb` | Neighbor list skin distance | 0.01-0.02 Å | Larger values reduce neighbor list rebuilding frequency |
| `nfft` | FFT grid dimensions (x,y,z) | 32-128 per axis | Larger grids improve reciprocal space accuracy |

For production MM/PBSA calculations, validate that `dsumtol` and the FFT grid size provide sufficient convergence by running sensitivity analyses on a subset of frames.

Sources: [test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh](test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh#L15-L26)

### Energy Command Integration

The `energy` command serves as a companion to `enedecomp`, providing total energy calculations that can be used for validation or decomposition verification. The `etype` parameter specifies the electrostatic treatment method, with options including PME, Ewald, and simple cutoff-based methods.

The decomposition results can be summed using cpptraj's dataset operations (e.g., `Total = sum(ATM)`) to verify that component-wise sums reproduce the total energy from the `energy` command. This cross-validation step is essential for ensuring the correctness of the decomposition before proceeding to MM/PBSA analysis.

Sources: [test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh](test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh#L14-L16), [test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh](test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh#L27-L29)

## Advanced Analysis Workflows

### Free Energy Protocol Integration

The TI and energy decomposition capabilities can be combined into comprehensive free energy protocols. A typical workflow involves:

1. Generating ∂H/∂λ data across λ windows during MD simulations
2. Performing TI analysis with bootstrapping for error estimates
3. Computing energy decomposition on representative snapshots from each window
4. Combining results for complete thermodynamic characterization

The framework supports reading pre-computed energy data via the `readdata` command, enabling post-processing of externally generated data from various MD engines including Amber, CHARMM, and GROMACS.

Sources: [test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh](test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh#L8-L11)

### Parallel Execution Considerations

For large-scale TI calculations with many λ windows or long trajectories, consider the parallel execution capabilities of cpptraj. Both OpenMP and MPI parallelization are supported, with different advantages depending on the analysis type:

- OpenMP: Effective for parallelizing individual TI calculations across frames or bootstrap samples
- MPI: Superior for handling multiple independent calculations or very large trajectory datasets

When using parallel execution, ensure that random number seeds are properly managed to maintain reproducibility across different thread/process configurations.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L103-L118)

## Best Practices and Recommendations

### Convergence Assessment

Establish convergence through multiple complementary metrics:

1. Compare results from different `nskip` values to identify equilibration
2. Use `avgincrement` analysis to verify temporal stability
3. Assess bootstrap error estimates; decreasing error with increased frames suggests convergence
4. Cross-validate energy decomposition totals against standalone energy calculations

For publication-quality free energy calculations, convergence should be demonstrated across at least three independent metrics.

Sources: [test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh](test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh#L13-L22)

> [!TIP]
> When performing TI analysis with limited data, use smaller `bs_pts` values (e.g., 50-70) to reduce bootstrap variance while maintaining sufficient statistical power. For well-converged systems with extensive sampling, increase `bs_pts` to 100-200 to maximize error estimate reliability.

### Data Management

Free energy calculations generate substantial output data including individual frame energies, bootstrap samples, and intermediate analysis files. Implement a structured naming convention and organize output by calculation type:

- `*_ti.agr`: TI curves and integrated free energy values
- `*_bs.dat`: Bootstrap sample results
- `*_incr.agr`: Incremental analysis results
- `*_decomp.dat`: Energy decomposition tables

This organization facilitates automated analysis pipelines and simplifies post-processing for publication figures.

Sources: [test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh](test/Test_TI/RunTest.sh#L6-L7), [test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh](test/Test_EneDecomp/RunTest.sh#L7)

## Next Steps

To explore related functionality in the cpptraj ecosystem:

- **Energy Extraction and Analysis**: For fundamental energy calculation techniques, see [Energy Extraction and Analysis](20-energy-extraction-and-analysis)
- **Atom Selection**: For precise mask specification in energy decomposition, see [Atom Selection and Mask Expressions](6-atom-selection-and-mask-expressions)
- **Parallel Processing**: For optimizing large-scale free energy calculations, see [OpenMP Multi-threading](29-openmp-multi-threading) or [MPI Parallelization](30-mpi-parallelization-for-large-scale-analysis)
- **PME Calculations**: For detailed PME implementation details, see [PME Calculations](28-pme-particle-mesh-ewald-calculations)


# Lipid Order Parameters



Lipid order parameter analysis in CPPTRAJ provides quantitative metrics for characterizing membrane structure and dynamics by measuring the orientational ordering of lipid acyl chains. This analysis is fundamental for understanding membrane fluidity, phase behavior, and lipid-lipid interactions in biological membranes and model lipid bilayers.

## Mathematical Foundations

Lipid order parameters quantify the orientation of molecular bonds relative to a defined reference frame, typically the membrane normal (z-axis). The primary order parameter calculated is the deuterium order parameter (SCD), derived from NMR quadrupolar splitting measurements and directly computable from molecular dynamics trajectories.

The order parameter Sα for a molecular vector relative to a reference axis α is defined as:

Sα = (3⟨cos²θ⟩ - 1)/2

where θ is the angle between the molecular vector and the reference axis α, and ⟨⟩ denotes ensemble averaging. For C-H bonds in lipid tails, the SCD parameter relates to the probability distribution of bond orientations, providing insight into chain conformational disorder.

## Implementation Architecture

CPPTRAJ provides two complementary commands for lipid order parameter analysis, each optimized for specific use cases:

| Command | Primary Purpose | Input Requirements | Output Format |
|---------|----------------|-------------------|---------------|
| `lipidorder` | General lipid order parameter calculations with customizable reference axis | Carbon atom masks, optional unsaturated bond specification | Sx, Sy, Sz components with standard deviations |
| `lipidscd` | Specialized SCD order parameter calculations per carbon position | Lipid residue selection, automatic C-H bond identification | Per-carbon SCD values with hydrogen-specific data |

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Trajectory Input] --> B{Analysis Type}
    B -->|General Order Parameters| C[lipidorder]
    B -->|SCD Calculations| D[lipidscd]
    C --> E[Reference Axis Specification]
    E --> F[Carbon Chain Definition]
    F --> G[Unsaturation Handling]
    G --> H[Component Calculation Sx/Sy/Sz]
    D --> I[Residue Selection]
    I --> J[C-H Bond Identification]
    J --> K[Per-Carbon SCD Calculation]
    H --> L[Output Generation]
    K --> L
    L --> M[Order Parameter Files]
```

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_LipidOrder/RunTest.sh#L14-L24), [RunTest.sh](test/Test_LipidSCD/RunTest.sh#L16-L25)

## LipidOrder Command

The `lipidorder` command provides flexible order parameter analysis with control over the reference axis direction and handling of unsaturated bonds within lipid tails.

### Core Parameters

- **Reference Axis**: Specifies the molecular axis along which order parameters are calculated (x, y, z)
- **Carbon Masks**: Atom mask expressions defining sequential carbon atoms along lipid acyl chains
- **Unsaturation**: Optional specification of double bond positions to modify calculation behavior
- **Tail Distance Analysis**: Calculates end-to-end distances for lipid tails with customizable resolution

> [!TIP]
> The `z` axis is typically used as the reference direction for planar lipid bilayers, aligning with the membrane normal. For vesicular systems or curved membranes, consider adjusting the reference frame based on local surface normals.

### Command Syntax

Basic lipid order parameter calculation for a single tail:
```
lipidorder out results.dat z \
  ":Lipid@C2" ":Lipid@C3" ":Lipid@C4" ... ":Lipid@C18"
```

Advanced calculation with unsaturation handling and tail distance:
```
lipidorder out sn1_est.dat z unsat ":Lipid@C9 | :Lipid@C10" \
  taildist e2e_sn1.dat delta 0.1 \
  tailstart ":Lipid@C2" tailend ":Lipid@C18" \
  ":Lipid@C2" ":Lipid@C3" ... ":Lipid@C18"
```

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_LipidOrder/RunTest.sh#L14-L24)

### Output Structure

The `lipidorder` command generates comprehensive output with multiple order parameter components:

```
#Cn         Sx     sd(Sx)         Sy     sd(Sy)         Sz     sd(Sz)      SCD_z     SCD_xy
  2 -0.1286853  0.0000000 -0.1839300  0.0000000  0.3126154  0.0000000  0.1563077  0.1471002
  3 -0.1788536  0.0000000 -0.1215643  0.0000000  0.3004179  0.0000000  0.1502090  0.1597572
  ...
```

- **Cn**: Carbon position number along the tail (relative numbering)
- **Sα**: Order parameter component along axis α
- **sd(Sα)**: Standard deviation of order parameter component
- **SCD_z**: Deuterium order parameter along z-axis (Sz/2)
- **SCD_xy**: Combined xy-plane order parameter

Sources: [sn1_est.dat.save](test/Test_LipidOrder/sn1_est.dat.save#L1-L4)

## LipidSCD Command

The `lipidscd` command provides specialized order parameter analysis specifically designed for comparing with experimental NMR measurements, automatically handling C-H bond identification and per-atom order parameter extraction.

### Simplified Interface

The `lipidscd` command streamlines the analysis workflow through:
- **Automatic residue detection**: Selects lipid molecules by residue name or type
- **C-H bond pairing**: Automatically identifies hydrogen atoms bonded to each carbon
- **Per-residue statistics**: Calculates order parameters separately for different lipid species

> [!TIP]
> Use the `lipidscd` command when you need direct comparability with NMR experiments or require analysis of multiple lipid types within the same system. It handles the atom naming conventions automatically.

### Command Syntax

Basic analysis of specific lipid types:
```
lipidscd :LipidName1,LipidName2 out results.dat
```

Advanced analysis with error formatting:
```
lipidscd :OL,PC out ol1.dat
lipidscd :OL2,PC out ol2.dat
lipidscd out ol3.agr xydy prec 10.7 xprec 3.0
```

Sources: [RunTest.sh](test/Test_LipidSCD/RunTest.sh#L16-L25)

### Output Structure

The `lipidscd` output provides per-carbon, per-hydrogen order parameters:

```
#Cn  OL_C11_H1 sd(OL_C11_H1)  OL_C11_H2 sd(OL_C11_H2)  OL_C11_H3 sd(OL_C11_H3)
  2  0.1911444     0.0000000  0.2222481     0.0000000  0.2222481     0.0000000
  3  0.1834894     0.0000000  0.1191841     0.0000000  0.1191841     0.0000000
  ...
```

- **Cn**: Carbon position along the tail
- **Residue_Cn_HX**: SCD value for specific carbon-hydrogen pair
- **sd()**: Standard deviation across trajectory frames

Sources: [ol1.dat.save](test/Test_LipidSCD/ol1.dat.save#L1-L4)

## Practical Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Load Trajectory] --> B[Define Lipid Selection]
    B --> C{Choose Analysis Method}
    C -->|Manual Control| D[lipidorder]
    C -->|Automated Detection| E[lipidscd]
    D --> F[Specify Carbon Chain]
    F --> G[Set Reference Axis]
    E --> H[Provide Residue Names]
    G --> I[Run Analysis]
    H --> I
    I --> J[Process Results]
    J --> K[Compare with Experiment]
```
